The merge experiment ran with real git and pytest on macOS in a temporary repository. Descriptions of GitHub merge queues, pull_request merge refs and branch protection come from documentation and were not run. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: Strategies compared
docs.text:
Strategy Shape Integration frequency Fits Trunk-based development Everyone commits to main (or merges very short-lived branches, under about a day or two) behind feature flags Continuous Teams practising CI/CD seriously; needs strong tests and flags (Level 3 · 02) GitHub flow Short-lived feature branches, pull request, review, merge to main, deploy from main Daily to weekly Most web/SaaS teams GitFlow develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*, main Per release Software shipped in discrete versions with long support windows; heavy for continuous delivery Release branches off trunk Trunk plus release-1.4 branches receiving only fixes Continuous on trunk Products with several supported versions

Longer-lived branches mean bigger, riskier merges and delayed feedback; the research-backed practice behind high-performing teams is small batches and frequent integration (Level 3 · 09). Whatever you choose, make main always releasable.

docs.title: Pull request checks
docs.text: A PR pipeline should answer, within minutes: Does it build? Do tests, lint and type checks pass? Are there security findings? Does it need review from the owners of these files? Configure branch protection / rulesets so these are mandatory, and combine with human review (at least one approval, code owners for sensitive paths, dismissing stale approvals on new pushes).

docs.title: Checks must run on what will actually merge
docs.text:
Here is why. In a throwaway git repository I created two branches from the same base:

  • rename-func renames price() to total_price() and updates its test.
  • new-caller adds report.py, which calls price(), with its own test.

Each branch's test suite is green on its own:

branch rename-func alone: 1 passed
branch new-caller alone:  2 passed

Merging them produces no textual conflict, but the merged result is broken:

merge of both (no textual conflict): git says 0 conflicts; tests: ERROR test_report.py ... Interrupted: 1 error during collection

report.py imports a name that no longer exists. Both PRs were green when reviewed, and the breakage appears only on the combination: a semantic conflict. The defences:

  1. Require branches to be up to date before merging, so the PR's checks ran against the current main. Cost: rebase/update churn on busy repositories.
  2. Merge queues (GitHub merge queue, Gerrit, Bors/Mergify-style tools): the queue builds the merge of each queued PR on top of the ones ahead of it and tests that combination before merging, giving serialisation with parallel testing.
  3. Test the merge commit. GitHub's pull_request event checks out a temporary merge of the PR into the base branch by default (documented behaviour; I did not verify it here), which already tests the combination at the time the PR last updated; but main can move afterward, which is why (1) or (2) is still needed.
  4. Run the full test suite on main after every merge and treat a red main as a stop-the-line event (revert first, then diagnose).

docs.title: Reviews, ownership and automation
docs.text:
• Keep PRs small (reviewable in minutes); large PRs get rubber-stamped.
  • CODEOWNERS routes reviews to owners of paths; required for sensitive areas (pipelines, infrastructure, auth).
  • Bots can label, check PR titles (conventional commits for changelogs; Level 3 · 07), enforce size limits and update dependencies (Dependabot, Renovate); give dependency PRs the same CI as human PRs, and consider automerge only for patch versions with strong tests.
  • Protect the pipeline definition itself: changes to .github/workflows/ or the Jenkinsfile deserve owner review, because a PR can change what runs (and, on some triggers, with which secrets).

docs.title: Commit and merge hygiene that helps CI
docs.text: Prefer squash or rebase merging for a linear, bisectable history on main; make each merged commit buildable so git bisect works. Keep commit messages informative (they feed changelogs). Use git revert to undo a bad merge on shared branches rather than force-pushing; never force-push to protected branches.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Required checks are named in branch protection and match the real job names.
  • Stale approvals are dismissed when new commits arrive.
  • Pipeline files have a code owner who is not the author of the change.
  • Secrets are not exposed to workflows triggered from forks.
  • PR titles or commit messages follow the convention the release tool expects.
  • A merge queue or up-to-date requirement prevents green-alone, red-together merges.
  • Long-lived branches are rebased or merged often enough that CI results stay meaningful.
  • Draft PRs run a cheaper subset of checks.
  • The default branch is protected against force-pushes.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A pull request is a pair of refs (head and base) plus metadata. When it is opened or updated, the hosting service fires an event; for GitHub's pull_request workflows it also creates a merge ref that represents "base plus head", and the workflow builds that. Branch protection is evaluated by the service at merge time: it looks up the required status checks for the base branch, requires each to have reported success for the PR's head (or merge) commit, and refuses the merge button otherwise. A merge queue adds a temporary branch holding the stack of queued changes, runs the required checks on it, and fast-forwards main only if they pass. The git experiment above shows why a purely textual merge algorithm cannot protect you: git merges lines, not meaning.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Long-lived branches.
  • Required checks configured to pass when skipped (or not required at all).
  • Allowing merges with stale checks on busy repositories.
  • Letting administrators bypass protections routinely.
  • Huge PRs and rubber-stamp reviews.
  • A red main left red while others keep merging.
  • Unreviewed changes to the pipeline files.
  • Force-pushing shared branches.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the rename-versus-new-caller experiment in your own repository, then write the branch protection or merge-queue settings that would have caught it before main broke.
  2. Measure how long your PR pipeline takes and how many PRs merge per day; estimate how often two PRs in flight could conflict semantically.
  3. Write the CODEOWNERS entries for pipeline files, infrastructure and a security-sensitive module.
  4. Draft your team's "main is red" policy: who reverts, how fast, and who may merge while it is red.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Local CI Runner You Can Run
docs.text:
The best way to understand a CI system is to build a tiny one. This project's minici runs a YAML pipeline on your machine and exhibits the core behaviours from Level 1: dependency ordering with parallelism, matrix expansion, cache keys, artifacts, conditions, timeouts, and failure propagation. It is a teaching model, not a product: it is not GitHub Actions or Jenkins and does not behave identically to either.

What was run

Everything in this lesson was run on macOS: the runner's 15 pytest tests, and the pipeline runs shown, which used a small Python demo project. The step that installs dependencies is simulated by a 2 s sleep so the cache effect is visible and repeatable. The deploy job only echoes. The matrix varies the TZ environment variable (there was only one Python version available). The runner has no sandboxing or security hardening: do not run untrusted pipeline files with it. See Lesson 01.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Parse a YAML pipeline with jobs, needs, steps (run, env, if, timeout, continue-on-error).
  2. Run jobs with no unmet dependencies in parallel; skip jobs whose dependencies failed unless if: always().
  3. Expand a matrix (cross product with include and exclude) into separate runs, with fail-fast.
  4. Cache directories by a key derived from file contents and matrix values; save only on success.
  5. Collect artifacts from successful jobs only.
  6. Enforce step timeouts and run scripts with set -eo pipefail.
  7. Refuse unsupported ${{ }} expressions instead of silently ignoring them.

docs.title: The runner
docs.text:
"""minici: a tiny local CI runner that demonstrates how pipeline engines work (jobs, needs, matrix, caching, artifacts, conditions, timeouts).
Pipeline files are YAML. This is a teaching tool, not GitHub Actions or Jenkins, and supports only the features documented below."""
import hashlib, itertools, json, os, re, shutil, subprocess, sys, threading, time
from pathlib import Path
import yaml

def expand_matrix(matrix):
    if not matrix: return [{}]
    include = matrix.get("include", []); exclude = matrix.get("exclude", [])
    keys = [k for k in matrix if k not in ("include", "exclude")]
    combos = [dict(zip(keys, vals)) for vals in itertools.product(*(matrix[k] for k in keys))] if keys else []
    combos = [c for c in combos if not any(all(c.get(k) == v for k, v in ex.items()) for ex in exclude)]
    for inc in include:
        match = [c for c in combos if all(c.get(k) == v for k, v in inc.items() if k in keys)] if keys else []
        if match:
            for c in match: c.update(inc)
        else: combos.append(dict(inc))
    return combos or [{}]

def subst(text, matrix, env):
    def repl(m):
        expr = m.group(1).strip()
        if expr.startswith("matrix."): return str(matrix.get(expr[7:], ""))
        if expr.startswith("env."): return str(env.get(expr[4:], ""))
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported expression ${{{{ {expr} }}}}")
    return re.sub(r"\$\{\{(.*?)\}\}", repl, text)

def topo_levels(jobs):
    done, levels, remaining = set(), [], dict(jobs)
    while remaining:
        ready = [j for j, spec in remaining.items() if set(spec.get("needs", [])) <= done]
        if not ready: raise ValueError(f"dependency cycle or unknown job among {sorted(remaining)}")
        levels.append(sorted(ready)); done |= set(ready); [remaining.pop(j) for j in ready]
    return levels

def cache_key(spec, matrix, workdir):
    parts = [json.dumps(matrix, sort_keys=True)]
    for f in spec.get("cache", {}).get("key_files", []):
        p = Path(workdir) / f; parts.append(hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() if p.exists() else "missing")
    return hashlib.sha256("|".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

class Runner:
    def __init__(self, workdir, store, log=print):
        self.workdir, self.store, self.log, self.lock = Path(workdir), Path(store), log, threading.Lock()
        self.results = {}                                    # job id -> "success"/"failure"/"skipped"
        self.timings = []                                    # (job, matrix, status, seconds, cache)

    def run(self, pipeline):
        jobs = pipeline["jobs"]; env = {str(k): str(v) for k, v in pipeline.get("env", {}).items()}
        for level in topo_levels(jobs):
            threads = []
            for jid in level:
                t = threading.Thread(target=self._run_job, args=(jid, jobs[jid], env)); t.start(); threads.append(t)
            for t in threads: t.join()
        return all(s in ("success", "skipped") for s in self.results.values())

    def _run_job(self, jid, spec, env):
        needs = spec.get("needs", [])
        if any(self.results.get(n) != "success" for n in needs) and spec.get("if") != "always()":
            self.results[jid] = "skipped"; self._say(f"[{jid}] skipped (a needed job did not succeed)"); return
        combos = expand_matrix(spec.get("strategy", {}).get("matrix")); fail_fast = spec.get("strategy", {}).get("fail-fast", True)
        failed = threading.Event(); statuses = []
        def one(m):
            if failed.is_set() and fail_fast: self._say(f"[{jid} {m}] cancelled (fail-fast)"); statuses.append("cancelled"); return
            s = self._run_combo(jid, spec, m, env)
            statuses.append(s)
            if s != "success": failed.set()
        ts = [threading.Thread(target=one, args=(m,)) for m in combos]
        [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
        self.results[jid] = "success" if all(s == "success" for s in statuses) else "failure"

    def _run_combo(self, jid, spec, matrix, env):
        label = f"{jid}{(' ' + json.dumps(matrix, sort_keys=True)) if matrix else ''}"
        t0 = time.time(); cache_state = "none"; status = "success"
        cdir = None
        if "cache" in spec:
            key = cache_key(spec, matrix, self.workdir); cdir = self.store / "cache" / key
            if cdir.exists():
                cache_state = "hit"
                for p in spec["cache"]["paths"]:
                    src = cdir / p
                    if src.exists(): dst = self.workdir / p; shutil.rmtree(dst, ignore_errors=True); shutil.copytree(src, dst)
            else: cache_state = "miss"
        failed_step = False
        for i, step in enumerate(spec.get("steps", []), 1):
            cond = step.get("if", "success()")
            if (cond == "success()" and failed_step) or (cond == "failure()" and not failed_step): continue
            e = dict(os.environ); e.update(env); e.update({str(k): subst(str(v), matrix, env) for k, v in step.get("env", {}).items()})
            cmd = subst(step["run"], matrix, env)
            try:
                p = subprocess.run(["bash", "-c", "set -eo pipefail\n" + cmd], cwd=self.workdir, env=e, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=step.get("timeout", 600))
                out, rc = (p.stdout + p.stderr).strip(), p.returncode
            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as ex:
                out, rc = f"timed out after {step.get('timeout', 600)} s", 124
            ok = rc == 0 or step.get("continue-on-error", False)
            self._say(f"[{label}] step {i} {subst(str(step.get('name', cmd[:30])), matrix, env)!r}: {'ok' if ok else 'FAILED rc=' + str(rc)}" + (f"\n    | " + out.replace("\n", "\n    | ")[:600] if (not ok or step.get("show")) and out else ""))
            if not ok: failed_step = True; status = "failure"
        if status == "success" and cdir is not None and cache_state == "miss":
            for p in spec["cache"]["paths"]:
                src = self.workdir / p
                if src.exists(): shutil.copytree(src, cdir / p)
        if status == "success":
            for pat in spec.get("artifacts", []):
                for f in self.workdir.glob(pat):
                    dst = self.store / "artifacts" / jid / f.name; dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); shutil.copy(f, dst)
        self.timings.append((jid, matrix, status, round(time.time() - t0, 2), cache_state))
        return status

    def _say(self, msg):
        with self.lock: self.log(msg)

def main(argv):
    pipeline = yaml.safe_load(open(argv[1])); workdir = argv[2] if len(argv) > 2 else "."; store = argv[3] if len(argv) > 3 else ".minici"
    r = Runner(workdir, store); ok = r.run(pipeline)
    print("--- summary"); [print(f"{j:<10} {json.dumps(m, sort_keys=True) if m else '':<28} {s:<8} {d:>6}s cache={c}") for j, m, s, d, c in sorted(r.timings, key=lambda x: (x[0], json.dumps(x[1], sort_keys=True)))]
    print("RESULT:", "success" if ok else "failure"); return 0 if ok else 1

if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main(sys.argv))

A tiny Python package (app/calc.py with a total() function) and three tests, pipeline:

  lint:

  test:
    needs: [deps, lint]
    strategy: {matrix: {tz: [UTC, Asia/Kolkata, America/New_York]}}
    steps:
      - {name: "tests under ${{ matrix.tz }}", run: "TZ=${{ matrix.tz }} python3 -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests", show: true}
  package:
    needs: [test]
    artifacts: ["*.tar.gz"]
    steps: [{name: build artifact, run: "tar -czf app-1.0.0.tar.gz app"}]
  deploy:
    needs: [package]
    steps: [{name: "deploy (simulated)", run: "echo deploying app-1.0.0.tar.gz", show: true}]

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: topo_levels repeatedly selects jobs whose needs are all complete, building the DAG's layers; Runner.run starts one thread per job in a layer and joins them before the next, which is simple but coarser than a real scheduler (which starts a job the instant its own dependencies finish). Each job expands its matrix and runs combos in threads; each step is a subprocess.run of bash -c in the workspace with an environment assembled from the pipeline, the step and the matrix. Cache keys are sha256(matrix JSON | hashes of key files). A real system adds what this omits: isolation (VMs/containers), secrets handling, log streaming and storage, retries, concurrency groups, matrix max-parallel, a persistent queue, authentication and a UI.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating this as a security boundary: pipeline steps run arbitrary shell as you.
  • Cache keys that omit relevant inputs (here the key includes the matrix and the listed files only).
  • Assuming local results equal hosted ones: a clean hosted runner has different tools, environment variables and network access.
  • Skipping the clean-run test (delete .minici and run again).
  • Fixing flaky tests with retries instead of understanding them.

docs.title: Level 2 · Pipelines in Depth
docs.text:
Level 1 built one pipeline end to end. Level 2 makes pipelines fast, trustworthy and maintainable at the size real teams have: dozens of jobs, several platforms, a monorepo, and a test suite that is occasionally wrong about itself.

What was run, and what wasn't

Nothing in this course was run on GitHub Actions or Jenkins: no account or server was available. What was run, on macOS: matrix expansion and cache keys in the Level 1 minici runner, a 20,000-run flaky-test simulation, a real coverage demonstration, a tested wait-for-port helper using real sockets, a tested changed-files-to-projects mapper that drives real git diff, a stale-workspace demo, and a 17-test workflow linter. Platform behaviour (GitHub limits, environments, caches, Jenkins syntax) comes from docs.github.com and jenkins.io as read in October 2026 and is labelled as such. Check limits against the current documentation.

Prerequisites: Level 1.

docs.title: 01 · Matrix Builds & Parallelism
docs.text:
A matrix runs the same job many times with different parameters: operating system, language version, database version, a shard number. It is the cheapest way to answer "does it work everywhere we claim it does?" and also the cheapest way to burn your CI budget, because the number of jobs is a product. This lesson shows exactly how a matrix expands, how include and exclude change it, what the documented limits are, and how to split one slow test suite across parallel jobs.

What was run

The expansion results below were computed by the expand_matrix function in the Level 1 minici runner (src/minici.py), which implements the documented rules in a simplified form. It is not GitHub's implementation; where the real service differs the platform's behaviour wins. The limits quoted (256 jobs per matrix, concurrency by plan) come from docs.github.com as read in October 2026 and were not exercised on GitHub. Jenkins' matrix syntax is described from jenkins.io and not run.

docs.title: Expansion is a product
docs.text:
strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu, windows, macos]
    python: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
    exclude:
      - {os: macos, python: "3.11"}
    include:
      - {os: ubuntu, python: "3.14", experimental: true}

Running expand_matrix on that block produced 9 jobs: the 3 × 3 = 9 product, minus the one excluded pair, plus the one extra include entry:

ubuntu/3.11  ubuntu/3.12  ubuntu/3.13
windows/3.11 windows/3.12 windows/3.13
macos/3.12   macos/3.13
ubuntu/3.14 (experimental: true)

Three rules explain every matrix you will meet:

  1. Each key with a list contributes a dimension; the job list is the Cartesian product of all dimensions.
  2. exclude removes combinations that match all the keys given (a partial pattern removes every combination containing those values).
  3. include either adds a key to existing combinations it matches (if every original key it mentions matches) or, when it matches none, adds a new combination. That is how experimental: true can be attached to one cell, or a lone extra cell can be added.

The second rule of include is the one people trip on. In minici, {os: ubuntu, python: "3.14"} matches no product cell (no 3.14 in the list), so it becomes a new job. Had it said {os: ubuntu, experimental: true}, it would have been merged into all three Ubuntu cells instead. The same line of YAML is "add a job" or "annotate three jobs" depending on what the product contains. Print the expanded list in a test or a dry run before you trust it.

docs.title: Sizes grow fast
docs.text:
Matrix Jobs 3 OS × 3 Python 9 3 × 3 × 2 databases × 2 feature flags × 3 shards 108 4 × 4 × 4 × 5 320

Per the GitHub documentation, a matrix can generate at most 256 jobs per workflow run. The 108-job matrix fits; the 320-job one does not and the workflow is rejected. Fitting is not the same as sensible: 108 jobs at 4 minutes each is 7.2 job-hours for one push, and on hosted runners you pay (or consume free minutes) for each job's wall time, usually rounded up per job. Concurrency is also capped by plan; the documented hosted-runner concurrent-job limits are 20 (Free), 40 (Pro), 60 (Team) and 500 (Enterprise) as I read them. A 108-job matrix on a 20-job plan queues most of itself, so total wall time is bounded by the cap, not by your longest job.

docs.title: Fail-fast and "experimental" cells
docs.text:
By default, on GitHub Actions, if one matrix job fails the in-progress and queued siblings are cancelled (fail-fast: true). That is good for saving money on a broken commit and bad when you want the full compatibility picture: you fix the Windows failure, then discover macOS also failed, one full cycle later. A common stance:

  • Pull requests: fail-fast: true, small matrix (one OS, oldest and newest language version).
  • Main branch / nightly: fail-fast: false, the full matrix, because the goal is the complete table.
  • Cells that may fail without blocking: continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }} so a pre-release interpreter reports but does not turn the whole run red.

Jenkins declarative pipelines express the same with a matrix { axes { axis {...} } } block and excludes; the product rule is identical, and failFast true on the parent stage is the analogue.

docs.title: Sharding: splitting one suite across jobs
docs.text:
A matrix over a shard index is how you make a 20-minute suite finish in 5. The runner needs a rule that assigns each test to exactly one shard. Two common rules:

  • By file, round-robin: shard i of n takes test files i, i+n, i+2n, ... in a sorted list. Simple and deterministic, but unbalanced when file durations differ.
  • By recorded duration: greedily give the longest remaining file to the lightest shard, using last run's timings. Needs stored timing data, which can go stale.

Whatever the rule, three properties must hold or you get false greens: every test runs exactly once (no gaps, no overlaps), the assignment is stable between the planning step and the running step (sort the list!), and a failing shard fails the build (see "required checks" below).

docs.title: Required checks and matrix names
docs.text: Branch protection (Lesson 09 of Level 1) requires status checks by name. A matrix produces one check per cell, named like test (ubuntu, 3.12). If you rename a dimension or remove a cell, the required check with the old name never reports, and PRs wait forever on "expected". A robust pattern is a final gate job with needs: [test] and if: always() that fails unless needs.test.result == 'success', and to require only that one stable name. The if: always() matters: without it, a failed matrix makes the gate skipped, and a skipped required check is treated as passing by some configurations.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A matrix is evaluated at workflow-planning time, before any runner is allocated. The service takes the strategy block, computes the list of parameter sets, and creates one job object per set, each with its own copy of the steps and a matrix context. Expressions such as ${{ matrix.python }} are substituted when the job starts. That is why a matrix value cannot depend on the output of a step in the same job; it can be computed by an earlier job and passed in through fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix), which is the standard way to make a dynamic matrix (for example, one cell per changed package; Lesson 09).

Because every cell is an independent job on a fresh runner, they share nothing but what you explicitly cache or upload as artifacts. Parallelism is therefore free of data races but not free of cost: each cell pays checkout, setup and dependency installation again, which is why the cache design in Lesson 02 matters more as the matrix grows.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Counting cells in your head and discovering the product is 300 jobs only when the bill arrives.
  • Using include to "add a row" when it merges into existing rows (or vice versa).
  • Leaving fail-fast on for a compatibility matrix, hiding failures behind the first one.
  • Quoting versions wrongly: python: [3.10] is parsed by YAML as the float 3.1. Quote version strings ("3.10").
  • Requiring matrix cell names directly in branch protection and then changing the matrix.
  • Unsorted or time-dependent shard assignment, so shards overlap or skip tests.
  • Matrices for things that do not vary: if no failure has ever differed between two cells, drop one.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run python3 src/minici.py against a pipeline with the 9-cell matrix above (or call expand_matrix directly) and confirm the list. Then change the include entry to {os: ubuntu, experimental: true} and predict the new job count before running it.
  2. Write a function shard(files, i, n) and a test proving that for several n, the union of all shards equals the file list and no file appears twice. Add a test that shuffling the input does not change the result.
  3. Take a real project's workflow. Compute its matrix size and estimate minutes per push. Which cell has never failed alone in the last 50 runs?
  4. Design the gate job for a 6-cell matrix so that a cancelled or skipped cell blocks the merge.

docs.title: 02 · Cache Design: Keys, Scope & Poisoning
docs.text:
Level 1 showed that a cache hit turns a 2-second install into a near-instant restore. Here we go a step further and look at how to design the key, because a cache is only as good as its key. Too narrow and you never hit; too broad and you restore the wrong thing and get a build that passes for the wrong reason.

What was run

Key values below were produced by minici.cache_key (SHA-256 of the matrix plus the contents of key files, first 16 hex digits) on a two-line req.txt. The restore-key fallback output comes from a small function I wrote that models the documented "exact key, else newest entry matching a prefix" behaviour; it is a model, not GitHub's cache service, which was not run. Limits quoted (10 GB per repository, eviction by age and size) are from docs.github.com as read in October 2026.

docs.title: What the key must capture
docs.text:
A cache entry is valid for a build if, and only if, everything that determined its contents is the same. Hash the inputs, not the date:

base       9fd107a23ce57c5f      matrix {os: ubuntu, py: 3.12} + req.txt
same again 9fd107a23ce57c5f      deterministic: same inputs, same key
py 3.13    8e9ff372b7f5030e      different interpreter => different key
dep bumped fa9115e3be8ef890      pytest 8.0.0 -> 8.0.1 in req.txt => different key
reverted   9fd107a23ce57c5f      change it back => the original entry is a hit again

Four properties are visible there. The key is deterministic; it changes when the lockfile changes (so a dependency bump rebuilds the cache); it changes with the matrix cell (a Python 3.13 wheel set must not be restored on 3.12); and it is reversible, meaning an old state finds its old entry. The key should include: the OS and architecture, the language or tool version, and a hash of the file that pins the dependencies. It should not include a timestamp or the commit SHA, which would make every run a miss and defeat the purpose.

Hash a lockfile, not a loose requirements list: flask>=3 resolves to different packages next month while its file hash stays the same, so the key says "same" while the contents differ. That is a stale-cache bug that shows up as "works on CI, differs on my laptop."

docs.title: Restore keys: partial hits
docs.text:
When the exact key misses (you bumped one dependency), restoring nothing wastes the 99% of packages that did not change. Most cache systems allow ordered fallback prefixes: if no exact match, restore the most recent entry whose key starts with a prefix, then save a fresh entry under the exact key at the end of the job. My model of that behaviour, with three stored entries:

key pip-ubuntu-bbb2, prefixes [pip-ubuntu-]  -> exact hit
key pip-ubuntu-ddd4, prefixes [pip-ubuntu-]  -> restored pip-ubuntu-bbb2 (partial hit; save a new entry at job end)
key pip-windows-eee5, prefixes [pip-windows-] -> miss
key pip-ubuntu-ddd4, prefixes [pip-]          -> restored pip-macos-ccc3   <-- WRONG PLATFORM

The last line is the danger. A prefix that is too short matches an entry from a different OS, so you restore binaries that cannot run, or worse, silently pass. Make the fallback prefix contain every dimension that must match (pip-ubuntu-3.12-), and only drop the content hash.

Partial restores are safe only when the tool re-validates what it restored. pip, npm, Gradle and Maven caches are content-addressed downloads, so a stale cache just means a few extra downloads. Caching a build output directory (compiled objects, node_modules as installed state, a virtualenv) with a partial restore can leave stale files that the build does not notice; for those, prefer an exact key or a clean build.

docs.title: Scope, size and eviction
docs.text:
The documentation states a default limit of 10 GB of cache per repository, with least-recently-used eviction when it is exceeded and eviction of entries not accessed for a period (seven days, as I read it). Implications:

  • A big matrix with one large cache per cell can fill the budget, so the entries evict each other and the hit rate collapses just when the matrix grows. Cache the download directory, not the installed tree, and keep cells that share contents on one key.
  • Caches are scoped by branch: a pull request can read entries made on its base branch, but not entries from sibling branches, and a PR's entries are not visible to other PRs. Warm the cache from main so every branch starts hot.
  • Entries are immutable: saving under an existing key does not update it. If your key never changes while the contents do, you will restore the first version forever.

docs.title: Cache poisoning
docs.text:
A cache is also an input to later builds. If an untrusted workflow (a fork's pull request) can write an entry that a privileged workflow (a release) later restores, the attacker's code runs in the privileged job. Defences are structural, not clever: privileged jobs should not restore caches written by untrusted triggers, release builds should use exact keys scoped to protected branches, and anything you ship should be built from a clean (uncached) build or verified. The real check for "is the cache hiding a bug" is a periodic cold build; if cold and warm builds ever disagree, you have found a key that is too broad.

Level 1's tarball experiment is the same idea from the other side: a cache hit is only trustworthy if the build is deterministic enough that a rebuild would have produced the same bytes.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• The key contains the OS, architecture, tool version and a hash of the lockfile.
  • The key contains no timestamp, run number or commit SHA.
  • Fallback prefixes keep every dimension that must match and drop only the content hash.
  • Installed state is cached only with an exact key; downloads can use fallbacks.
  • Entries are warmed from the default branch so feature branches start hot.
  • Release builds never restore a cache written by an untrusted trigger.
  • Total cache size across all cells stays well under the repository limit.
  • The hit rate is logged per job, and a job with a hit rate near zero is investigated.
  • Saving happens even when a later non-critical step fails, if your platform allows it.
  • A cold-cache build is run regularly and compared with the warm one.
  • The pipeline prints the key and whether it hit, so a slow run can be explained.
  • Cache contents never include secrets or credentials.
  • Large binary caches are compressed once, not per job.
  • Matrix cells that share dependencies share a key.
  • Someone is responsible for deleting caches after a dependency compromise.
  • Cache paths are absolute or relative to a known directory, not to a changing workspace.
  • Restores are verified (a marker file or version check) before the build trusts them.
  • The team can explain, in one sentence, what makes each key change.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The cache service is a key-value store with a restore step before your job and a save step after it. On restore the runner sends the exact key and the ordered list of prefixes; the service answers with the best matching entry's archive, which the runner unpacks at the paths you configured. On save (normally in a post-job hook) the runner checks whether the exact key already exists; if so it skips the upload, otherwise it archives the paths and stores them under that key. Two consequences follow from this design. First, save happens only if the job succeeds by default, so a flaky test can leave you without a fresh cache and cause misses on the next run. Second, because the key is checked before the job and written after, two parallel jobs with the same key both miss and both try to save; one wins and the other is wasted work. Warm a shared cache in an early job and let matrix cells depend on it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Keying on the commit SHA or date, so every run is a cold build.
  • Hashing an unpinned requirements file so the key does not change when the resolved packages do.
  • A fallback prefix shorter than the platform dimension, restoring the wrong OS's files.
  • Caching installed state with partial restore and getting stale-file bugs.
  • Never measuring the hit rate; a cache that always misses costs time to save.
  • Writing caches from untrusted PRs that privileged jobs later read.
  • Assuming a cache is always there: every pipeline must work, slowly, on a miss.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Use minici.cache_key to show the key changes when (a) you add a trailing newline to the lockfile and (b) you change only a comment in a file that is not listed as a key file. Which of these results is a feature and which a hazard?
  2. Run the Level 1 demo pipeline twice and then change one dependency version; record the three install times. Explain each.
  3. Write a fallback prefix for a Node project cached per OS and Node major version, and say what happens on the first run after a Node upgrade.
  4. Your cache is 8 GB and the repository limit is 10 GB. A matrix with 6 cells each saving 2 GB is proposed. What happens, and how do you fix it?

docs.title: 03 · Reusable Pipelines: Workflows, Actions & Shared Libraries
docs.text:
Fifteen repositories with fifteen copies of the same 80-line workflow means fifteen places to fix the next security patch. Sharing pipeline logic is the CI equivalent of extracting a function, and it has the same trade-offs: one fix reaches everybody, and one mistake breaks everybody.

What was run

I parsed a small reusable-workflow file with PyYAML to check its structure (the output is shown). No workflow was executed on GitHub, and no Jenkins shared library was run. The semantics of workflow_call, uses: and composite actions come from docs.github.com (October 2026); Jenkins shared libraries from jenkins.io. The syntax shown is therefore documentation-derived and untested.

docs.title: Three kinds of reuse on GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Mechanism Granularity Defined in Called with Reusable workflow A whole job or several jobs A workflow file with on: workflow_call jobs.<id>.uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@ref Composite action A sequence of steps inside one job action.yml with runs: using: composite steps[*].uses: owner/repo/path@ref Template / generator Whole repo or file Anywhere Copy at creation time (no live link)

Pick by what is shared. If the shared unit needs its own runner, permissions or matrix, it is a reusable workflow: the caller delegates a job. If it is "set up Python, restore the cache, install", it is a composite action: it runs as steps within the caller's job, on the caller's runner, sharing its filesystem.

docs.title: The contract of a reusable workflow
docs.text:
A reusable workflow declares its interface under on.workflow_call. Parsing a sample with PyYAML printed:

sections: ['inputs', 'outputs', 'secrets']   inputs: ['python-version']
secrets: ['deploy-token']   outputs: ['artifact-name']   jobs: ['build']

and shows the YAML 1.1 trap from Level 1 again: the top-level on key is read as the boolean True, so the code that found it had to look up d[True]. Tools that read workflow files (like this course's linter, Lesson 10) must handle that.

The interface is a typed contract:

  • inputs are plain values (string, boolean, number); they are not secret.
  • secrets are passed explicitly (secrets: {deploy-token: ${{ secrets.X }}}) or all at once with secrets: inherit. Prefer explicit: inherit hands the callee every secret the caller can see.
  • outputs map to job outputs, which map to step outputs written to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, a three-link chain that people routinely break by skipping a link.

A caller treats the callee like a function: it passes inputs, reads outputs, and cannot see inside. Per the documentation, reusable workflows can be nested to a limited depth and a workflow can call a limited number of others; check the current limits before designing a deep hierarchy.

docs.title: Versioning is the whole game
docs.text:
uses: org/ci/.github/workflows/build.yml@main means every caller picks up the newest commit of that file on its next run. That is convenient for the platform team and dangerous for everyone else: a bad merge to main breaks all repositories at once, and you cannot reproduce last Tuesday's build because the pipeline logic changed underneath it.

A sane policy:

  • Callers pin to a tag or a full SHA (a SHA is the only immutable form; tags can be moved, as the linter's W003 rule flags).
  • The platform team publishes versioned releases (v3.2.0), keeps a moving major tag (v3) only for low-risk consumers, and documents breaking changes.
  • Changes to the shared workflow are tested in a canary repository or against a matrix of representative callers before a tag moves.
  • Inputs are additive: new optional inputs with defaults do not break existing callers; renaming or removing one does.

docs.title: Jenkins shared libraries
docs.text: Jenkins' equivalent is a shared library: a Git repository with vars/ (global steps callable from any Jenkinsfile, such as buildApp(...)) and src/ (classes), loaded by @Library('name@version') _. The same lessons apply, and Jenkins adds its own risk: library code runs on the controller with Groovy sandbox rules unless the library is marked trusted, and a trusted library can do anything the controller can. Pin the version (@v3) rather than a branch, and keep libraries small, tested functions, not a framework.

docs.title: When sharing hurts
docs.text:
• Premature abstraction. Two repositories with similar-looking workflows may diverge next quarter; one shared workflow with twenty if: inputs is harder to read than two files.
  • Debugging across a boundary. An error in a reusable workflow shows the callee's steps in the caller's run, but fixing it means a change, review, release and re-pin in another repository.
  • Hidden permissions. A callee can use at most the permissions the caller grants it, but a caller who grants contents: write to a workflow it has not read has delegated trust; read what you call.
  • Blast radius. A shared deploy workflow that gets a permissive change is a network-wide incident (Level 4 · 05 covers audit and change control).

A rule of thumb that has held up: share after the third copy, share the boring parts (set up, build, publish) rather than the decisions (what to deploy, when), and make the interface small.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• The callee's inputs, secrets and outputs are documented next to the workflow.
  • Callers pin a tag or SHA, never a branch.
  • The platform team has a canary repository for testing changes.
  • New inputs are optional with defaults; removals go through deprecation.
  • Secrets are passed explicitly, not with blanket inheritance.
  • There is a policy for how many versions are supported at once.
  • A test or example caller exists for every reusable workflow.
  • Composite actions are used for step sequences and reusable workflows for whole jobs.
  • Failures in shared code name the callee and its version in the log.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When a workflow run starts, the service resolves each uses: reference to a commit in the other repository, reads that file at that commit, and inlines it into the run as additional jobs, wiring inputs, secrets and outputs between them. The callee's jobs appear under the caller's job name in the UI and count against the caller's concurrency and billing. A composite action is simpler: its steps are expanded into the caller's job at execution time and run sequentially on the same runner, which is why a composite action can modify files the next step sees, and a reusable workflow cannot (it runs on a different runner; pass files as artifacts, Lesson 07 in Level 1).

Access to the callee is checked at resolution: a private repository's workflow can be reused by other repositories only if its sharing settings allow it. This is why a "works in the platform repo, fails in the product repo" error is often a permission setting, not a YAML bug.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Referencing @main and being surprised when old commits stop building.
  • secrets: inherit everywhere, over-sharing credentials.
  • Reusable workflow where a composite action fits (and the reverse), then fighting runner or file-sharing limits.
  • Breaking the interface by renaming an input without a deprecation period.
  • Forgetting a link in the output chain (step output, job output, workflow output).
  • No tests for the shared logic, so a bug ships to every consumer at once.
  • Sharing decisions instead of mechanics, until every team needs a special case.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a reusable workflow build.yml with one required and one optional input and one output, parse it with PyYAML, and list its contract as the sample did. Where is the on key?
  2. Write a composite action that sets up Python and installs from a lockfile. State two things it can do that a reusable workflow cannot, and two that it cannot do.
  3. Draft a versioning policy for a platform team supporting 20 repositories: tags, canary, deprecation notice, and the rollback procedure when v3.2.0 is bad.
  4. Take two similar workflows in repositories you know. Would you share them today? Write the argument for waiting.

docs.title: 04 · Containers in CI: Images, Services & Readiness
docs.text:
Containers appear in CI in three roles: the environment your job runs in (container: or a Docker agent), services your tests talk to (a database, a cache, a message broker), and the artifact your pipeline produces (an image you build and push). Each has its own failure modes. The most common one is mundane: the test starts before the database accepts connections.

What was run, and what wasn't

No container was built or run: there is no container runtime on the machine used for this course. The Dockerfile, container: and services: snippets are from docs.github.com and docs.docker.com as read in October 2026 and are untested. What I did run is the readiness helper waitfor.py (4 pytest tests against real local sockets), which is the part of this lesson you can verify without Docker.

docs.title: Containers as the job environment
docs.text:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: python:3.12-slim        # steps run inside this image
    services:
      db:
        image: postgres:16
        env: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_DB_PASSWORD }}}
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres"
          --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-sha>
      - run: pytest         # reaches the database at host `db`, port 5432

Documented behaviour: with container: set, the job's steps run inside that image and service containers are reachable by their service name over a private network. Without container: (steps on the runner itself) services are reached on localhost through published ports. Mixing the two up is a classic connection refused.

Benefits: the environment is described in one line and is identical for everyone who uses that image tag. Risks: the tag is mutable. python:3.12-slim changes when a new patch release is published, so a green pipeline can turn red with no commit. Pin the digest (python@sha256:...) for reproducibility and update it deliberately with a bot, or accept the drift knowingly and watch for it.

docs.title: Readiness: "started" is not "ready"
docs.text:
A service container is started when its process launches. It is ready when it accepts the first query, which for a database can be seconds later, after crash recovery and initialization. A health check in the service options makes the platform wait until the container reports healthy before running your steps; the Docker daemon runs the command at the interval and marks the container healthy after it passes, unhealthy after the configured retries.

When you cannot rely on that (a service started by your own script, a local compose stack), wait explicitly. Waiting with a fixed sleep 10 is wrong both ways: too short on a slow runner (flaky), too long on a fast one (wasted minutes on every run). Wait for the condition, with a deadline:

def wait_for_port(host, port, timeout=30.0, initial=0.1, factor=2.0, max_delay=2.0, ...):
    deadline, delay, attempts = clock() + timeout, initial, 0
    while True:
        attempts += 1
        try:
            with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=...): return attempts
        except OSError:
            if clock() + delay > deadline: raise NotReady(...)
            sleep(delay); delay = min(delay * factor, max_delay)

The four tests (all passed; the full file is src/waitfor.py with src/test_waitfor.py):

  1. A service already listening returns on the first attempt.
  2. A service that starts 0.6 s late (a thread binds the port after a delay) is detected: more than one attempt, and elapsed time between 0.5 s and 3 s.
  3. A port nobody listens on raises NotReady with a message naming host, port, attempts and timeout, after ~0.5 s.
  4. The backoff delays, driven by a fake clock so the test is instant and deterministic, are exactly [0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.0] then capped at 1.0.

Test 4 injects clock and sleep. Injecting time is the technique that makes retry logic testable without making the test suite slow or flaky; the alternative is a test that really sleeps for ten seconds.

A TCP connect proves the port is open, not that the application is ready (some servers accept connections before they can serve queries). Prefer a protocol-level check where one exists (pg_isready, a PING to Redis, an HTTP /health that touches its dependencies) and use the port check only as the first gate.

docs.title: Building images in a pipeline
docs.text:
Image builds use layer caching: Docker reuses a layer when the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. Order the Dockerfile from least to most frequently changing, or the cache is invalidated early:

FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest>
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .             # changes rarely
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt     # cached until requirements change
COPY . .                            # changes every commit; keep it last

Putting COPY . . first would invalidate the dependency layer on every commit. On hosted runners the layer cache from the previous run is gone unless you export it (a registry cache, or the platform's cache backend); this is the same keying problem as Lesson 02, with the same poisoning concerns. Tag images with an immutable identifier (the commit SHA or a version), push latest only as a convenience, and deploy by digest. Never bake secrets into a layer: they remain in the image history even if a later layer deletes them (Lesson 08 of Level 1).

docs.title: Containers and the Docker socket
docs.text: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a job container gives that job control of the host's Docker daemon, which is effectively root on the host. Treat it as a privileged configuration that untrusted pull requests must never reach. Alternatives are rootless builders (BuildKit, Kaniko, Buildah) that build without the host daemon.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Service containers on a hosted runner are ordinary containers started by the runner before your steps, attached to a user-defined Docker network. That network provides DNS, so the name db resolves to the container's address; this is why the service name works inside a container: job. When the job is not itself in a container, the runner has to publish the service's port on the host, so you connect to localhost:<mapped-port>. The health check is the daemon's HEALTHCHECK machinery: it executes your command inside the service container periodically and tracks consecutive failures. The runner waits for the healthy state with its own timeout before starting step one. All of this disappears when the job ends: containers and the network are torn down, so service state (a seeded database) never persists between runs, which is a feature for isolation and a cost for slow seeding.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• sleep N instead of waiting on a condition.
  • Mutable image tags that change under a green pipeline.
  • localhost vs service name confusion between container and non-container jobs.
  • Declaring "ready" on an open port while the application is still initializing.
  • COPY . . before dependency install, defeating layer caching.
  • Secrets passed as build arguments or copied into layers.
  • Mounting the Docker socket into jobs that run untrusted code.
  • Retries with no deadline, which turn an outage into a hung job.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_waitfor.py -v and read the fake-clock test. Add a fifth test where the service appears after exactly two failed attempts and assert the returned attempt count.
  2. Write a HEALTHCHECK or --health-cmd for a Redis service and say what exit codes mean to Docker.
  3. Reorder a Dockerfile of your own so dependency installation is cached, and describe how you would prove the layer was reused (build twice and compare the output).
  4. Explain why a database seeded with 2 GB of test data in a service container may be slower than restoring it from a cache, and how you would measure it.

docs.title: 05 · Test Reports & Flaky Tests
docs.text:
A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. One flaky test is an annoyance; a few hundred make the pipeline random, teach everyone to press "re-run" without reading the failure, and eventually hide a real bug behind the habit. The cure starts with arithmetic, because flakiness compounds in a way intuition underestimates.

What was run

The pass-rate table compares a formula with a 20,000-run Monte Carlo simulation I ran in Python (seeded random numbers, independent flakes). The simulation is a model: real flakes are often correlated (a slow runner makes many tests flaky at once) and not independent. The rerun estimate and the retry arithmetic are computed from the formulas shown. No real CI system's flake data was used or exists here.

docs.title: How flakes compound
docs.text:
Suppose a suite has n tests and each one independently fails spuriously with probability p even when the code is correct. The suite passes only if none of them flake:

P(green) = (1 − p)ⁿ

Tests (n) Per-test flake rate (p) Formula Simulated 100 0.001 (0.1%) 0.905 0.903 100 0.01 (1%) 0.366 0.360 500 0.01 0.007 0.007 1000 0.002 0.135 0.135

The simulation agrees with the formula to within about 0.006, which is the sampling noise you expect from 20,000 runs. Read the table slowly:

  • A suite of 100 tests where each flakes one time in a thousand is green only 90% of the time: one run in ten is red for no reason.
  • At 1% per test, a 500-test suite is green 0.7% of the time. It would be unusable, and the team would already have noticed. The dangerous region is the middle, where a suite is green often enough that people keep trusting "just re-run it."
  • 1000 tests with p = 0.2% pass 13.5% of runs. Per-test rates that look negligible are not, at scale.

So the target is not "few flaky tests" but a flake budget: to keep a 1000-test suite green 99% of the time on correct code you need p below about 0.00001 per test, one in a hundred thousand.

docs.title: Measuring one test's flake rate
docs.text: You rerun a suspect test 200 times on one commit and see 18 failures. The estimate is 18/200 = 0.090, with a 95% interval of about ±0.040 (the normal approximation, roughly 1.96 × √(p(1−p)/n)). So the true rate is plausibly between 5% and 13%, and 200 runs cannot tell you whether it is 6% or 12%. Fewer runs would give a wider interval. If someone claims "I fixed it" after 10 clean runs, the probability of seeing 10 clean runs from a 9%-flaky test is (0.91)¹⁰ ≈ 0.39, so 10 clean runs prove very little. You need a few dozen to be moderately convinced and hundreds to be sure for rates this low.

docs.title: Retries: a bandage with a cost
docs.text:
Automatic retry of failed tests is common (pytest-rerunfailures, Jenkins retry, test framework options). The arithmetic:

A test that fails 8% of the time, with 2 retries (3 attempts total), still fails the build with probability 0.08³ = 0.00051, about 1 in 1950. Retries do reduce red builds by orders of magnitude, which is why teams love them. The costs:

  1. They hide real intermittent bugs in the product (a race condition, a timeout). A retry-green result of "passed on third attempt" must be reported, not discarded.
  2. They multiply time when the failure is slow.
  3. They rescue tests that should fail: a test that really is 70% failing (0.7³ = 0.34 still fails, but 0.3 flakiness will pass often) passes enough to ignore.

Policy that works: retry is allowed, but every retried-then-passed test is recorded, counted per test, and when a test exceeds a threshold it is quarantined and a ticket is created with an owner and a due date.

docs.title: Quarantine without losing the signal
docs.text:
Quarantine means: keep running the test, but do not let its result gate the merge. Implementations include a marker (@pytest.mark.quarantine) with a separate non-blocking job that runs those tests, or a skip list stored in the repository. Rules that keep it honest:

  • Quarantine is temporary and visible: a list with owners and dates; its size is a dashboard metric.
  • Quarantined tests still run, so you can see when one has gone stable and when it finally fails for a real reason.
  • A flaky test that covers critical behaviour is a bug to fix, not a thing to skip.

docs.title: Reading failures: test reports
docs.text:
Raw logs are hard to scan at 20,000 lines. Test frameworks can emit JUnit XML (pytest --junitxml=report.xml), a de-facto format that CI systems parse to show a table of failures, durations and history (Jenkins' junit step and GitHub Actions test-reporter actions both consume it; I describe this from their documentation and did not run them). What a good report gives you:

  • The failing test name and message first, not the 5,000 passing lines.
  • Duration per test, to find the slow ones (and to shard by time, Lesson 01).
  • History: whether this test failed on other unrelated commits, which is the strongest flake signal available. A test failing on 12 different PRs in a week and never on main's own runs is not a bug in those 12 PRs.

Always publish the report even when the job failed (if: always()), or you will have the report only on green builds, when you need it least.

docs.title: Causes, in order of frequency
docs.text:
1. Shared state and ordering: tests that depend on each other or on a database left by a previous test.
  2. Time: sleeping instead of waiting for a condition (Lesson 04), tests that assume the current date, time zones, or that two timestamps differ.
  3. Concurrency: races inside the code under test or in the test's own threads.
  4. Resources: a fixed port, a shared temp file, an overloaded runner making a timeout too tight.
  5. External services: a test that calls the real network.
  6. Randomness: unseeded random data. Print the seed on failure so you can reproduce.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A test runner reports each test's outcome to the framework's reporter, and CI infrastructure stores or parses the result. The compounding formula holds because the build result is a conjunction of every test's outcome: any single failure turns it red. Retries change the conjunction to "each test passes within k attempts", reducing the effective per-test failure probability from p to pᵏ when attempts are independent. The independence assumption is the weak point: a flaky cause that affects the whole machine (an overloaded runner, a full disk) correlates failures, so retrying immediately on the same runner helps less than the formula suggests, and retrying on a fresh runner helps more. This is also why rerunning the entire job often works when rerunning a test does not: you get a different runner.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• "Just re-run it" as the team's standard answer, with no tracking.
  • Retrying everything without recording what needed a retry.
  • Concluding a flake is fixed after a handful of clean runs.
  • Deleting a flaky test that covers real behaviour instead of fixing the race.
  • Sleeping to fix a timing flake, trading flakiness for slowness.
  • Not publishing reports on failure.
  • Unseeded randomness with no logged seed.
  • Treating a flake rate as per-suite when the formula is per-test.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Compute P(green) for 300 tests at p = 0.003, then simulate 10,000 runs in Python and compare. How close is it?
  2. You rerun a test 50 times and see 3 failures. Give the estimate and a rough 95% interval. How many more runs would halve the interval's width?
  3. Design a quarantine policy: where the list lives, who owns entries, the maximum age, and how the dashboard metric is computed.
  4. Write a pytest plugin sketch or conftest.py hook that records every test that passed only after a retry to a file for the nightly report.

docs.title: 06 · Quality Gates: Coverage, Lint & Analysis
docs.text:
A quality gate is a check whose failure blocks a merge or a deployment: tests pass, coverage does not drop, lint is clean, no known-vulnerable dependency, no secret in the diff. Gates turn standards into something the machine enforces consistently. They also turn a number into a target, and a target people optimise stops being a good measure. This lesson shows that with a demonstration.

What was run

The coverage demonstration was run on macOS with Python's coverage package and pytest, on a tiny shop.py module (a discount function with a normal and a VIP branch) that I wrote for this purpose. The numbers are from that one toy module; they illustrate the mechanism and say nothing about what coverage levels real projects achieve. Lint, SAST and vulnerability-scanning tools are described from their documentation and were not run here.

docs.title: What a coverage number measures
docs.text:
Line coverage is the fraction of lines executed during the test run. Branch coverage counts whether both outcomes of each if were taken. Neither measures whether the tests check anything.

The demonstration, step by step:

  1. A weak test that calls both code paths and asserts nothing. coverage reported shop.py: 6 statements, 0 missed, 4 branches, 0 partial, 100%. Full line and branch coverage.
  2. I then introduced a bug: the VIP discount factor changed from 0.8 to 0.08 (a customer who should pay 80% now pays 8%).
  3. The weak suite still passed. A 100%-covered module with a gross pricing error and a green build.
  4. A strong suite (the same inputs, with assertions on the returned prices) caught it: 1 failed, 2 passed.
  5. The strong suite on the correct code also reached 100% branch coverage. So the two suites have identical coverage and opposite value.
  6. A partial test that exercised only the VIP path reported 40% line / 57% total with branches; useful to see that the report does show unexecuted code correctly.

The conclusion is not "coverage is useless". It is exactly this: coverage finds code that no test touches (a real and valuable signal); it cannot find code that no test checks. A low number means missing tests; a high number means nothing alone.

Better evidence that tests check behaviour comes from mutation testing: automatically make small changes (> to >=, 0.8 to 0.08) and check that some test fails. A surviving mutant is a bug your suite would not catch. Mutation testing is slow, so teams run it on changed files or nightly. I did not run a mutation tool; my change in step 2 was a manual mutation.

docs.title: How to gate on coverage sensibly
docs.text:
• Gate on the diff, not the total: "new and changed lines are at least X% covered" is achievable and meaningful, while a project-wide threshold punishes a 1-line fix in a legacy file.
  • Use a ratchet: the total may not decrease. It blocks regression without demanding a rewrite.
  • Never make 100% a requirement; people write assertion-free tests to satisfy it, which is the weak test above.
  • Review the report, not just the number: look at which lines are uncovered and whether they matter.
  • Configure the tool to fail below the threshold (coverage report --fail-under=80 returns a non-zero exit status), so the gate is code in the pipeline and not a person's opinion.

docs.title: The other gates
docs.text:
Gate Catches Typical false-positive source Formatter check (black --check, gofmt -l) Style drift None if the formatter is deterministic; fix with auto-format Linter (ruff, eslint) Unused names, likely bugs Rules that do not fit your code; tune rather than disable everything Type checker (mypy, tsc) Interface mismatches Third-party libraries without types SAST (static security analysis) Injection, unsafe functions High noise; triage and baseline Dependency scan Known-vulnerable versions Vulnerabilities in code paths you never call Secret scan (Level 1 · 08) Committed credentials Test fixtures that look like keys License check Incompatible licenses Ambiguous metadata Performance budget Slower endpoints, bigger bundles Noisy shared runners

Rules for adding a gate: it should be fast (feedback in minutes), deterministic (same code, same answer), actionable (the message says what to change), and rare to bypass. A gate that is red for weeks gets muted; a gate with many false positives trains people to ignore the real ones.

docs.title: Introducing a gate to an existing codebase
docs.text: You cannot turn on a linter with 4,000 existing violations. Options: record a baseline (existing findings are accepted, only new ones fail), fix by directory over time, or make the gate advisory (report, don't block) for a trial period with a date to enforce. Whichever you choose, write the date down. "Advisory" with no end date is "disabled."

docs.title: Gates as code
docs.text: Policy must live in the repository, versioned like code: pyproject.toml or .coveragerc for thresholds, a lint config, a workflow file. A gate configured only in a web UI cannot be reviewed, diffed, or reproduced locally. It must also be runnable locally with one command (make check) that mirrors CI; if a failure can only be reproduced after a push, developers will stop running gates before pushing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Coverage is gated on changed lines or as a ratchet, never as a fixed 100% rule.
  • Coverage reports list the uncovered lines for reviewers.
  • Mutation testing or manual mutation spot-checks are run on critical modules.
  • Lint, format and type checks are one local command that mirrors CI.
  • New gates start with a baseline of accepted existing findings.
  • Advisory gates carry an enforcement date.
  • Each gate has an owner and a documented process for false positives.
  • Gate results are deterministic: same code, same answer.
  • Gates report within minutes, so developers wait for them.
  • Dependency and secret scans run on a schedule as well as on pull requests.
  • Threshold changes go through review like code changes.
  • Suppressions carry a reason and an expiry date.
  • Excluded files are listed and reviewed periodically.
  • A failing gate message states what to change.
  • Teams are trained to read the report, not just the colour.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: coverage works through Python's tracing hooks: it is notified as each line of the measured code executes and records (file, line) pairs (and (from_line, to_line) pairs for branches). After the run it compares the set of executed lines against the set of executable lines it derives from the bytecode and reports the difference. It never looks at assertions, return values or test names, so a test that calls a function inside try: ... except: pass covers it perfectly. The gate itself is just a process exit status: the pipeline step that runs coverage report --fail-under=80 exits non-zero when the total is below 80, and the CI system marks the step, job and required check as failed. Everything a gate does reduces to that: a command, its exit status, and branch protection that refuses to merge a red required check.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating coverage as a quality score rather than a map of untested code.
  • A project-wide threshold that nobody can meet in a legacy file.
  • Assertion-free tests written to satisfy the number.
  • Gates that only run in CI, with no local equivalent.
  • Advisory forever: a gate with no enforcement date.
  • Disabling a failing check instead of fixing or baselining it.
  • Excluding files from coverage until the number looks good.
  • Gating on tools that are non-deterministic (network-dependent scans), which makes merges random.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the demonstration: write discount(price, vip) with two branches, a weak test, and a strong test. Show 100% coverage for both, then mutate a constant and show only the strong test fails.
  2. Configure --fail-under and confirm that the command exits with status 2 (or whatever your version returns) when the threshold is missed; record it with echo $?.
  3. For a repository you know, propose a baseline strategy for adding a type checker: what is accepted today, what is enforced from now, and the date.
  4. List three gates for a service that handles payments and say what each must never do (be slow, be flaky, produce unactionable messages).

docs.title: 07 · Environments, Approvals & Concurrency
docs.text:
Building and testing are safe to repeat. Deploying changes something people use. A pipeline therefore needs a way to say "this job touches production, so it needs extra conditions": who may trigger it, who must approve it, which credentials it can see, and that only one deployment to a target runs at a time. GitHub Actions calls the target an environment; Jenkins expresses the same ideas with input steps, credentials scopes and the lock plugin.

What was run, and what wasn't

No approval, environment or protection rule was exercised: that needs a GitHub repository with environments configured, and I did not create one for this lesson. Everything about environments is from docs.github.com and Jenkins documentation as read in October 2026. The numbers quoted (a 30-day wait for approval) are documented limits. What is verifiable locally is the lint rule that flags a deploy job lacking concurrency:, which Lesson 10's tested linter implements (rule W006).

docs.title: What an environment is
docs.text:
An environment is a named deployment target (staging, production) attached to jobs with environment: production. Per the GitHub documentation it can carry:

  • Required reviewers: the job waits, paused, until a listed person or team approves. Up to a small number of reviewers can be listed and one approval releases the job.
  • Wait timer: a delay before the job starts, which gives a window to cancel.
  • Branch / tag restrictions: only workflows on main (or a release/* pattern) may deploy to it.
  • Environment secrets and variables: values visible only to jobs that target that environment, and only after protection rules pass.
  • Custom protection rules: a third-party check (change-management system, health check) the platform consults before releasing.

A job waiting for approval is not consuming a runner, but it is still waiting: documentation states a workflow run waiting for approval is cancelled after 30 days. A deploy that "needs a Friday approval" can expire quietly over the weekend of a holiday.

docs.title: Why secrets belong to the environment
docs.text:
A repository-level secret is visible to every job in the repository, including a pull request's workflow if permissions allow. An environment secret is only released to a job that has passed the environment's rules. So PROD_DEPLOY_KEY stored as a production environment secret cannot be read by the test job or by a PR-triggered workflow. This is the practical meaning of "least privilege" in a pipeline (Level 1 · 08): the credential exists only where the check has happened.

Combined with OIDC federation (Level 3 · 08), the environment name can appear in the token's claims so the cloud provider itself refuses to issue production credentials to a job that is not in the production environment.

docs.title: What an approval does and doesn't prove
docs.text:
It proves a person with the right account clicked "approve" on this run. It does not prove:

  • that the person read the diff (rubber-stamping is the normal failure; a reviewer approving 20 times a day cannot be a control);
  • that the approval was independent: by default the person who triggered the run may be able to approve it unless "prevent self-review" is enabled;
  • that the thing approved is the thing deployed unless the deploy uses the exact artifact built and tested earlier in the run (build once, promote the same artifact; Level 1 · 07). If the deploy job rebuilds, the approver approved a commit but the system shipped a rebuild.

An approval gate is a control only when these three properties are designed in. Otherwise it is a ritual that adds a delay.

docs.title: Concurrency: one deployment at a time
docs.text:
Two pushes in quick succession start two workflow runs. If both deploy, they race: the older one can finish last and leave production on the older version. GitHub Actions' answer is the concurrency key:

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false      # queue, do not cancel a deploy already running

Key points from the documentation: runs in the same group execute one at a time; a newer pending run replaces an older pending one (so at most one waits); cancel-in-progress: true cancels the running one, which is right for tests on a branch (newer commit supersedes) and wrong for deploys (you would abort a deployment half-way, e.g. between a migration and the app update). So: cancel-in-progress: true for CI, false for deployment.

Note the replacement behaviour: if three deploys queue, the middle one is dropped. That is acceptable only if each deploy ships "the latest state", which is true for deploying main and false for deploying a specific release tag that someone asked for.

Jenkins offers disableConcurrentBuilds() per job and the Lockable Resources plugin's lock(resource: 'prod') for finer control; the semantics differ slightly, so read the plugin documentation for what happens to waiting builds.

docs.title: Promotion between environments
docs.text:
A typical flow: build once → deploy to dev automatically → run smoke tests → deploy to staging → run integration tests → manual approval → production. Each environment gets the same artifact and different configuration. The three things allowed to differ are configuration values, scale, and credentials; if the code or the build differs, staging stops being evidence about production.

Keep configuration in the repository as code or a config service, not edited by hand on servers, so that "what is deployed where" is answerable from version control (Lesson 06 of Level 3 on GitOps).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Environment names are defined once and referenced by constant, not typed freehand.
  • Production deploys use the same artifact that passed the earlier stages.
  • Self-review is prevented for production approvals.
  • Environment secrets exist only in the environments that need them.
  • Deploy jobs use a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress false.
  • Branch restrictions limit which refs can deploy to production.
  • Approval notifications reach people who can actually act on them.
  • Approvals expire visibly rather than silently.
  • Rollback uses the same environment protections as a forward deploy.
  • Approval and deploy records are exported to long-term storage.
  • A break-glass path exists, is rare, and is reviewed afterwards.
  • Staging differs from production only in configuration, scale and credentials.
  • Smoke tests run after every deploy, and a failure triggers the rollback procedure.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a job declares environment: production, the scheduler evaluates the environment's protection rules before assigning a runner. If a rule needs a human, the job enters a "waiting" state and a notification is sent to the reviewers; the run's UI shows the pending review. On approval the scheduler records who approved and when (this record appears in the run and in the audit log), releases the environment's secrets to the job's context, and queues it for a runner. A branch restriction is checked against the ref that triggered the run, which is why a deploy job triggered from a feature branch is rejected even if a reviewer would have approved. Concurrency groups are enforced at the same scheduling layer: the group's lock is acquired before the job starts, and a run that cannot get the lock is shown as pending.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deploy secrets stored at repository level, visible to untrusted workflows.
  • Reviewer approval without independence (self-approval allowed, or the same two people approve everything).
  • Rebuilding in the deploy job, so the approved commit and the deployed bytes differ.
  • cancel-in-progress: true on deploys, aborting half-applied changes.
  • No concurrency control, allowing an older deploy to finish after a newer one.
  • Different artifacts per environment, destroying the meaning of staging.
  • Long approval waits that expire silently.
  • Environment names as free text with typos (prodction) that silently create a new, unprotected environment.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a workflow with build, deploy-staging and deploy-production jobs where production uses environment: production and a concurrency group. Run python3 src/wflint.py on it and fix every finding.
  2. Draft the protection rules for a production environment in your organisation: reviewers, self-review policy, wait timer, branch rule. Justify each setting in one line.
  3. Two commits land one minute apart and both start a deploy. Describe, step by step, what happens with and without concurrency, and what the final deployed version is in each case.
  4. List what you would check to confirm an approval was meaningful. What data would you need to log?

docs.title: 08 · Runners & Agents: Where Your Jobs Actually Run
docs.text:
A pipeline definition is only instructions. The runner (GitHub's term) or agent (Jenkins') is the machine that executes them. Where it runs and what survives between jobs determines your cost, speed, security and, most surprisingly, whether your builds are repeatable.

What was run, and what wasn't

I ran a small experiment with the Level 1 minici runner to show the stale persistent workspace problem (output below). I did not register a self-hosted runner, run a Jenkins agent, or measure autoscaling. Descriptions of GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners and the documented limits come from docs.github.com as read in October 2026 (hosted job limit 6 hours, self-hosted job limit 5 days). Jenkins agent behaviour is from jenkins.io and not run.

docs.title: Hosted vs self-hosted
docs.text:
Hosted (provided by the CI vendor) Self-hosted (you run the machine) Setup None Install the runner/agent, keep it patched Isolation A fresh VM per job, discarded afterwards Whatever you build: VM, container, or bare machine reused Hardware Vendor's sizes (larger ones cost more) Anything: GPUs, ARM, mainframes, private network access Cost Per minute (some free allowance) Machines, power, people Network Public internet Can reach your private systems Max job time 6 hours (hosted, documented) 5 days (self-hosted, documented)

Choose self-hosted for a reason: needing special hardware, reaching a private network, very large caches, or cost at high volume. "It is cheaper" is true only after you count the engineers who patch it.

docs.title: Ephemeral vs persistent
docs.text:
The more important axis is whether a runner is reused.

  • Ephemeral: a runner takes one job, then is destroyed (a fresh VM or a container). Every job starts from a known image. Nothing leaks from one job to the next. This is the default for hosted runners and recommended for self-hosted when jobs may run untrusted code.
  • Persistent: the machine lives on and runs many jobs. Faster (warm caches, installed tools) but jobs share a filesystem, a Docker daemon, and any lingering process.

docs.title: The stale-workspace demonstration
docs.text:
I wrote a one-step pipeline whose test passes only if a leftover file from an earlier run is present, a deliberately silly stand-in for a build that reads a stale cache, an installed package, or an uncleaned output directory. Running it twice in the same working directory:

run 1: no cache: building from scratch              RESULT: failure
run 2: using stale cache from a previous build -> passes    RESULT: success

Same pipeline, same commit, different result, because run 1 created .cache_ok and run 2 found it. On a persistent runner the second build is green only because of the first.
