The human steps are the decisions: approve, and for risky releases watch the canary (Lesson 01). A release process that is a wiki page of manual steps will eventually miss one.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text: Be able to answer, from a running system: which version is this, which commit, which build, which pipeline run, who approved. Embed the version and commit SHA in the artifact (a /version endpoint, an image label), emit it in logs and metrics, and keep the release record. In an incident this saves the first twenty minutes.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Release tags are protected from moving or deletion.
  • Commit or PR title format is linted in CI.
  • Version and commit are embedded in the artifact and reported at runtime.
  • A human can override the computed version in the release pull request.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The version bump is a pure function from (current version, list of commit messages) to a new version, which is why it is easy to test exhaustively. The surrounding automation does I/O: read tags to find the previous release, git log previous..HEAD to list the commits, compute the version, update version files, write the changelog, commit, tag and push. Each of those has failure modes the pure function hides: a missing previous tag (first release), a merge commit history that makes git log ordering confusing, concurrent releases on two branches both computing 1.5.0, and a push that succeeds for the commit and fails for the tag. Release tooling should be idempotent: running it again after a partial failure must not create 1.5.1 just because 1.5.0 half-exists.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Mislabelling a breaking change as minor.
  • Trusting commit messages blindly with no lint, so unparseable messages vanish from the release.
  • Auto-generated changelogs published as-is, full of noise.
  • Forgetting to forward-port a hotfix, so the bug returns.
  • Moving a tag after publishing, so two builds share one version.
  • No version embedded in the artifact or reported at runtime.
  • Manual release steps that drift from the written checklist.
  • Versioning an application like a library (or the reverse) without a reason.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_semrel.py -v. Add a type revert: handled by the rules and decide what it should do. Write the tests first.
  2. Write a CI check that validates each pull request title against the Conventional Commits header regex and gives a helpful error message.
  3. For a library you use, read its last three releases and judge whether each version number matched the actual compatibility impact.
  4. Design the hotfix procedure for your branching model, with the forward-port step as an explicit checklist item.

docs.title: 08 · Supply-Chain Security for Pipelines
docs.text:
Your software is mostly other people's code: libraries, base images, build tools, CI actions. A supply-chain attack compromises one of those inputs, or the build process itself, so that malicious code reaches your users with your signature on it. The attack surface is the whole path from source to running artifact; this lesson covers what a pipeline can do to shrink it.

What was run, and what wasn't

I ran one local demonstration: computing a SHA-256 checksum of an archive, verifying it, tampering with the file and verifying again. I did not run signing tools (Sigstore/cosign, GPG), generate an SBOM, produce provenance attestations, or scan dependencies. Descriptions of those tools, and of frameworks such as SLSA, are from general knowledge and public documentation as I know it; check their current docs. Nothing here substitutes for a security assessment.

docs.title: Where attacks enter
docs.text: Entry point Example Defence Direct dependency A maintainer account is taken over and a new version ships malware Pin versions, review updates, use lockfiles with hashes Transitive dependency A library of a library is compromised SBOM, scanning, fewer dependencies Typosquatting / dependency confusion A public package with the same name as your private one wins resolution Scoped/namespaced registries, explicit index config Base image or tool A mutable tag now points to a different image Pin by digest CI action or plugin A tag on a third-party action is moved to malicious code Pin to a commit SHA (Lesson 10's rule W003) Build system A compromised runner or poisoned cache injects code into your artifact Ephemeral runners, isolated builds, provenance Your own pipeline A pull request exploits script injection to steal secrets Hardening (Level 4 · 01) Distribution Someone swaps the artifact on the download server or registry Checksums, signatures

docs.title: Integrity: checksums and pins
docs.text:
A checksum binds a name to content. The demonstration:

$ shasum -a 256 app.tar > SHA256SUMS
2a02380a339b...baf7a  app.tar
$ shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
app.tar: OK
(change one line inside app.py, rebuild the tar)
$ shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
app.tar: FAILED
shasum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match        (exit status 1)

Any change to the content, even adding ; import os to one line, changes the digest, and the check fails with a non-zero exit status, which is what makes it usable as a pipeline gate. Two limits are crucial. First, a checksum stored next to the file proves only that the download was not corrupted; an attacker who can replace the file can replace the checksum. It must come over a different trusted channel, or be a signature by a key the attacker lacks. Second, a checksum identifies content but not who built it or from what; that is provenance.

For dependencies, the package managers support this directly: pip's hash-checking mode (--require-hashes) refuses packages whose digest is not in your requirements file, and lockfiles in npm, Cargo, Go (go.sum) and others record hashes. The trade-off is maintenance: updates mean regenerating hashes, which is why a bot that opens update pull requests (with tests and changelog links) is the practical way to stay both pinned and current. I did not run pip's hash mode here.

docs.title: Pin everything that executes
docs.text:
• Dependencies: lockfile, committed, with hashes where the tool supports them.
  • Base images: by digest (image@sha256:...), updated by a bot.
  • CI actions and plugins: by full commit SHA. A tag can be re-pointed; a SHA cannot.
  • Tools downloaded in scripts: version plus checksum. curl https://x | sh runs whatever the server says today.

Pinning protects against silent change, not against a malicious version you deliberately adopt, which is why review of updates and scanning still matter. It also freezes security fixes unless you keep updating; "pinned" must not mean "forgotten".

docs.title: Know what you ship: SBOM and scanning
docs.text: A Software Bill of Materials lists the components in an artifact (name, version, hash, licence), commonly in SPDX or CycloneDX formats. Generating one in the pipeline gives you an answer to "are we affected by vulnerability X?" in minutes instead of days: search the SBOMs. Vulnerability scanners match components against advisory databases. Caveats: scanner output is noisy (a vulnerable function you never call), version matching is imperfect, and a clean scan means no known issues, not no issues. Triage by reachability and severity, and set a fixed time budget for fixing critical findings.

docs.title: Provenance and signing
docs.text: Signing proves an artifact was produced by a holder of a key. Provenance is a signed statement of how an artifact was built: which source commit, which builder, which inputs. Frameworks like SLSA describe levels of assurance, from "provenance exists" up to "built on a hardened, isolated, non-forgeable builder." Tools such as Sigstore's cosign support keyless signing, where the builder authenticates with its CI identity (OIDC) and gets a short-lived certificate recorded in a transparency log, so no long-lived signing key can leak. The value is in the verification step: the deploy system must refuse artifacts whose signature or provenance doesn't match policy (built from the main branch of this repository, on our CI). Signing without enforced verification is decoration.

docs.title: The build system is the trust root
docs.text: Everything above assumes the thing that signs is honest. If the build environment is compromised, it signs malware. Defences from Level 2 matter here: ephemeral isolated runners, no shared persistent state between untrusted and trusted builds, no cache poisoning from pull requests, minimal credentials, and hermetic builds that do not fetch arbitrary network resources at build time. A reproducible build (Level 1 · 06: identical output for identical inputs; I measured the gzip filename quirk in that lesson) lets a second independent builder verify the first, turning "trust the builder" into "check the builder".

docs.title: A practical order of work
docs.text:
1. Lockfiles and pinned base images and actions (cheap, high value).
  2. Secret scanning and least-privilege tokens (Level 1 · 08).
  3. Dependency update bot with required tests.
  4. SBOM generation and vulnerability scanning with an agreed response time.
  5. Signing and enforced verification at deploy time.
  6. Provenance and a hardened builder, for software with high stakes.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text: • Lockfiles are committed and, where supported, include hashes.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 maps any input to a fixed 256-bit digest such that finding two inputs with the same digest, or an input for a given digest, is computationally infeasible. That makes the digest a content-addressed name: pinning to it means "exactly these bytes." Signatures add authenticity: the signer uses a private key to sign the digest, and anyone with the public key (or a certificate chain to a trusted root) verifies it. A signature over a digest therefore authenticates the whole artifact transitively. Provenance is a signed document whose subject is the artifact digest and whose predicate lists the build inputs; verification checks the signature and then that the predicate satisfies policy. Every mechanism rests on a root of trust you must decide on: the registry, the CI identity provider, or the keys.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Checksum next to the download, which proves nothing about tampering.
  • Pinning by mutable tag (@v4, :latest) and calling it pinned.
  • Pinning and never updating, accumulating known vulnerabilities.
  • Generating SBOMs nobody queries.
  • Signing without verifying at deploy time.
  • curl | sh in build scripts.
  • Trusting any CI-signed artifact, including those built from pull-request branches.
  • Ignoring the build system's own security while hardening everything else.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the checksum demo. Then place the checksum file in a separate location with restricted write access and describe what that changes in the threat model.
  2. List every external input to one of your builds (packages, images, actions, scripts fetched) and mark which are pinned by immutable identifier.
  3. Write the deploy-time policy for signature verification: what identity must have signed, from which repository and branch.
  4. Decide your response-time target for a critical vulnerability in a transitive dependency, and the pipeline steps that make it achievable.

docs.title: 09 · Measuring Delivery: The DORA Metrics
docs.text:
How do you know whether your delivery pipeline is any good? Opinions are plentiful and unreliable. Research from the DORA programme identified four measures that correlate with software delivery performance and, in that research, with organisational outcomes. They are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Throughput and stability together: shipping fast and shipping safely turned out not to be a trade-off for the teams studied.

What was run

src/dora.py and its 6 pytest tests were written and run, using a four-deployment hand-made fixture; no real team's data was used and the results below describe the fixture only. The definitions follow common usage as I understand it; DORA's published definitions have been revised over time (the current set and exact wording should be checked at the source), and teams define "deployment", "failure" and "restore" differently. Claims about the research are summarised from memory of the published work, not re-read for this lesson.

docs.title: The four measures
docs.text:
Measure Question Pipeline-level data you need Deployment frequency How often do we ship to production? Timestamps of production deploys Lead time for changes How long from commit to running in production? Commit time and deploy time per change Change failure rate What share of deploys cause a failure needing remediation? A record of which deploys led to incidents, rollbacks or hotfixes Time to restore How long to recover when a deploy goes wrong? Failure start and recovery time

The first two measure speed; the last two measure stability. A team that deploys ten times a day with a 40% failure rate is not elite, and neither is one that deploys monthly with a 0% failure rate (because it ships so rarely that every release is a large, risky batch).

docs.title: Computing them
docs.text:
On the fixture of four deployments (times in hours since an arbitrary origin): lead times 2, 4, 6 and 1 hours; deployments 2 and 4 failed, restored after 1 hour and 2 hours; window of 2 days.

deploys_per_day     2.0     4 deployments / 2 days
median_lead_time_h  3.0     sorted leads 1, 2, 4, 6 -> median (2 + 4) / 2
change_failure_rate 0.5     2 failed of 4
median_restore_h    1.5     median of 1 h and 2 h

Details that matter and that the tests pin down:

  • Median, not mean. Lead time and restore time are skewed: one three-week outlier ruins a mean. Medians (and percentiles such as p90) describe typical and bad cases separately.
  • A failed deploy with no recorded restore time counts in the failure rate but not in the restore median (a test checks this). Otherwise an unresolved incident would silently improve the numbers.
  • An empty window returns None, not zero: "no data" and "perfect" must look different.
  • The fixture is tiny, so the numbers are arithmetic, not evidence. Real metrics need enough deployments for the median and rate to be stable; with 4 deploys a single extra failure changes the rate by 25 points.

docs.title: Where the data comes from
docs.text:
• Deploys: the pipeline's deploy job emits an event (to a log, a metrics system or a table) with service, version, commit and time. This is better than inferring deploys from Git tags.
  • Commit time: the first commit of the change (or the PR open time, or the merge time, which gives a shorter "lead time" that omits waiting in review). Pick one definition and state it. Note that the shorter definition hides the very thing you may want to see: time spent waiting.
  • Failures: link incidents, rollbacks and hotfix deploys back to the deploy that caused them. This is the hardest data to collect honestly, because it requires humans to tag incidents with a cause. A proxy: a deploy followed within N hours by a rollback or an emergency fix.
  • Restore: incident start and resolution times from the incident tool, not from when someone "stopped looking".

docs.title: Using them without ruining them
docs.text:
Goodhart's law applies fully: a measure that becomes a target ceases to be a good measure.

  • Deployment frequency is gamed by splitting changes into trivial deploys or by counting no-op deploys. Count only deploys that change production behaviour.
  • Lead time is gamed by redefining the start (measure from merge, not first commit), or by merging half-finished work behind flags.
  • Change failure rate is gamed by not declaring failures. If people are punished for incidents, incidents stop being recorded. Blameless culture is a precondition for honest numbers.
  • Time to restore is gamed by declaring incidents "resolved" early or by never opening one.

Use the metrics to find constraints and watch trends for a team, never to rank people or compare teams with different contexts (a firmware team and a web team differ legitimately). Pair every metric with a question: lead time is long; where is the wait: review queue, tests, approvals, release trains?

docs.title: Diagnosing from the numbers
docs.text: Pattern Likely cause Where to look Low frequency, long lead time Big batches, slow gates, manual approvals Level 4 · 02 (speed and cost); trunk-based development High frequency, high failure rate Weak tests, no canary, no flags Lessons 01, 02 and the quality gates in Level 2 Low failure rate but slow restore No rollback path, poor observability Lesson 04; Level 4 · 07 Everything fine but unhappy engineers The metrics miss something Ask them: flaky tests? toil? on-call load?

docs.title: Beyond four
docs.text: The DORA research and other work (SPACE framework and others) also point to developer experience, reliability, and team wellbeing. Pipeline-adjacent measures worth tracking: CI duration (p50 and p90), flaky-test rate (Level 2 · 05), queue time for runners (Level 2 · 08), time to first feedback on a PR, and rework rate. Treat them as diagnostics.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Deploy events are emitted by the pipeline, not reconstructed from tags.
  • Definitions of deploy, failure and restore are written beside the dashboard.
  • Medians and percentiles are reported, not means alone.
  • Metrics are used for trends within a team, never for ranking people.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each metric is a statistic over events. Frequency is a count per window; lead time and restore time are durations computed per event and summarised with medians; failure rate is a proportion. The code is therefore a few lines, as metrics() shows. All the difficulty lives upstream, in event capture and definitions: deciding which timestamp is "commit", linking an incident to its cause, and handling multiple services deployed together. A change can touch several services; do you count one deploy or several? Whatever you choose, apply it consistently, publish the definitions next to the dashboard, and never compare numbers computed under different definitions.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using mean instead of median for skewed durations.
  • Treating the numbers as targets or comparing people and teams.
  • Counting no-op deploys to inflate frequency.
  • Not recording failures (or punishing the people who do).
  • Mixing definitions between teams or over time.
  • Too few data points to say anything.
  • Optimising a metric without asking what it is supposed to improve.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_dora.py -v. Add a fifth deployment with a very long lead time (500 hours) and compare the median to the mean.
  2. Define, for your own team, what counts as a deploy, a failure and a restore. Write them in three sentences each.
  3. Instrument a pipeline's deploy job to emit one JSON line per production deployment, and write the query that computes weekly frequency from the log.
  4. Pick the metric that looks worst for your team, list three possible causes, and design one cheap experiment to test the likeliest.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Canary Release Simulator
docs.text:
This project builds the decision engine of an automated canary release and then measures how it behaves: how quickly it catches a bad release, how often it wrongly rolls back a good one, and what the choices (traffic steps, sample sizes, threshold) cost. The traffic is synthetic. The point is to understand the trade-offs before you put such a rule in front of production.

What was run

src/canary.py (about 35 lines) and src/test_canary.py (11 tests) were written and run on macOS. Traffic is generated with Python's seeded random module: each request independently fails with the configured probability. Real traffic has bursts, correlated failures, varying request mixes and delayed metrics, none of which are modelled, so real detection performance will be worse than shown. The statistical test is a standard one-sided two-proportion z-test using the normal approximation. I did not use any canary tool (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker).

docs.title: The design
docs.text:
def run_canary(true_stable, true_canary, steps=(1, 5, 25, 50, 100), requests_per_step=20000,
               min_canary=400, z_limit=2.33, seed=0):

At each step the simulator splits requests_per_step between the canary (a pct share) and stable, draws errors, accumulates counts across steps, computes

z = (p_canary − p_stable) / sqrt( p_pool · (1 − p_pool) · (1/n_canary + 1/n_stable) )

and rolls back if n_canary >= min_canary and z > z_limit; otherwise it moves to the next step, and promotes after the last. Three design choices are worth defending:

  1. One-sided. We only care whether the canary is worse. A significantly better canary is good news, not a reason to stop (a test asserts z < 0 for a better canary).
  2. A minimum sample (min_canary). With 1% of 20,000 = 200 canary requests, a single burst of errors can look dramatic. The rule refuses to decide until it has 400. The test test_min_sample_prevents_decision_at_1_percent checks the first step has 200 requests and no rollback is declared from it alone.
  3. Pooled variance assumes the null hypothesis (rates are equal) to estimate the standard error, the usual form for this test.

Edge cases are tested because they are where production code breaks: no data (z = 0.0, never raise), zero errors on both sides (standard error is zero; return 0 instead of dividing by zero), and equal rates giving exactly 0.

docs.title: Running the scenarios
docs.text:
For each scenario, 300 runs with seeds 0–299, stable error rate 1.0%:

canary 1.0%  rollback 13/300 = 0.04   (false alarms)         median stop pct = 5
canary 1.2%  rollback 234/300 = 0.78                           median stop pct = 50
canary 1.5%  rollback 300/300 = 1.00                           median stop pct = 25
canary 2.0%  rollback 300/300 = 1.00                           median stop pct = 5
canary 5.0%  rollback 300/300 = 1.00                           median stop pct = 5

and a single traced run (canary 5%, seed 1):

pct  1: n_canary 200,  canary_err 0.090, stable_err 0.0112, z 10.18   (below min sample: no decision)
pct  5: n_canary 1200, canary_err 0.055, stable_err 0.0110, z 13.58   -> rollback

That trace makes the minimum-sample rule visible: the 1% step already had z of 10, but only 200 canary requests, so the decision waited one step.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
• False alarms are 4%, higher than a naive reading of 2.33 (about 1%) suggests. Five looks at the data, each with a 1% false-positive chance, accumulate: up to roughly 1 − 0.99⁵ ≈ 4.9% if the looks were independent (they are not, because counts accumulate, so the true rate is lower, and 4.3% observed is plausible but I did not derive it). Repeated testing inflates false positives; the fix is a stricter z_limit or a sequential-testing method designed for repeated looks.
  • Sensitivity depends on the effect size. A 5× worse canary is caught almost immediately; a 20% relative worsening (1.0 → 1.2%) is caught in 78% of runs and typically only at 50% of traffic, by which time many users have been exposed.
  • More traffic per step buys sensitivity. Because the z statistic grows with the square root of the sample size, quadrupling the requests roughly doubles z for the same effect. You can test that with requests_per_step.

I made one wrong prediction during development: I wrote a test expecting the 1.0 → 1.2% regression to be usually missed (more than 100 of 200 seeded runs), and it failed: only 47 of 200 were missed. The test now asserts the measured behaviour with a conservative floor (more than 55 of 100 seeds caught). The lesson for real canary design: don't guess detection power, measure it.

docs.title: Experiments to try
docs.text:
1. Threshold sweep. Run the equal-rates scenario for z_limit of 1.64, 2.33 and 3.09 and plot false-rollback rate against detection rate for 1.0 → 1.2%. You are drawing an ROC-like curve; choose your operating point deliberately.
  2. Fewer steps. Use steps=(5, 100). Detection is cheaper to compute but a bad release now hits 100% sooner. How many requests are exposed to the bad version before a rollback, per scenario? Add a counter for "failed requests served by the canary" and compare designs by cost of bad releases, not just by whether they were caught.
  3. Low traffic. Set requests_per_step=1000. How often is the 5% canary decided at all? This is the situation of a low-volume service, and the answer ("rarely") should push you to longer bake times or synthetic traffic.
  4. Correlated failures. Make errors arrive in bursts (a 30-second window of 50% failures) and see how the independent-requests test misjudges it.

docs.title: From simulator to production
docs.text: To turn this into a real component you need: metrics from the actual system, time-aligned comparison of canary and stable over the same window; delay handling (metrics lag); multiple signals (latency, saturation, business metrics) with a combination rule; a safe response to missing data (stop, don't promote); an audit record of every decision; and a human override. Mature tools implement these; evaluate them against this simulator's questions: what are your false-rollback and detection rates for the effect sizes you care about?

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Every threshold in the rule has a recorded false-alarm and detection rate.
  • The step schedule and sample sizes are chosen from the effect size you must detect.
  • Simulated results are never presented as production evidence.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The error counts per step are binomial draws; summed across steps they remain binomial in the total number of requests, so the estimated rates converge to the truth as n grows and their difference has a standard error shrinking like 1/√n. The z statistic scales the observed difference by that standard error, so a given true difference becomes statistically visible once the sample is large enough for the noise to fall below it. The step schedule controls exposure: small early steps limit the damage from a catastrophic release; later large steps supply the sample size needed to detect subtle regressions. The decision rule is therefore a joint design of schedule, sample size and threshold, which is why changing one number silently changes the false-alarm and miss rates.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deciding on tiny samples, rolling back on noise or promoting on luck.
  • Ignoring repeated-looks inflation of the false-alarm rate.
  • Testing only error rate, missing latency and saturation.
  • Comparing against historical data rather than the concurrent stable fleet.
  • Treating missing metrics as success.
  • Never measuring detection power for the regression size you care about.
  • Tuning on the simulator and trusting the numbers for a real system.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_canary.py -v, then reproduce the five-row scenario table with your own script and compare numbers (they are deterministic for the same seeds).
  2. Do experiment 1 and write a one-paragraph recommendation for the threshold, with the trade-off stated in numbers.
  3. Add a latency signal: draw latencies from two distributions and combine "error rate worse" OR "mean latency worse" into the decision; measure the resulting false-alarm rate.
  4. Write the canary policy for a payment service: steps, minimum samples, thresholds, who is paged on rollback, and what happens when metrics are missing.

docs.title: Level 4 · Pipelines at Scale
docs.text:
Level 4 is about running delivery for many teams: securing it, making it fast and affordable, governing it, testing it, recovering when it breaks, changing it, and making the right way the easy way.

What was run, and what wasn't

No Jenkins server, GitHub organisation, cloud account or real incident was involved. What was run, on macOS: a pipeline performance model with critical-path analysis (7 tests), an M/M/c queue simulation checked against the closed-form Erlang C result (6 tests), a hash-chained audit log with its limits tested (9 tests), a workflow converter that reports what it cannot translate (8 tests), a golden-path generator verified by the workflow linter (8 tests), contract tests that run a pipeline on good and broken inputs (4 tests), and a release-readiness check (6 tests). Platform controls, limits and organisational practices are from documentation or general experience and are labelled.

Prerequisites: Levels 1, 2 and 3.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Threat-Modelling the Pipeline: assets, boundaries, twelve attack paths and the controls that address them.
  2. Speed & Cost: the critical path, billed minutes, and queue time as a nonlinear effect.
  3. Jenkins at Scale: controller limits, configuration as code, agents, and a measured pool-fragmentation effect.
  4. GitHub Actions at Scale: documented limits, organisation policy, runner groups, cost governance.
  5. Audit & Compliance: separation of duties, evidence, and a tamper-evident log with known gaps.
  6. Testing Pipelines: contract tests for gates, and the python3 that was not the one I expected.
  7. Pipeline Incidents: runbooks for broken main, leaked secrets, outages and compromise.
  8. Migrating CI Systems: inventory, parallel run, cutover, and a converter that refuses to lose steps silently.
  9. Golden Paths: a generator whose output must pass the linter.
  10. Capstone: A Release-Readiness Check: four independent checks, one explainable decision.

docs.title: After Level 4
docs.text: You have a mental model of how delivery systems work from commit to production, a set of tested tools that make the ideas concrete, and a clear sense of which claims in this course were measured and which are documented. The next step is to apply them to a real system you can run.

docs.title: 01 · Threat-Modelling the Pipeline
docs.text:
A CI/CD system holds the keys to production: deploy credentials, signing keys, access to source and the ability to run arbitrary code on powerful machines. That makes it one of the most valuable targets in an organisation, and its attack surface is unusual because it executes untrusted input by design: a pull request is a stranger's code that your system builds and tests. This lesson applies a simple threat-modelling method to a pipeline and connects each threat to a control you can check.

What was run, and what wasn't

This lesson is mostly analysis. The controls it points to were built and tested earlier in this course and re-used here: the workflow linter (17 tests, Level 2 · 10), the secret scanner (12 tests, Level 1 · 08), the Jenkinsfile linter (11 tests, Level 1), and the audit-log chain in Lesson 05. No attack was carried out against any real system, and no real vulnerability is demonstrated. Descriptions of attack classes come from public security guidance such as GitHub's security-hardening documentation as I know it (October 2026); verify against current documents. A threat model is a structured argument, not a measurement.

docs.title: Step 1: What are you protecting?
docs.text:
List assets and what compromising each would allow:

Asset If compromised, an attacker can... Deploy credentials / cloud roles Change production directly Source repository write access Insert code that every later build trusts Signing keys / signing identity Make malicious artifacts look genuine Secrets in the CI system Reach databases, registries, third-party APIs Build artifacts and caches Ship tampered binaries without touching source The runners themselves Pivot into internal networks; persist between jobs Pipeline definitions Change what is checked (turn off the gates) Logs and reports Leak secrets; hide evidence

docs.title: Step 2: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
Draw where data crosses from less to more trusted:

  1. Contributor → repository (a fork's pull request, an issue title, a comment).
  2. Repository → runner (the code and workflow files that execute).
  3. Runner → secret store / cloud (the credentials a job receives).
  4. Third-party code → your job (actions, plugins, base images, dependencies).
  5. Build → registry → production (the artifact's journey).
  6. People → approval (who may change what, and how that is recorded).

Every threat is a way to move something across a boundary the designers did not intend.

docs.title: Step 3: The common attack paths
docs.text: # Threat How it works Control (and where in this course) T1 Script injection ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} is pasted into a run: script; the title contains shell commands Pass via env:; linter rule W005 (Level 2 · 10) T2 "Pwn request" A pull_request_target workflow (privileged) checks out and runs the PR's code No head checkout in privileged triggers; linter rule W002 T3 Unpinned third-party action A tag is moved to a malicious commit; every pipeline using @v4 runs it Pin to full SHA; linter rule W003; update bot (Level 3 · 08) T4 Over-broad token The default token can write contents; a compromised step pushes code Least-privilege permissions:; linter rule W001 T5 Secret exposure Secret echoed to logs, written into an artifact, or committed Masking, scanner (Level 1 · 08), short-lived OIDC credentials T6 Cache poisoning An untrusted run writes a cache that a privileged run restores Separate scopes; no cache restore in release builds (Level 2 · 02) T7 Persistent runner compromise Malware left on a reused self-hosted runner reads the next job's secrets Ephemeral runners, isolation (Level 2 · 08) T8 Dependency compromise A malicious package version is pulled in Lockfiles with hashes, review, scanning (Level 3 · 08) T9 Pipeline tampering An attacker with write access edits the workflow to skip tests or exfiltrate Protected branches, CODEOWNERS on pipeline files, required reviews T10 Artifact tampering The package in the registry is replaced after the build Signing and verification at deploy; digests T11 Approval abuse Self-approval, or a reviewer who rubber-stamps Prevent self-review; audit trail (Lesson 05) T12 Insider with legitimate access A trusted engineer misuses access Separation of duties, logging, anomaly review

docs.title: Reading T1 and T2 closely
docs.text: T1 is a code-injection bug of the classic kind: untrusted data becomes part of a program. The workflow engine substitutes the expression into the script text before the shell parses it, so quoting inside the script cannot help. T2 combines two properties that should never meet: privilege (secrets and a write token, which pull_request_target provides) and untrusted code (the PR head). Each property is fine alone: unprivileged PR builds run fork code safely because they get no secrets (that is the point of the default pull_request trigger for forks), and privileged workflows are safe if they only run code already on the base branch. The linter encodes exactly those two rules, and I tested them in both directions.

docs.title: Step 4: Rank and decide
docs.text:
Not every threat deserves equal effort. Score each by likelihood (is the attacker's step cheap? is the target reachable?) and impact (what does it unlock?). A reasonable ordering for a typical public GitHub project: T1/T2 (cheap, high impact), T3 and T8 (supply chain, widely exploited), T4 and T5 (limit blast radius), T6/T7 (depends on runner choices), then the rest. For a private monorepo with no outside contributors the weights shift toward T9, T11 and T12: the likely adversary is a compromised account or an insider.

Write down accepted risks with an owner and review date. "We know the self-hosted runner is persistent; accepted until Q2; mitigated by network isolation" is a decision. A silent gap is not.

docs.title: Step 5: Turn controls into checks
docs.text:
A control that depends on people remembering will fail. Put it in the pipeline:

  • Lint workflow files on every change to .github/workflows/ (the Level 2 linter, with exit status 1 on findings).
  • Run the secret scanner on every push and on history periodically.
  • Require CODEOWNERS approval for pipeline files, and protect the branches those workflows run on.
  • Alert on changes to org-level settings: new secrets, new runners, new third-party app installations.
  • Run a periodic clean-room rebuild of a release and compare outputs (Level 1 · 06 showed why determinism makes that possible).

Then test the controls: deliberately introduce a bad workflow in a sandbox repository and confirm the lint fails, the review is required and the alert fires. An untested control is a hope.

docs.title: What the tools in this course do not cover
docs.text: The workflow linter reads YAML text; it cannot see that a script downloaded in a step is malicious, that a legitimate action has a vulnerability, or that a maintainer's account was taken over. The secret scanner uses patterns, so it misses secrets with unusual shapes. Neither addresses Jenkins plugin vulnerabilities, runner OS patching, network egress control, or what a legitimately privileged person might do. A threat model is the document that says which of those you have decided to handle, and how.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Threat modelling works by forcing you to enumerate flows and ask "what if the data on this flow is hostile?" at each trust boundary, rather than listing vulnerabilities you already know. In a pipeline, the flows are unusually rich because the build system is a general-purpose code executor wired to credentials. The structural defence is privilege separation by trigger and environment: untrusted events run in unprivileged contexts with no secrets; privileged contexts run only code that has passed review; the highest-privilege step (deploy, sign) runs in a protected environment that releases credentials only after policy checks. Almost every control in the table is an application of that single idea, enforced by the CI platform or by checks like the linters.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Listing tools instead of flows, and missing the boundary that matters.
  • Treating CI as "internal" and not as a high-value target.
  • Giving every job the same broad credentials.
  • Controls that need people to remember, not automated checks.
  • No test that the controls work.
  • Modelling once and never revisiting after adding a runner, an integration or a new trigger.
  • Accepting risks silently without an owner or date.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Draw the data-flow diagram for a pipeline you operate, marking the six trust boundaries. Which boundary has the fewest controls?
  2. Run python3 src/wflint.py on your real workflows. Map each finding to T1–T12 and decide fix, accept or suppress.
  3. For T6 (cache poisoning) write the precise conditions under which your own pipeline would be vulnerable, and one test that would show it.
  4. Pick two threats you would accept for an internal-only repository and write the acceptance statements with owner and review date.

docs.title: 02 · Speed & Cost
docs.text:
A slow pipeline is a tax on everyone: engineers context-switch while waiting, batches grow bigger because each run is expensive, and flaky failures become more costly to retry. A costly pipeline is a budget problem that tends to show up as a sudden constraint. Both are usually fixed by understanding where the time goes, which is rarely where intuition says.

What was run

src/pipeperf.py (7 tests) computes the critical path of a job graph and billed minutes; the example numbers below are the fixture in its tests, not measurements of any real pipeline. The cost function takes a rate you supply: I use an arbitrary illustrative number (0.5 per minute) and make no claim about any provider's prices. The queueing results are from a simulation (Lesson 03 and Level 2 · 08).

docs.title: Two different quantities
docs.text:
• Wall-clock time (latency): how long a developer waits. Determined by the critical path, the longest chain of dependent jobs.
  • Compute time (cost): total machine-minutes billed, the sum over all jobs, including every matrix cell.

Parallelism trades one for the other: splitting a 12-minute job across 3 runners cuts wall-clock time but not total compute (and adds startup overhead for each).

docs.title: The critical path
docs.text:
Consider a graph: lint (1 min), build (4), unit (6, a 3-cell matrix, needs build), e2e (12, needs build), deploy (2, needs unit, e2e and lint).

critical path: 18.0 minutes   build (4) -> e2e (12) -> deploy (2)
billed minutes: 37            lint 1 + build 4 + unit 6x3 = 18 + e2e 12 + deploy 2

Two experiments from the tests:

  1. Make a non-critical job faster. Cutting unit from 6 minutes to 1 changes the path to ... nothing: still 18.0. The 3-cell unit job was never on the critical path (it finishes at minute 10; e2e finishes at 16). All that effort saves cost and no waiting.
  2. Make the critical job faster. Cutting e2e from 12 to 3 minutes drops the total only to 12.0, and the critical path moves: build -> unit -> deploy (4 + 6 + 2). A 9-minute saving in one job gave a 6-minute saving overall because another path took over. After you shorten the longest path, the second longest becomes the target.

Practical consequence: measure before optimising. Take the actual job durations from a dozen recent runs (median and p90), compute the critical path, and only work on jobs on it. Optimising a job off the path is a cost project, not a speed project, and should be justified as one.

docs.title: Where time actually goes
docs.text:
Typical breakdown of a job, and the lever for each:

Phase Lever Waiting for a runner Pool size, autoscaling (see below) Checkout Shallow clone (but see Level 2 · 09), sparse checkout for monorepos Setup and dependency install Caching with a good key (Level 2 · 02), prebuilt images Build Incremental or remote-cached builds, parallel compilation Tests Sharding (Level 2 · 01), run only affected tests (Level 2 · 09), fix slow tests Packaging, upload, publish Skip on PRs; compress less; upload once Fixed overhead per job Fewer, larger jobs vs more parallelism

Test the overhead assumption: a job that does 10 seconds of work after 90 seconds of setup should probably be merged into its neighbour, because each job pays setup again.

docs.title: Cost: the matrix multiplies
docs.text:
billed_minutes sums per-cell minutes, rounding each job up to whole minutes in the default model (many providers bill per started minute; check yours). A job of 0.2 minutes in a 10-cell matrix is billed as 10 minutes, not 2. In the tests: 10 cells of 0.2 min → 10 billed minutes versus 2.0 without rounding. Fixture total: 37 billed minutes, at the arbitrary 0.5 rate = 18.5 units per run. Multiply by runs per day to see the monthly effect; a team pushing 200 PR updates a day at that fixture's 37 minutes spends 7,400 billed minutes per day, which is the sort of figure that gets noticed.

Cost levers: reduce wasted runs, shrink matrices on PRs and run the full matrix on main, cancel superseded runs (concurrency with cancel-in-progress: true for CI, never for deploys; Level 2 · 07), skip jobs when only docs changed, avoid retrying whole pipelines for single flakes, and clean up old artifacts and caches that count toward storage limits. Self-hosted runners change the accounting from per-minute to fixed capacity.

docs.title: Queue time: the hidden component
docs.text:
Developers experience wait time as time-to-result, and part of it is waiting for a free runner. I simulated a pool of 8 runners, jobs averaging 5 minutes, arriving randomly (Poisson), first-come-first-served (an M/M/c queue):

Utilisation Mean wait (simulated) 90th percentile wait Closed-form (Erlang C) mean 50% 0.08 min 0.00 0.07 70% 0.56 2.06 0.56 80% 1.41 4.65 1.43 90% 4.43 12.25 4.38 95% 11.67 29.64 10.55 98% 32.88 80.65 29.25

The simulation and formula agree closely up to 90% (within about 2%); at 95% and 98% the simulated mean deviates by about 10–12% from the formula, which I attribute to slow convergence of a nearly saturated queue in a finite run, not a different model (I did not verify that by longer runs). The shape is the message: wait time is nonlinear in utilisation. Going from 80% to 90% busy triples the mean wait; at 98% a job waits half an hour on average. A pool that looks "efficient" at 90% average load delivers terrible latency, and real load is burstier than Poisson (everyone pushes at 9:30), so the real numbers are worse.

Pool size matters too, at the same utilisation: at 90% busy, mean wait is 21.5 min with 2 runners, 4.4 min with 8, 0.74 min with 32 (simulated; Erlang C gives 21.3, 4.4, 0.72). Larger pools absorb variation better, which is the statistical argument for shared pools over per-team pools.

Plan capacity for a target such as "90th percentile wait under 2 minutes at peak", not for average utilisation.

docs.title: A sensible order of work
docs.text:
1. Measure: collect per-job durations, queue times and costs. Without data you will optimise the wrong thing.
  2. Fix the critical path; re-measure; repeat.
  3. Cut waste: duplicate runs, unneeded matrix cells, jobs triggered by irrelevant changes.
  4. Cache and shard.
  5. Revisit pool sizing and autoscaling.
  6. Only then consider heavier changes (a build system with remote caching, bigger machines).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The pipeline is a directed acyclic graph with a duration on each node. The earliest finish time of a node is its own duration plus the latest finish among its dependencies, computed by a memoised recursive walk (finish[n] = max(finish[deps]) + minutes[n]). The graph's total time is the maximum finish over all nodes, and following the via pointers back from that node recovers the critical path. This is the same algorithm project managers use for critical-path analysis. A queue changes the picture because a job's ready time is no longer its start time: start = ready time + wait, and the wait depends on the pool's state, which depends on every other pipeline running at the same time. Hence local optimisations (making one pipeline faster) can be swamped by a global effect (the pool saturating).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Optimising a job that is not on the critical path.
  • Parallelising without counting per-job overhead.
  • Averages instead of percentiles for runtime and queue time.
  • Ignoring the matrix multiplier in cost.
  • Running the full matrix on every PR update.
  • Sizing the runner pool for average utilisation.
  • Measuring once, not after changes; the critical path moves.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_pipeperf.py -v, then model your own pipeline in the same dict format and compute its critical path. Which job would you speed up first?
  2. Pick a job off the critical path and argue for or against optimising it.
  3. Using the queue table, a pool of 8 runners reaches 90% utilisation at peak. Propose a change and use src/queuesim.py to predict the new mean and 90th percentile waits.
  4. Estimate monthly billed minutes for your pipeline from run counts and per-job durations, then find the three largest contributors.

docs.title: 03 · Jenkins at Scale
docs.text:
A single Jenkins server for a few jobs is easy. Jenkins as a shared platform for dozens of teams and thousands of jobs is a different system: configuration drift, plugin upgrades that break pipelines, a controller that becomes a bottleneck, and security assumptions that no longer hold. This lesson describes the common failure points and the practices that address them.

What was run, and what wasn't

No Jenkins server was run for this course. Everything about Jenkins here is from the Jenkins documentation (jenkins.io, as read in October 2026) and general practice; I did not test configuration snippets. What I did run is the course's Jenkinsfile linter (src/jenkinslint.py, 11 tests; Level 1 · 04) and the runner-pool queue simulation from Lesson 02, which applies to Jenkins agents as much as to any runner pool.

docs.title: Architecture in one paragraph
docs.text: A Jenkins controller holds configuration, job definitions, credentials and build history, schedules builds and serves the UI. Agents (nodes) run the work. The classic mistake is running builds on the controller itself ("built-in node"): the code under test then runs next to the credentials and configuration of every team. The documentation recommends not running builds on the controller; set its executors to zero and do everything on agents.

docs.title: What breaks as it grows
docs.text:
1. Controller load. Pipeline scripts run in the controller's JVM (the Groovy CPS interpreter), and heavy logic in a Jenkinsfile (large loops, JSON parsing of big payloads) burns controller CPU and memory while agents sit idle. Rule: pipelines orchestrate, shell steps on agents compute.
  2. Build history and disk. Unbounded logs and artifacts fill the controller's disk. Set build discarders (keep N builds or N days) by default, and ship logs and artifacts to external storage.
  3. Plugin sprawl. Hundreds of plugins from many maintainers: each is code running with controller privileges, with its own update cadence and vulnerabilities. Upgrading one can break another; some are abandoned. Keep the set small, track the security advisories Jenkins publishes, and test upgrades in a staging controller with copies of representative jobs first.
  4. Configuration drift. Settings changed by clicking in the UI are not versioned, not reviewable and not reproducible. A rebuilt controller loses them.
  5. Credentials sprawl. Credentials in the global scope are visible to every job; teams copy secrets into job configs.
  6. Groovy sandbox escapes and trusted libraries. Pipelines run in a sandbox that restricts calls; administrators approve exceptions ("script approval"). Approving a dangerous method for convenience weakens isolation for everyone.
  7. One shared queue. A single team's burst of 500 jobs delays everyone else's (see below).

docs.title: Practices that scale
docs.text:
Configuration as Code (JCasC). The Configuration as Code plugin describes the controller (security realm, credentials references, nodes, global settings) in YAML checked into Git and applied on start-up. Combined with a container image whose plugin list is pinned, the controller becomes disposable and reproducible: you can build a staging copy, test an upgrade, and roll back by redeploying the previous image. I did not run it; check the plugin's documentation for the schema of your version.

Job definitions in the repository. Use Jenkinsfile in each repository (and multibranch or organisation-folder jobs to discover repositories) so that pipeline changes go through code review with the code they build. Avoid hand-created freestyle jobs.

Shared libraries (Level 2 · 03) for the common parts, versioned and tested. A library is code that every team's pipeline trusts; treat changes with the discipline of a platform release.

Ephemeral agents. Create agents on demand (containers or cloud VMs), run one build, and destroy them (Level 2 · 08). Persistent agents drift, accumulate state and hold the stale-workspace problem I demonstrated with minici.

Credentials scoping. Use folder-level credential stores so a team's secrets are visible only to that team's jobs, and prefer short-lived credentials (cloud OIDC, tokens fetched at job time) to long-lived ones stored in Jenkins.

Controller sizing and isolation. Many organisations run several controllers, one per business unit or trust level, instead of one giant one, trading central management for blast-radius containment. Whichever model: back up the controller's home directory (with credentials encrypted) and test the restore.

docs.title: Queue behaviour
docs.text:
With a fixed set of agents, Jenkins queues builds when no executor with a matching label is free. Lesson 02's simulation (8 runners, 5-minute jobs, Poisson arrivals) applies directly:

  • at 70% utilisation the mean wait was 0.56 min, at 90% it was 4.4 min, at 98% 33 min;
  • at 90% utilisation, 2 executors gave a 21.5-minute mean wait, 8 gave 4.4 and 32 gave 0.74.

Real Jenkins queues add complications the model lacks: labels fragment the pool (a job waiting for a gpu label cannot use idle linux agents), job priorities, and "throttle concurrent builds" settings. Fragmentation hurts, and I measured it: at 90% utilisation one pool of 8 gave a mean wait of 4.43 min (90th percentile 12.25), while each of two separate pools of 4 at the same utilisation gave 9.96 min (90th percentile 26.03), more than double. Keep the label vocabulary small.

docs.title: Linting Jenkinsfiles
docs.text: Level 1's jenkinslint.py catches mistakes before they run: unbalanced braces, missing agent, a deploy stage without an input or approval, steps with no timeout. On a deliberately bad copy of the sample Jenkinsfile it reported 4 findings; on the clean sample, none (both were recorded in Level 1 · 04). It is a text-pattern linter, not a Groovy parser, so it can be fooled. Jenkins offers a built-in validation endpoint for declarative pipelines (documented; I did not use it), which parses with the real grammar and is the better check where available.

docs.title: Upgrades and security hygiene
docs.text:
• Track the Jenkins security advisories; critical controller or plugin vulnerabilities are patched in coordinated releases, and unpatched public-facing controllers have been a frequent target.
  • Use the long-term support (LTS) release line for controllers, upgrade on a schedule, and keep a staging controller.
  • Disable anonymous access, use SSO/LDAP, apply role-based access (matrix or folder-based) with least privilege, and enable CSRF protection (default in recent versions).
  • Do not expose the controller to the internet if you can avoid it; put it behind a VPN or an authenticating proxy.
  • Restrict who can edit Jenkinsfiles that run in trusted contexts; pull-request builds from forks should not get credentials.

docs.title: When to move on
docs.text: Jenkins is flexible and mature, and its flexibility is exactly the cost: the platform team maintains a lot. Reasons teams migrate (Lesson 08) include the maintenance burden, plugin risk, and wanting CI close to source hosting. Reasons to stay: heavy investment in pipelines and plugins, special integrations, on-premises requirements. Migrate for a measured reason, not fashion.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Controller executors are set to zero; builds run on agents.
  • The plugin list is pinned, minimal and tracked against security advisories.
  • Controller configuration is code and rebuilds reproducibly.
  • Build discarders are set globally.
  • Credentials are scoped to folders, not global.
  • Agents are ephemeral and created on demand.
  • Upgrades are tested on a staging controller first.
  • Backups are restored in a drill at least once a year.
  • Heavy computation runs in shell steps on agents, not in Groovy.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The controller keeps the build state in files under JENKINS_HOME (job configs, build records, credentials encrypted with keys stored alongside). A pipeline build is a durable state machine: the Groovy script is executed by the CPS interpreter, which serialises its program state to disk so a build survives a controller restart; steps that take time run on agents and report back. This is why a Jenkinsfile's Groovy has restrictions (not all Java constructs are serialisable) and why heavy computation in it is painful: it is interpreted, checkpointed and single-threaded per build on the controller. Agents connect to the controller over an agent protocol (inbound or outbound) and execute the shell commands and file operations the steps request; they need only enough credentials for the job at hand.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running builds on the controller.
  • Heavy Groovy logic in the Jenkinsfile.
  • UI-only configuration that cannot be rebuilt.
  • Unbounded build history.
  • Approving script exceptions casually.
  • Global credentials visible to all jobs.
  • Skipping upgrades, then facing a large, risky jump.
  • No tested restore of the controller backup.
  • Label sprawl that fragments the agent pool.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a checklist to audit an existing Jenkins controller against the points above and rate each answer red, amber or green.
  2. Run python3 src/jenkinslint.py on your own Jenkinsfile and list what it cannot detect.
  3. Using src/queuesim.py, reproduce the pool-of-8 versus pool-of-4 comparison, then try three pools of 3 and one pool of 9 and explain the trend.
  4. Draft the plan for a controller upgrade: staging, which jobs you test, how you roll back, and who signs off.

docs.title: 04 · GitHub Actions at Scale
docs.text:
Actions is easy to start and easy to leave ungoverned. Across hundreds of repositories you need to answer: which actions may be used, who may use which runners, how secrets are scoped, how workflows are kept consistent and what it costs. This lesson collects the platform-level controls and the documented limits that shape designs.

What was run, and what wasn't

Nothing in this lesson was run on GitHub. Limits and settings are from docs.github.com as read in October 2026 and change over time, and some depend on plan (Free, Pro, Team, Enterprise): verify against the current documentation for your account before relying on any number. The quoted limits are the ones I recorded for this course: job time 6 hours on hosted and 5 days on self-hosted runners, 256 jobs per matrix, 10 GB cache per repository, workflow runs deleted or limited after 35 days (as I recorded it), approval wait 30 days, 50 re-run attempts, and concurrent-job caps of 20 / 40 / 60 / 500 by plan. The queueing numbers come from the simulation in Lesson 02.

docs.title: Limits shape designs
docs.text:
Limit (documented) Design consequence Hosted job ≤ 6 h Long jobs (full-fleet integration, model training) need self-hosted runners or must be split Self-hosted job ≤ 5 days Still not a place for week-long batch work; use a scheduler built for it ≤ 256 jobs per matrix Large fan-out needs several workflows or dynamic matrices split in chunks (Level 2 · 01) Cache 10 GB per repository, LRU Many large caches evict each other; share keys, cache downloads (Level 2 · 02) Concurrent jobs by plan (20/40/60/500) A busy org queues; the cap, not your longest job, sets wall time (Lesson 02) Approval wait ≤ 30 days Long-pending production approvals silently expire Re-runs ≤ 50 attempts Don't build a "retry until green" habit; fix flakes (Level 2 · 05) Log and artifact retention Download evidence you need for audit before it expires, or export it (Lesson 05)

Use the platform's numbers as constraints in your platform design doc, with a date, so the next engineer knows they came from a specific reading.

docs.title: Who may run what: organisation policies
docs.text:
At organisation (or enterprise) level you can typically control, per the documentation:

  • Allowed actions: all actions, only those from your organisation, or an allowlist of specific actions (optionally requiring SHA pinning). For a regulated environment the allowlist plus SHA pinning policy is the strongest control against T3 (Lesson 01): the platform rejects a workflow that uses an unlisted or unpinned action, so the linter is no longer the only line of defence.
  • Default workflow token permissions: set the default to read-only so jobs must ask for write access explicitly. This turns the linter's W001 finding into a baseline.
  • Fork pull request handling: whether workflows from forks run automatically, need approval for first-time contributors, or never run; and whether they can access secrets (they should not).
  • Runner groups: sets of runners, with access limited to named repositories or organisations. Put sensitive deploy runners in a group that only the deploy repositories can target, and keep untrusted PR builds on ephemeral hosted runners.
  • Secrets and variables at org level, with a repository-selection list so a secret is available only to repositories that need it, and environment secrets for production (Level 2 · 07).
  • Required workflows / rulesets: organisation-level rules that require certain checks (a security scan, a lint) on all repositories matching a pattern. The product has changed its mechanism for this over time; check the current documentation for what your plan supports.

Apply policy to the platform with configuration as code (Terraform GitHub provider, a settings app, or scripts using the API) so that settings are reviewable and drift is detectable, as in Level 3 · 05.

docs.title: Workflows as a platform
docs.text:
The pattern from Level 2 · 03 becomes central at scale: a platform repository publishes reusable workflows and composite actions (build-python, deploy-service), versioned with tags and SHA pins, and the "golden path" (Lesson 09) generates caller workflows that use them. What to decide:

  • Where reusable workflows live (a dedicated repository with restricted write access) and who reviews changes to them.
  • Versioning and deprecation policy (Level 2 · 03): breaking changes need a new major tag and a migration window.
  • Observability of the platform: which repositories use which version of which workflow, so you know who to notify when v2 is retired. Query the workflow files across the org (code search or an inventory job) and store the result.
  • Ownership of failure. When a reusable workflow breaks, thirty teams are red. Give the platform team an on-call rotation and canary releases of the workflow itself (Level 3 · 01 applies to pipelines too).

docs.title: Runners at scale
docs.text: For self-hosted runners at scale, run them as ephemeral instances created on demand by an autoscaler (a controller that watches the job queue, a Kubernetes-based runner controller, or a cloud scale-set), one job per instance, destroyed afterward. Questions for the design: how long does a new runner take to become ready (affects queue time); what network access and credentials does it have; how do you patch the image (rebuild on a schedule); how do you isolate untrusted workloads; and how do you cap spend. The queue arithmetic from Lesson 02 applies: size for a target 90th-percentile wait at peak, and keep the label set small so the pool is not fragmented.

docs.title: Cost governance
docs.text:
• Visibility: the platform exposes usage per repository and workflow; export it regularly and attribute spend to teams.
  • Budgets and spending limits on the account, so a runaway matrix or a loop that triggers itself does not generate a surprise bill. A workflow that pushes a commit can trigger itself; the platform has loop protection for the default token, but a workflow using another token can still loop, which is a known pitfall.
  • Waste reduction: path filters (Level 2 · 09), concurrency cancellation for CI, skipping jobs on docs-only changes, scheduled workflows reviewed periodically (an unattended nightly job running for three years is classic waste), and artifact and cache retention set to what you need.
  • Right-size runners: larger machines cost more per minute but can finish faster; measure total cost, not minute price.

docs.title: Governance and observability
docs.text:
• Alert on new workflow files that use pull_request_target, self-hosted, or secrets: inherit, which the Level 2 linter can flag in a central scan.
  • Track workflow failure rates and durations per repository and surface the worst offenders to their owners.
  • Keep an inventory of third-party actions in use with their pinned SHAs, plus a process to review and bump them via a bot with changelog links.
  • Make audit logs available (who changed org settings, secrets, runner groups, approvals), exported to a log store you control (Lesson 05).

docs.title: Migrating between scales
docs.text: A repository starts with a hand-written workflow; ten later repositories copy it; a hundred repositories need a platform. Resist building the platform too early (Level 2 · 03's "share after the third copy"), and resist letting it stay ad hoc past the point where a vulnerability fix needs a hundred pull requests.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Allowed actions and SHA pinning are set by organisation policy.
  • The default token permission is read-only.
  • Fork pull request workflows need approval and never see secrets.
  • Reusable workflows are versioned, inventoried and canaried.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Organisation-level policy is evaluated by the control plane at several moments: when a workflow file is parsed (is every uses: allowed and pinned?), when a job is scheduled (does this repository have access to this runner group, environment or secret?), and when a token is issued (what permissions does this job's GITHUB_TOKEN get, given the defaults and the permissions: block?). Enforcing at those points, in the platform and not in the repository, is what makes the controls reliable: a repository's own workflow cannot opt out of an organisation allowlist. Reusable workflows are resolved the same way: a caller's allowed-actions policy applies to the actions inside the callee as well, which can surprise platform authors who forget to put their own actions on the allowlist.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Relying on documentation numbers from memory or from an old plan.
  • Write-by-default tokens across the organisation.
  • No action allowlist for sensitive repositories.
  • Self-hosted runners shared by trusted and untrusted work.
  • Platform workflows referenced by @main, so every change is a fleet-wide deploy.
  • No inventory of workflow versions in use.
  • No spend limit, and scheduled jobs nobody owns.
  • Settings changed in the UI only, never in code.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write the policy for your organisation: allowed actions, default token permissions, fork PR behaviour, runner groups. Justify each choice in one line, and say what a developer sees when a workflow breaks the policy.
  2. Draft the inventory query that lists, per repository, every uses: reference and flags any not pinned to a SHA (the course's linter already finds the pins; extend it to scan a directory tree).
  3. Propose the autoscaling target for a runner pool using the queue table, with the numbers that justify it.
  4. Plan the retirement of platform-workflows@v2: how you find users, notify them, track migration and finally turn it off.

docs.title: 05 · Audit & Compliance
docs.text:
Regulated environments, customer security reviews and ordinary incident investigations all ask the same questions about your delivery process: who changed what, who approved it, what was deployed, and can you prove it? Compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA and others) phrase this differently, but a pipeline that records the right facts, controls who can act and keeps evidence will answer most of the technical questions. This lesson is about building that pipeline; it is not legal or audit advice, and I did not consult any framework text for this lesson.

What was run

src/auditlog.py (a hash-chained audit log, 9 tests) was written and run. The log is a teaching model of tamper evidence; it is not a certified audit system and does not satisfy any specific regulation on its own. Statements about what auditors typically expect are general, from my background knowledge, and must be checked against the framework and auditor you actually face.

docs.title: What an auditor wants to see
docs.text:
Translate the typical control objectives into pipeline facts:

Question Evidence the pipeline should produce Was this change reviewed by someone other than its author? Pull-request approvals, with identities and timestamps, enforced by branch protection (not just policy) Was it tested and scanned? Required-check results tied to the exact commit Who approved the production deployment? Environment approval record (Level 2 · 07), with approver identity What exactly was deployed? Version, artifact digest, commit SHA, build ID (Level 3 · 07 traceability) Could the same person write, approve and deploy a risky change? Access reviews showing separation of duties Were emergency changes handled properly? Break-glass records with after-the-fact review Can anyone tamper with the history? Immutable or tamper-evident logs, restricted deletion rights Is access reviewed? Periodic access review output for repositories, runners, secrets

docs.title: Separation of duties
docs.text:
The principle: no single person should be able to push a change and approve it and deploy it and erase the record. In pipeline terms:

  • Branch protection requires at least one approval from someone who is not the last pusher, with dismissal of stale approvals on new commits. (Platform settings, not the course's code; check what your plan supports.)
  • CODEOWNERS for the pipeline files themselves, so changing the gates needs a review by the platform team.
  • Environment protection with reviewers other than the triggering user and "prevent self-review" on (Level 2 · 07).
  • Administrators can bypass protections on many platforms; either disable bypass for production repositories or log and alert whenever it is used.
  • For small teams where full separation is impractical, document compensating controls: post-hoc review of every production deploy, extra alerting.

docs.title: Evidence: make it automatic, not archaeological
docs.text:
Collecting screenshots before an audit is expensive and incomplete. Instead have the pipeline write an evidence record at deploy time: who triggered, commit, artifact digest, approvals (from the platform's API), test result IDs, scan results, timestamps. Store it outside the CI system (a write-once bucket or log store) because CI retention is limited (logs, artifacts and run records expire; Lesson 04) and CI administrators can alter things.

Keep the mapping from deploy to change request if your organisation uses tickets: a commit message or PR template field with the ticket ID, validated by a check, so the link is machine-readable.

docs.title: A tamper-evident log, built and tested
docs.text:
A log that can be quietly edited is weak evidence. A cheap strengthening is to chain the records: each stores the hash of the previous one plus its own content, so changing any earlier record invalidates every later hash.

def append(log, event):
    prev = log[-1]["hash"] if log else GENESIS
    log.append({"event": event, "prev": prev, "hash": sha256(prev + canonical_json(event))})

verify(log) recomputes the chain and returns the index of the first bad record. The nine tests establish what it does and what it does not:

Attack on a 3-record log Detected? Edit a field in record 1 (version changed to 9.9.9) Yes: reported at index 1 Delete record 1 Yes: index 1 (the next record's prev no longer matches) Swap records 1 and 2 Yes: index 1 Insert a forged record at position 1 Yes: index 1 Change the first record Yes: index 0 Truncate the tail (drop the last record) No: the remaining chain is internally consistent Rewrite the whole chain consistently No: a forger who can recompute hashes can make a valid chain

The last two rows are the honest limit, and the tests include them as tests of the known gaps so nobody mistakes the log for more than it is. The defence is to anchor the head hash outside the attacker's reach: publish it periodically to a different system (a separate account, an append-only store, a timestamping service, or even a signed commit), so a later rewrite cannot reproduce the published head. Digital signatures per record (Level 3 · 08) add authenticity for records written by the system. Using a managed immutable storage feature (object lock or write-once retention) offers a similar guarantee by a different mechanism; I did not run any.

Also decide what goes into the log. Record the minimum needed: identities, actions, object identifiers, timestamps, outcomes. Do not record secrets or personal data beyond what is necessary; an audit log is a long-lived data store with its own privacy obligations.

docs.title: Retention and time
docs.text: Compliance regimes often require retaining evidence for a fixed period (commonly measured in years; the number depends on the framework, jurisdiction and contract: check yours). Plan for it: export logs before platform retention expires, keep clocks synchronised (timestamps from different systems must be comparable: use UTC and NTP-synced hosts), and test that you can actually retrieve a record from three years ago in a readable format.

docs.title: Emergency changes
docs.text: Production incidents need fast changes. A break-glass procedure allows an authorised person to bypass the normal approval, with controls: it is rare, it raises an alert, the reason is recorded, and a review within a defined time confirms the change was legitimate and brings the code back through the normal process. Count break-glass uses; a high number means the normal path is too slow (see Lesson 02, and the delivery metrics of Level 3 · 09).

docs.title: Compliance as code
docs.text: Express controls as checks that run continuously, not as annual documents: a scheduled job that queries repository settings and fails if any production repository lacks branch protection; a policy check on infrastructure plans (Level 3 · 05); a report of secrets older than the rotation period; an alert when a workflow uses a disallowed trigger. The output of those checks is itself evidence. Beware of checkbox compliance: passing an audit and being secure are different things, and the threat model (Lesson 01) is what tells you which controls matter.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A cryptographic hash chain turns a sequence of records into a structure where each element commits to everything before it. Changing record k changes its hash, which is part of record k+1's input, so verify finds the first mismatch. This is the same construction as a Git history (each commit includes its parent's hash, which is why rewriting history changes every descendant's ID) and as the Merkle structures behind transparency logs. What it cannot provide is completeness (that no record was dropped from the end) or authorship (who wrote it), because both require a reference that lives outside the chain: an externally published head, or signatures. All audit-log designs reduce to "who holds the reference copy, and can the writer alter it?"

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Controls that exist only as policy, not enforced by the platform.
  • Evidence kept only in the CI system, subject to retention and admin edits.
  • Admins able to bypass protections silently.
  • Logs with no anchor, trusting chain integrity alone.
  • Secrets or personal data in audit logs.
  • Unsynchronised clocks across systems.
  • Break-glass used routinely.
  • Annual evidence scramble instead of continuous checks.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_auditlog.py -v. Modify verify to also accept an expected head hash, and add a test that truncation is now detected.
  2. List the evidence you would need to answer "who approved the production deployment of version X last March?" and where each piece lives today. Which would have expired?
  3. Design the break-glass procedure for your team: who may use it, what it alerts, and how the review works.
  4. Write three compliance-as-code checks for your GitHub or Jenkins setup, with the query each runs and the failure condition.

docs.title: 06 · Testing Pipelines
docs.text:
A pipeline is code that decides whether other code ships. If it is wrong, it can fail to catch a broken build (a false green) or block good ones (a false red) and either is expensive. Yet pipelines are often the least tested code in a repository, changed by editing YAML and pushing to see what happens. This lesson shows how to give a pipeline automated tests, using the course's minici runner as the system under test.

What was run

src/test_pipeline_contract.py (4 tests) runs the Level 1 demo pipeline through minici on copies of the demo project and asserts the behaviours it promises. These are tests of a local teaching runner; GitHub Actions and Jenkins can be tested with different tools (below, described and not run here), and their execution semantics differ from minici. The contract-test idea transfers; the harness does not.

docs.title: What there is to test
docs.text:
1. The pipeline's promises: if tests fail, nothing is deployed; if lint fails, tests do not run; every matrix cell runs; artifacts are produced only on success.
  2. The gates themselves: does the security scan actually fail on a known-bad input? A gate that never fails may not be running (a scan that quietly finds nothing because the path is wrong).
  3. Pipeline code: scripts, shared libraries, composite actions: ordinary unit tests apply (the course's tools each have their own).
  4. Configuration validity: YAML syntax, expression errors, references to jobs and secrets that don't exist: a linter's job (Level 2 · 10).

docs.title: Contract tests with a local runner
docs.text:
The four tests, each copying the demo project to a temporary directory, optionally breaking something, running the pipeline and checking per-job results:

  1. Green pipeline deploys: all jobs succeed, including package and deploy.
  2. A failing unit test blocks packaging and deployment: replace the test file with assert False; expect test = failure and package = skipped and deploy = skipped. This is the central promise of a CD pipeline, and it is a regression test for the needs wiring: if someone removes needs: [test] from package, this test fails.
  3. A syntax error fails lint and skips tests: the lint job fails and test is skipped, confirming the dependency order.
  4. Every matrix cell ran: three test cells, all successful (a test against silently shrinking matrices).

All four passed. They did not pass the first time. The first run had two failures: the green-pipeline test and the matrix test reported failure. The cause was environmental, not the pipeline logic: each pipeline step runs python3 -m pytest, and in the subprocess python3 resolved to the system Python, which has no pytest; the interpreter running my tests (a virtual environment) did. With the virtual environment's bin directory first on PATH, all four pass. I fixed the test harness by prepending the running interpreter's directory to PATH inside the test, with a comment explaining why.

That failure is a small, real instance of the problem this lesson is about: a pipeline's behaviour depends on its environment, and the environment is part of what you must pin and test. The identical YAML gave green or red depending on which python3 was found first. On CI the same issue appears as "works on my machine, fails on the runner" (Level 2 · 08), and the fix is the same: declare the interpreter explicitly (a setup-python step with a version, a container image with a pinned tag or digest) and verify with a step that prints the resolved path and version.

docs.title: Techniques for real platforms
docs.text:
These are described from public documentation and general practice, and I did not run them for this course.
