  • Run workflows locally with an emulator (tools such as act run GitHub Actions workflows in containers). Useful for fast iteration, but it is an emulation, not the platform: contexts, permissions, caches, secrets, OIDC and hosted-runner contents differ. Treat a local pass as "likely", and the platform run as truth.
  • A test repository. Keep a sandbox repository where pipeline changes are exercised on real runners with harmless payloads, including deliberately failing cases, before the change is released to the shared workflow tag (Level 2 · 03).
  • Canary the pipeline change: switch one low-risk repository to the new reusable-workflow version first.
  • Jenkins: a pipeline unit-testing library can run Jenkinsfiles with mocked steps in a JVM; the declarative linter validates syntax against the real grammar. For shared libraries, unit-test the Groovy classes.
  • Property: the pipeline must be able to fail. For every gate, keep (or generate) a deliberately failing input in a test fixture and assert the gate rejects it. In this course, the linters were all tested on both good and bad samples for exactly that reason.

docs.title: Mutation testing a pipeline
docs.text: The contract tests above can themselves be tested: mutate the pipeline (delete a needs: line, remove the if: on the deploy job, change a threshold) and check that some test fails. A mutant that no test catches reveals an untested promise. It is the same technique as mutation testing for code (Level 2 · 06) applied to configuration. Doing this by hand once for each critical promise ("deploy needs test", "tests need lint") is cheap and instructive; automating it is a small script that edits a copy of the YAML and runs the suite.

docs.title: Testing for the failure modes you fear
docs.text:
List the worst things a pipeline could do, then test each:

Fear Test Deploys when tests fail Break a test, assert no deploy (done above) Deploys from a pull request or a fork Run with a PR-like event context and assert the deploy job is skipped Leaks a secret to logs Run with a sentinel secret value and grep the logs for it (a masking test) Runs two deploys at once Trigger two runs and assert serialisation (needs the real platform) Passes with an empty test set Make pytest collect zero tests and assert the job fails (exit code 5 in pytest for "no tests collected") Succeeds when a step is skipped by mistake Count the steps that actually ran

The empty-test-set case is worth a special note: many runners treat "no tests found" as success, which turns a misconfigured path into a permanently green pipeline.

docs.title: Speed and flakiness of pipeline tests
docs.text: Pipeline tests are slow if they run real builds. Keep them small: a tiny sample project, stubbed installation (the contract test replaces the 2-second install with mkdir libs), parallel runs, and a split between fast contract tests on every change to pipeline files and slower end-to-end checks nightly. Pipeline tests flake like any other (shared ports, wall-clock dependencies) and the same discipline applies (Level 2 · 05).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Every critical promise has a contract test: no deploy on failure, no deploy from a fork, no deploy on zero tests.
  • Each gate has a deliberately failing fixture.
  • The interpreter and tool versions are pinned and printed by the pipeline.
  • Pipeline logic lives in testable scripts with unit tests.
  • Pipeline changes go through a sandbox repository first.
  • Reusable workflow changes are canaried on one low-risk repository.
  • Mutation of needs and if lines is checked at least once per critical promise.
  • Contract tests are fast and run on every change to pipeline files.
  • Slower end-to-end checks run nightly.
  • Emulator results are treated as likely, platform results as truth.
  • Test failures in the pipeline suite are triaged with the same flake discipline as product tests.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The contract tests work because minici's Runner is a library: it takes a parsed pipeline and a working directory and returns per-job results (success, failure, skipped) in a dictionary that the test can assert on. That separation, a runner you can call from code with an inspectable result, is the design property that makes a pipeline testable. Platform CI engines do not expose such an API for local use, which is why testing them needs either an emulator, a real sandbox run, or extracting the logic into scripts that are testable and keeping the YAML thin. The most effective strategy at scale is the last: put decisions in versioned scripts with unit tests (like this course's linters and guards), and let the pipeline file merely call them in order.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Never testing the pipeline, learning from production failures.
  • Gates that can never fail, with no failing fixture to prove they work.
  • Relying on a local emulator as proof.
  • Environment assumptions (which python3?) left implicit.
  • Treating "no tests collected" as success.
  • Big logic in YAML that cannot be unit tested.
  • No test of the deploy-skipping rules for PRs and forks.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_pipeline_contract.py -v. Remove needs: [test] from the package job in a copy of the demo pipeline and confirm which test fails. Restore it.
  2. Write a contract test that asserts deploy never runs when the event is a pull request (add an if to the pipeline and a way to pass the event).
  3. Write a test where the test suite collects zero tests, and make the pipeline fail on it.
  4. Build the mutation script: delete each needs entry in turn and report which mutants survive.

docs.title: 07 · Pipeline Incidents
docs.text:
The delivery system is production infrastructure for your engineers. When it fails, nothing ships, including the fix for whatever else is broken. And it can be the cause of incidents: a bad deploy, a leaked credential, a poisoned artifact. This lesson covers how to respond to each class, and how to learn from it.

What was run

This lesson is process and judgment; nothing was executed except small calculations with src/dora.py (Level 3 · 09) on a hand-made fixture. The runbooks are templates drawn from general incident-response practice, not from any particular organisation's procedure, and have not been exercised in a real incident. Adapt them, and rehearse them.

docs.title: Classes of pipeline incident
docs.text: Class Example First priority Broken main A merge turns the main branch red; nobody can merge Restore green quickly: revert or fix forward Pipeline outage The CI server, runner pool, registry or artifact store is down Restore the ability to ship; know the emergency deploy path Bad release shipped A deploy caused customer impact Stop the bleeding: rollback, flag off (Level 3 · 04) Secret leak A credential in a repository, a log or an artifact Revoke and rotate first, investigate second Compromised build A malicious dependency, action or runner Contain, preserve evidence, rebuild trust Cost spike A loop or matrix burns the budget Cancel the runs, cap spend, fix the trigger Data-affecting migration A migration locks or corrupts a table Halt, assess, restore (Level 3 · 03)

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Stabilise before diagnosing. Revert, roll back, turn the flag off, cancel the run. Understanding why can wait until the damage stops growing.
  2. One incident commander who coordinates; others investigate and act. Many people typing commands into production at once make things worse.
  3. A written timeline from the start (who did what, when). Memory is unreliable and the timeline is the core of the review.
  4. Communicate on a schedule, even when nothing has changed ("still investigating, next update in 30 minutes").
  5. Preserve evidence before cleaning up (logs, run records, the compromised runner's disk image), especially for security incidents; platform retention may delete it.
  6. Blameless reviews. Ask how the system allowed the mistake, not who made it. People who fear blame hide near misses, and then you learn nothing.

docs.title: Runbook: broken main
docs.text:
1. Announce in the team channel: "main is red, merges paused" and name an owner.
  2. Find the culprit commit: the first red run; use the CI history, git bisect if several commits landed together.
  3. Decide: revert or fix forward. Prefer revert when the cause is clear and the revert is clean, because it restores a known-good state in minutes. Fix forward only when the fix is trivial and certain.
  4. Verify: the revert's own pipeline must go green before announcing recovery.
  5. Follow up: why did this reach main? A missing required check, a semantic merge conflict (Level 1 · 09: green alone, red together), a flaky test that hid a real failure (Level 2 · 05), or a merge queue that wasn't used?

A merge queue (tests the combined result before merging) prevents most "green separately, red together" breakages and is the structural fix.

docs.title: Runbook: leaked secret
docs.text:
1. Revoke or rotate immediately. Assume the secret is already compromised: bots scan public repositories quickly. Deleting the commit or force-pushing does not un-leak a secret (clones, forks, caches, the platform's own records, and mirrors may keep it).
  2. Find the exposure window and use: when was it committed or logged, and what did the credential permit? Check the provider's audit logs for use of that key during the window.
  3. Clean up the repository history if policy requires it, and purge it from build logs and artifacts; this is hygiene, not remediation.
  4. Find the cause: a missing scanner (the Level 1 secret scanner finds patterns but not everything), a debug echo, a .env file committed. Add the control.
  5. Replace long-lived secrets with short-lived ones (OIDC federation) where you can, so the next leak has a short half-life.

docs.title: Runbook: pipeline outage
docs.text:
1. Declare an outage and tell engineers the state and the workaround.
  2. Know your emergency path before you need it: a documented, tested way to deploy a hotfix without the normal pipeline (a script run by a break-glass role, with logging and review afterward; Lesson 05). If the only way to ship the fix is the broken system, you have a circular dependency.
  3. Triage the dependency: the controller? the runner pool? a registry? a third-party service (a package index, a cloud region)? Check provider status pages, but also check your own quotas, expired tokens and certificates, which cause many "outages".
  4. Degrade deliberately: pause scheduled jobs to free capacity, restrict to the critical repositories, run a single priority queue.
  5. After recovery, check for lost or duplicated work: half-finished deploys, queued jobs that ran twice, caches written during the failure.

docs.title: Runbook: suspected compromised build input
docs.text:
1. Contain: disable the affected workflow, pause deployments, and revoke credentials those jobs could access.
  2. Scope: which builds used the bad input (an action version, a package version, a runner)? An SBOM and artifact metadata (Level 3 · 08) answer this in minutes; their absence makes it a days-long hunt.
  3. Assess artifacts: anything built in the window is suspect. Identify what was deployed where, and decide what to rebuild from a clean environment and redeploy.
  4. Preserve evidence from runners and logs, and rotate everything the build could read.
  5. Rebuild trust: pin to a verified version, rebuild on fresh ephemeral runners, compare outputs against the last known-good reproducible build where you have one (Level 1 · 06).

docs.title: Measuring and improving
docs.text: Track pipeline incidents like production ones. Using the DORA calculator on a fixture, one failed deploy that took 1 hour to restore and another that took 2 hours gave a median restore of 1.5 hours and a change failure rate of 0.5 (Level 3 · 09); the real numbers are yours to collect. Also track: time to detect (alert fired versus problem started), time to rollback specifically, number of incidents by class, and recurrence of the same cause. Use the review to produce concrete, owned, dated actions (a new test, a guard, a runbook step, a removed permission), and follow up on them. Reviews that end in "be more careful" change nothing.

docs.title: A review template
docs.text:
• Summary: what happened, impact, duration.
  • Timeline with timestamps (UTC).
  • Detection: how did we find out; could we have found out sooner?
  • Contributing factors: several, systemic (missing check, ambiguous docs, tool behaviour), not a single "root cause" person.
  • What went well: the things to keep doing.
  • Actions: each with an owner and due date, ranked by how much risk they remove.
  • Evidence appendix: logs, graphs, links.

docs.title: Rehearsal
docs.text: Run game days: simulate a leaked token, a broken main, a registry outage, in a safe environment. Time how long it takes to revoke a credential, to find which deployments used an artifact, to restore the pipeline from backup. The first time you do it, expect surprises: stale contact lists, missing access, a runbook referencing a decommissioned system. Finding those in a drill is the whole value.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Incident response is a feedback system with latency at each stage: detection (monitoring and alerts), decision (who decides, with what information), action (how fast the mechanism works: a flag flips in seconds, a rollback takes minutes, a rebuild takes hours), and verification (how you know it worked). The total damage is roughly impact rate × time to recovery, so improvements target the slowest stage. A team with good alerting but a rollback that takes an hour should invest in rollback; a team that can roll back in a minute but detects problems an hour late should invest in alerting and canary analysis. The runbooks above are mostly about shortening the decision stage by writing the decisions down beforehand.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Diagnosing before stabilising.
  • Deleting a leaked secret from Git without rotating it.
  • No emergency deploy path independent of the broken system.
  • Many people acting at once with no commander.
  • No timeline, so the review relies on memory.
  • Blameful reviews that suppress reporting.
  • Actions without owners or dates, never completed.
  • Never rehearsing, so the first run of the runbook is during an incident.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write the leaked-secret runbook for your organisation's most sensitive credential: exact commands or console steps to revoke it, who can do it at 3 a.m., and where the audit logs are.
  2. Test your emergency deployment path in a staging environment. Time it and record every manual step.
  3. Take a past incident and rewrite its review using the template. What action items have no owner?
  4. Design a game day: the scenario, injects, success criteria and how you would debrief.

docs.title: 08 · Migrating CI Systems
docs.text:
At some point most organisations change CI: Jenkins to GitHub Actions, a hosted service to self-managed, or a consolidation after an acquisition. Migrations fail in familiar ways: the inventory missed jobs, a "simple" translation lost behaviour silently, people were cut over before the new system proved equivalent, or the old system lingered for years. This lesson gives a method and shows the translation problem concretely.

What was run

src/wf2minici.py (8 tests) converts a simple GitHub Actions workflow into a minici pipeline and lists everything it cannot translate. It is a teaching converter between two simplified formats, not a Jenkins-to-Actions tool, and I did not use any real migration tool (Actions Importer or similar) or migrate a real system. The migration method is general practice, not measured here.

docs.title: Phase 0: Decide why
docs.text: Valid reasons: reduce platform maintenance (patching a controller, plugin risk; Lesson 03), consolidate on the system next to the source host, a feature you need, cost, or a policy requirement. Weak reasons: fashion. State the success criteria up front (time-to-green for a typical PR, cost per month, maintenance hours, security controls improved) so you can tell whether the migration worked. A migration with no measurable goal is a cost with no benefit.

docs.title: Phase 1: Inventory
docs.text:
You cannot migrate what you have not found. Collect, for every job or pipeline:

  • Triggers (push, PR, schedule, webhook from another system, manual).
  • Steps and the tools they use (compilers, scanners, deploy scripts, custom plugins).
  • Credentials and the systems they reach.
  • Agents/runners and special requirements (GPU, OS, network zone).
  • Downstream consumers: who relies on its artifacts, statuses, notifications, or on being a required check.
  • Usage: last run, run frequency, owner. Many jobs are dead. Delete them rather than migrate them; in a typical estate a large fraction of old jobs are unused, but measure yours instead of trusting that statement.
  • Hidden coupling: jobs that trigger other jobs, shared workspaces, shell scripts that live only on an agent.

Classify each pipeline: simple (build/test with standard tools), standard with extras, complex (custom plugins, fan-in/fan-out, manual gates, odd agents). Estimate the work by class, and migrate a few of each class first to calibrate.

docs.title: Phase 2: Translation and what gets lost
docs.text:
The converter takes a workflow, maps the constructs both formats share (jobs, needs, a matrix with fail-fast, global env, steps that are shell commands with name and env), and reports everything else instead of dropping it. On the course's sample workflow (src/ci.yml):

test.steps[0]: action `actions/checkout@v4` (must be replaced by shell commands)
test.steps[1]: action `actions/setup-python@v5` (must be replaced by shell commands)
package: `if` has no minici equivalent
package.steps[0]: action `actions/checkout@v4` (must be replaced by shell commands)
package.steps[2]: action `actions/upload-artifact@v4` (must be replaced by shell commands)

Five of the workflow's constructs could not be translated: four marketplace actions and one job-level if. The converted pipeline contains only the run: steps, so on its own it would run the tests without checking out code or installing Python. This is the central migration hazard: a translation that runs and goes green but does less than the original. The tests encode the design rule that prevents it:

  1. run steps convert; needs given as a string becomes a list; the matrix and fail-fast: false carry over; global env carries over.
  2. Anything unsupported is reported with its location: actions (uses:), environment, a step-level if, reusable-workflow calls.
  3. Nothing is silently dropped. A conversion with a non-empty "unsupported" list is not done.

Common translation gaps between real systems (general knowledge, not tested here): marketplace actions and Jenkins plugins have no direct counterparts, so each must be re-implemented or replaced; expression syntax and context objects differ; credentials models differ (Jenkins credentials vs repository/environment secrets, OIDC); caching and artifact semantics differ (keys, scopes, retention); concurrency and approval features differ; scheduled triggers use different time zones and semantics; matrix syntax has different rules (Level 2 · 01); agent labels map to runner labels and groups; and build numbers and URLs change, which breaks anything that links to them.

Prefer to move the logic into scripts in the repository (make test, ./ci/build.sh) that both systems call, so the CI definition is a thin wrapper and the next migration is cheap.

docs.title: Phase 3: Run in parallel, compare
docs.text:
Don't cut over on faith. For a period, run old and new CI on the same commits and compare:

  • Outcome: same pass/fail? Investigate every disagreement; both directions matter. A new system that is greener than the old may have lost a check.
  • Coverage of checks: the set of steps that ran (names and counts), not just the final colour. The contract-test idea from Lesson 06 applies: feed both systems a known-bad commit and confirm both fail.
  • Artifacts: same files, same digests where builds are reproducible (Level 1 · 06); if not byte-identical, understand the differences.
  • Time and cost: against the success criteria.
  • Notifications and statuses: that the right people get the right messages, and required checks have the right names for branch protection.

Mark the new status checks non-required during the trial, then swap which is required at cutover. The required-check names (Level 2 · 01) are a frequent cutover trap.

docs.title: Phase 4: Cutover
docs.text:
• Migrate in waves: low-risk repositories first, then standard, then complex and critical. Learn from each wave.
  • Have a rollback plan: the old system stays available and runnable until the new one has served a full release cycle; keep the old job definitions.
  • Freeze changes to the old pipelines during each repository's cutover so definitions don't diverge.
  • Move secrets deliberately: create new ones scoped to the new system, rotate rather than copy where possible, and revoke the old ones after cutover. Copying secrets from a system you are retiring is how stale credentials persist for years.
  • Update deployment targets that restrict access by CI IP or identity.
  • Communicate: dates, what changes for developers, where to get help, a migration guide with before/after examples.

docs.title: Phase 5: Decommission
docs.text: The step that gets skipped. Set a date to make the old system read-only, then to shut it down; archive build history and artifacts you must keep (compliance retention, Lesson 05); remove its credentials, DNS and firewall exceptions; update documentation and links. A zombie CI system with live credentials and no owner is a security liability.

docs.title: How to know it worked
docs.text: Compare against the success criteria from Phase 0: median time-to-green, cost, maintenance hours, incident count, developer satisfaction survey. Report the result honestly, including regressions. If the new system is slower for a class of jobs, say so and plan the fix.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Both CI systems implement a similar abstract model: a trigger creates a run; a run is a graph of jobs; each job executes ordered steps on an executor with an environment and credentials; results are statuses and artifacts. The converter works on the intersection of two concrete syntaxes for that model. Anything outside the intersection (marketplace actions, plugins, platform-specific contexts) is a place where behaviour lives in the platform, not in your file, which is why it cannot be translated mechanically. The way to reduce migration risk is to keep as much behaviour as possible on your side of that line: in scripts and containers you control, with the CI file only wiring them together.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Migrating without success criteria.
  • Incomplete inventory, including dead jobs.
  • Mechanical translation that silently drops steps.
  • No parallel run, so differences surface after cutover.
  • Comparing only the final colour, not what ran.
  • Required-check name mismatches at cutover.
  • Copying secrets to the new system.
  • Never decommissioning the old system.
  • Big-bang cutover across all repositories at once.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_wf2minici.py -v and then convert on one of your own workflows. How many unsupported items does it report, and what would you replace each with?
  2. Inventory ten pipelines you know. Classify them simple / standard / complex and estimate effort by class.
  3. Design the parallel-run comparison report: the columns, how disagreements are triaged, and the exit criteria for cutover.
  4. Write the decommission checklist for an old CI controller, including credentials, history and access.

docs.title: 09 · Golden Paths: Making the Right Way the Easy Way
docs.text:
If doing the secure, tested, observable thing takes a week of YAML archaeology, teams will skip parts of it. A golden path (or paved road) is a supported, opinionated, low-effort way to build and ship a typical service: a template repository or generator that gives you a working pipeline, tests, deploy configuration and monitoring on day one. Teams may leave the path, but the path is so convenient that most don't.

What was run

src/goldenpath.py (8 tests) generates a GitHub Actions workflow for a Python service from a few parameters, and the tests check that the output parses, passes this course's workflow linter with zero findings, and that the generator refuses unsafe input. It has not been used on a real platform, the generated workflow has not been run on GitHub, and it covers one language and one deployment style. The adoption and organisational points are general experience, not measurements.

docs.title: What belongs on the path
docs.text:
A useful golden path bundles the decisions that every team would otherwise remake (often poorly):

  • Repository layout and a README with how to run, test and release.
  • A CI workflow that lints, tests, scans and builds with caching and pinned tools.
  • Deployment pipeline with environments, approvals and concurrency (Level 2 · 07).
  • Security baseline: least-privilege token, pinned actions, secret scan, dependency updates.
  • Observability defaults: health endpoint, structured logs, standard metrics, dashboards, alerts.
  • Operational docs: a runbook skeleton, an on-call link, ownership metadata.
  • Versioning and release automation (Level 3 · 07).

The principle: encode requirements as defaults so compliance is automatic, and keep the surface for customisation small and explicit.

docs.title: A generator that refuses to guess
docs.text:
def generate(service, python="3.12", deploy_env=None, pins=None, timeout=15): ...

Design choices, each backed by tests:

  1. Pins are mandatory and must be full SHAs. The caller supplies {'actions/checkout': <40 hex>, 'actions/setup-python': <40 hex>}; a tag like v4 or a missing entry raises ValueError. The generator does not know the right SHAs and will not invent them; a platform team supplies the current approved pins from a central source and updates them with a bot. This keeps a hard-coded stale or wrong pin out of every generated repository.
  2. The generated workflow passes the linter with no findings, including permissions: set to read-only, a timeout on every job, and, when a deploy environment is given, a needs, a protected environment, and a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: false (so a running deploy is never aborted). That test is the contract: the template cannot drift from the policy without a test failing. The same linter runs on the generated code that runs on hand-written workflows.
  3. The service name is validated against ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,40}$. The name is interpolated into the YAML (workflow name, concurrency group), so a name like Orders; rm -rf / would otherwise inject text into a file that later executes. Input to a generator is untrusted input: a test confirms a hostile name is rejected.
  4. Version strings stay strings. python="3.10" is emitted quoted, and a test parses the result to confirm it is the string 3.10 rather than the float 3.1 (the YAML trap from Level 2 · 01).
  5. No deploy job unless asked. Without a deploy_env, only test exists.

Generated deploy job (excerpt), as printed by the generator for deploy_env="production":

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    environment: production
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-orders-production
      cancel-in-progress: false

The SHAs in the test fixtures (aaaa…, bbbb…) are dummy values and not real commits; a real run needs real pins.

docs.title: Templates vs enforcement
docs.text:
A template gives you a good start and then drifts: you copy it once, the platform improves it, and your copy stays old. Options:

Approach How updates reach teams Cost Copy-once template They don't, unless someone pushes a PR Cheap to build; drift over time Template + update bot A bot opens PRs when the template changes Moderate; needs tooling Thin caller + reusable workflows Teams reference a versioned workflow; updating the tag updates behaviour (Level 2 · 03) Moderate; coupling and version policy Central policy enforcement Org rules require checks regardless of the repo's own files (Lesson 04) Highest; strongest guarantee

Typically you combine them: generated callers of reusable workflows (so improvements flow by version bump), plus org-level required checks for the non-negotiable controls.

docs.title: Adoption is the hard part
docs.text:
A golden path nobody uses is a documentation project. What makes teams adopt it:

  • It is genuinely faster. A new service reaches "deployed to staging with CI" in an hour, not a week. Measure that time.
  • It is built with its users, not for them: pilot with two teams, take their pain seriously.
  • Escape hatches exist and are documented. Teams with unusual needs deviate; the path should make deviations visible (a tag in metadata) rather than forbidden, with the platform team learning from what they need. If too many teams need the same deviation, the path should grow.
  • Support is real: a channel, response times, office hours, a roadmap.
  • Value is visible: free dashboards, automatic dependency updates and security scanning that teams would otherwise maintain themselves.

Measure adoption (share of services on the path), the time to first deploy, lead time and change failure rate by path vs off-path (Level 3 · 09), and satisfaction. If services on the path do not deploy faster or fail less, the path is not working; you need that to be a finding, not an assumption.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Mandated, unusable paths that make teams hide their real workflow elsewhere.
  • Platform team as bottleneck: every change needs a ticket to them.
  • Too many options, which is just a framework with a new name.
  • A template with secrets or environment-specific values baked in.
  • No versioning or deprecation policy (Level 2 · 03).
  • Treating the path as finished. Languages, runners and threats move; the path needs a maintainer and a roadmap.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The generator is string construction guarded by validation, which sounds trivial and is the whole design: the tests are what make it a policy instrument. By running the generated YAML through the same linter that reviews hand-written workflows, any change to the template that violates a rule (removing the timeout, loosening permissions) fails in the platform team's CI before it reaches a single service. This turns an organisational standard from a document people may or may not read into an executable specification: the standard is what the tests accept. The same pattern scales beyond workflows: generated infrastructure modules verified by the plan guard (Level 3 · 05), service templates verified by a conformance suite, and so on.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Letting the generator guess unsafe values (default pins, default tags).
  • Unvalidated input interpolated into generated files.
  • No test tying the template to the policy.
  • Copy-once templates with no update path.
  • Forbidding escape hatches instead of making them visible.
  • Not measuring adoption or outcomes.
  • No owner or roadmap for the path.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/test_goldenpath.py -v. Add a node option producing a Node workflow, and make sure the linter still finds nothing. What tests do you add?
  2. Add a parameter matrix_python=["3.11","3.12"] and test that the output has the right job count and quoted versions.
  3. Design the update strategy: how does a security fix to the template reach 80 existing services?
  4. Define three metrics for the golden path's success and how you would collect them.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone — A Release-Readiness Check
docs.text:
The capstone joins the components built across the course into one decision: is this release ready to go out? It checks the pipeline definition (workflow linter), the infrastructure change (plan guard), the team's recent delivery health (DORA metrics) and the canary result (simulator), and it reports reasons when the answer is no. It never deploys anything. It is a small demonstration of the idea at the heart of a delivery platform: automated, explainable gates that combine several signals.

What was run, and what wasn't

src/capstone.py (about 20 lines) and src/test_capstone.py (6 tests) were written and run. Inputs are synthetic: a generated workflow, a hand-written plan fixture, a hand-made deployment history and a simulated canary. The decision thresholds (for example the 30% maximum change failure rate) are arbitrary defaults I chose for illustration and are not recommendations. All 173 tests in src/ pass on macOS (the whole-course total at the time of writing). Nothing was run on GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Terraform or a real deployment system.

docs.title: The design
docs.text:
def readiness(workflow_paths, plan, allow_destroy, deploys, window_days,
              stable_err, canary_err, seed=0, max_cfr=0.30): ...

It collects reasons from four independent checks:

  1. Workflows: run wflint.lint_file on each path (Level 2 · 10); each finding becomes a reason such as W003 test.steps[0].
  2. Infrastructure plan: run planguard.check (Level 3 · 05); destructive actions not on the allowlist become reasons.
  3. Delivery health: compute DORA metrics (Level 3 · 09); a change failure rate above the maximum is a reason.
  4. Canary: run the simulator (Level 3 · 10) and add a reason if it decides to roll back.

The result is {"ready": bool, "reasons": [...], "metrics": {...}, "canary": "promote"|"rollback"}. ready is true only when the list of reasons is empty. The most important property: every "no" comes with a reason a human can act on, and absence of reasons is the only way to be ready, so a new check that is added but broken in a way that finds nothing would make it easier to be ready; testing that each check can fail (Lesson 06) is what stops that.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The generated workflow for service orders with production deploy (from Lesson 09, with dummy pins), a plan with one in-place update and one replace of a database, and a six-deployment history in which one deploy failed and was restored after 1 hour (lead times 3 h each):

allow=[]                         canary 1.0% -> ready=False  reasons: ['plan: replace of aws_db_instance.main not allowed']
allow=['aws_db_instance.main']   canary 1.0% -> ready=True   reasons: []
allow=['aws_db_instance.main']   canary 5.0% -> ready=False  reasons: ['canary: rollback at 5% traffic (z=13.58)']
metrics: deploys_per_day 0.43, median_lead_time_h 3.0, change_failure_rate 0.167, median_restore_h 1.0

Walk through it:

  • Row 1: the workflow is clean (generated, so the linter finds nothing) and the metrics are healthy (CFR 0.167, under 0.30), but the plan would replace a database. Blocked, with the resource named.
  • Row 2: the replace is explicitly allowlisted (a reviewer made the call in the pull request, Level 3 · 05), so the answer is ready.
  • Row 3: the same allowlist, but the canary has a 5% error rate against stable 1%; the simulator rolls back at the 5% step with z of 13.58 (the same trace shown in Level 3 · 10). Blocked.

The six tests cover: all green; a destructive plan blocks; an allowlisted plan passes; a high failure rate blocks (3 of 5 deploys failing, CFR 0.6); a bad canary blocks (canary == "rollback"); and an unpinned workflow (@v4) blocks with a W003 reason.

docs.title: What this is, and isn't
docs.text:
It is a compact example of policy-as-code gating: independent checks, each tested, combined into one explainable decision.

It isn't a release system. A real platform would need: real data sources (the plan from the actual tool, deployments from an event store, canary metrics from monitoring); handling of missing or stale data (here a missing input would simply be an error, and a silently empty list would pass; the safe design treats absent evidence as a failure); persistent records of each decision (Lesson 05); an override process with approval and audit trail; and operational concerns such as timeouts and retries. Simulated canary traffic is also not evidence about your system: the readiness check should consume real analysis.

docs.title: Suggested extensions
docs.text:
1. Add supply-chain checks (Level 3 · 08): verify the artifact digest against a signed manifest and require an SBOM.
  2. Add a flag check: fail if a release flag older than N days is still present (Level 3 · 02).
  3. Add a migration check: fail if a destructive schema operation appears without a contract-phase approval (Level 3 · 03).
  4. Add evidence output: write the decision, inputs' hashes and reasons to the hash-chained audit log (Lesson 05).
  5. Replace the simulated canary with a function that fetches metrics for the canary and stable fleets over the same window and treats missing metrics as a failure.
  6. Wrap it in a pipeline job that runs before the deploy job and is a required gate (Level 2 · 06 and 07).

docs.title: What you have built across the course
docs.text:
All of these are in src/ and tested; run python3 -m pytest -q src (with the dependencies in the course README) to see the whole suite:

Level Components 1 minici runner (15 tests), Jenkinsfile linter (11), secret scanner (12), deterministic tarball helper, the demo project's own tests (3) 2 Path-filter mapper (9), wait-for-port helper (4), workflow linter (17) 3 Canary simulator (11), feature-flag evaluator (8), GitOps reconciler (8), plan guard (9), version-bump tool (12), DORA calculator (6) 4 Pipeline performance model (7), queue simulator (6), audit-log chain (9), workflow converter (8), golden-path generator (8), pipeline contract tests (4), readiness check (6)

Those counts sum to the 173 that pytest reports for src/ (I checked the per-file counts with pytest --collect-only).

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Run the same ideas on a real platform: set up a small repository with GitHub Actions or a local Jenkins, and port one component (the linter as a required check is a good first step).
  • Learn a build system with remote caching (Bazel, Gradle, Nx) to move from path filters to input hashing.
  • Study your platform's security documentation and the supply-chain frameworks in depth (SLSA, Sigstore).
  • Read incident reviews from public postmortems about CI/CD and supply-chain attacks, and apply the threat-model method (Lesson 01) to your own pipelines.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The check is a fold over independent evaluators: each produces zero or more reasons and the verdict is the conjunction of their silence. Independence matters: a failure in one evaluator does not hide another's findings, so the output lists everything wrong at once rather than the first thing wrong (a design choice that saves multiple fix-and-retry cycles). Determinism matters too: with a fixed seed the canary result is reproducible, so a failing decision can be replayed. The deeper pattern, which the whole course has been building toward, is that delivery safety comes from small, tested, explainable checks composed together, wired to the pipeline's control flow so that a "no" actually stops a deploy, and recorded so that you can later prove why.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Composing checks that can never fail, and calling the result a gate.
  • Treating missing evidence as success.
  • A single combined score that hides which check failed.
  • Thresholds with no owner and no review.
  • No override path, so people bypass the system.
  • No record of decisions.
  • Confusing a simulation with evidence.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run python3 -m pytest -q src and then add a fifth check of your own to readiness (for example the secret scanner on a directory). Write the tests first: one that makes it fail, one that makes it pass.
  2. Change readiness so that missing inputs (plan=None, an empty deploy list) produce a reason instead of passing silently. Which tests change?
  3. Write the policy statement for your organisation: which checks block a production deploy, which only warn, who may override, and where the decision is recorded.
  4. Draw the end-to-end flow from commit to production for a service of yours, marking where each course component would run and which control it provides.
